name: @wunderui/react
description: WunderUI — a design system and component library for React.

install.available: Core and Pro licence holders: the full library from the private GitHub repository wunder-ui/wunderui-core (Polar invites your GitHub account after the purchase). The npm package of the same name is WunderUI Free (free components only).
install.package: Accept the GitHub invitation, `git clone https://github.com/wunder-ui/wunderui-core`, run `npm install && npm run build` in it once, then in your project: `mkdir .wunderui`, `npm pack <wunderui-core>/packages/react --pack-destination .wunderui` and `npm install ./.wunderui/<the .tgz>`. The wunderui-setup agent skill does all of it.
install.doNot: `npm install @wunderui/react` installs WunderUI Free from npm: the free components only (no charts, data tables, AI or agent components). Core and Pro need the full library from the private wunderui-core repository — never install the npm package for them.
install.free: Free plan: the 83 free components are MIT source at https://github.com/wunder-ui/wunderui — add them with `npx wunderui-cli add <name>` (files, dependencies and styles), install the Free package with `npm install @wunderui/react`, or copy components/, lib/ and styles/wunderui.css (each free component in design.json has a sourceRaw URL). Core and Pro components come with a plan (https://wunderui.com/#pricing).

counts.exportsMethod: TypeScript compiler API: checker.getExportsOfModule(packages/react/src/index.ts). valueExports = exported values (components, hooks, functions, constants); typeExports = type-only exports; allExportNames = both, unique. catalogExports = names listed in components[].exports (values and types); otherExports = value exports outside the catalogue (hooks, providers, utilities, parts).

plans.free: WunderUI Free: the components with tier "free" are open source under the MIT License (https://github.com/wunder-ui/wunderui) — any project, commercial included. Every "pro" component needs WunderUI Core or Pro.
plans.core: WunderUI Core: every component, commercial license.
plans.pro: WunderUI Pro: everything in Core plus UI block and template source and all agent skills.

durations.use: Tooltip dismiss, press release. Barely reads as motion.
The default exit. Hover, focus ring, checkbox, switch track.
Dropdown, popover, context menu, backdrop, collapse.
Dialog, toast, switch thumb — a surface arriving.
Progress and meter fills. Data moving, not chrome.

easings.use: Anything arriving. Fast start, long settle. The house curve.
Anything repositioning while staying on screen.
Dialog, popover, switch. At most one per screen.
A sampled spring: one soft overshoot, then it settles. Something physical landing — a thumb, an arrow, a released sheet. Never on a data value.

amplitudes.use: Tooltip — stays glued to its anchor.

rules: **Duration and easing are class names, not numbers.** `duration-base`, `ease-entrance`. Tailwind has no `--duration-*` theme namespace, so WunderUI ships these as `@utility` rules that also set `--tw-duration` — which means they work on `animate-in` / `animate-out` too.
**Only `transform` and `opacity`.** Everything else goes through layout or paint. Height animates via `grid-template-rows: 0fr → 1fr`, never via `height`.
**Entrances decelerate, exits accelerate.** `ease-entrance` in, `ease-exit` out — and the exit is one step shorter on the duration scale, never the entrance duration reversed.
**Never fade in the LCP element.** An element at `opacity: 0` is not an LCP candidate, so a 600ms hero fade adds 600ms to your LCP. Render headline copy at full opacity; animate `transform` only.
**Restrain the travel.** Anything anchored to a trigger moves `--travel-xs` or `--travel-sm`. A menu that slides 20px looks like it fell in.

**One overshoot per screen.** `ease-overshoot` is punctuation. Two of them on one view and the interface reads as a toy. Never on a data value: a bar, gauge or bubble that swings past its number shows a wrong number for a moment.

**Reduced motion is opt-in, not a kill switch.** Wrap the animation in `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)` so the still state is the default and you cannot forget a selector. Reduced means calmer, not nothing: drop transforms and travel, keep opacity and colour changes (rule 15).

**Never `transition-all`.** Name the properties — `transition-[opacity,transform]` — or use bare `transition`, which covers colour, shadow, transform and opacity but no layout property. `transition-all` animates things you did not mean to animate, including on first paint.
**Loading keeps its height.** A skeleton occupies the same box as the content it stands in for, and crossfades — it never collapses and reflows.
**A looping ambient animation is the one place `ease-in-out` belongs.** A shimmer that runs forever has no entrance and no exit, so symmetry is correct there and nowhere else.

**Animate by frequency.** Keyboard-driven and 100+/day actions (command palette, shortcuts, moving between tooltips) get no motion; tens a day get a short fade; rare moments may delight. Tooltips skip their entrance when another one was just open (`data-open:data-instant:animate-none`).

**Anchored surfaces grow from their trigger.** Popover, dropdown, tooltip, hover card and select use `origin-(--transform-origin)`. Never start from `scale(0)` — start at 0.92–0.97 with opacity. Centred dialogs are exempt.

**Toggles stay interruptible.** Animate switches, checkboxes, tabs and other repeated state changes with transitions — they retarget from wherever they are — never with keyframes bound to the state, which restart from zero. An overshoot transition (`transition-transform duration-base ease-overshoot`) still swings past the end.

**Hover only where hover exists.** Tailwind v4's `hover:` is already gated to `(hover: hover)`; hand-written `:hover` in CSS goes inside `@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)`, so a tap on a phone does not leave a hover state stuck.

**Reduced motion keeps the fade.** WunderUI's global rule zeroes the scale, slide, spin and blur of every `animate-in` / `animate-out` and every transform transition, and keeps opacity and colour — so do not add `motion-reduce:transition-none` or `motion-reduce:animate-none` to a fade.

recipes.Overlay enter and exit:
/* Dialog, sheet, popover, dropdown, context menu — one pattern for all of them.
   Base UI exposes data-open / data-closed; tw-animate-css turns them into keyframes. */
<Dialog.Popup className="
  data-open:animate-in   data-open:fade-in-0   data-open:zoom-in-92
  data-open:slide-in-from-bottom-2
  data-open:duration-slow  data-open:ease-overshoot
  data-closed:animate-out  data-closed:fade-out-0 data-closed:zoom-out-96
  data-closed:duration-fast data-closed:ease-exit
" />

components.example:
<Accordion className="gap-0">
  <AccordionItem value="profile" variant="divider">
    <AccordionTrigger icon={<User />} iconVariant="plain" indicatorVariant="plus">

parts.name: Accordion
parts.description: Holds which items are open. Opening one item closes the open one unless you set `multiple`.

parts.name: AccordionItem
parts.description: One section, framed as a bordered `card` (the default) or as a `divider` row with a line above and below.

parts.name: AccordionTrigger
parts.description: The header row, a `<button>` with `aria-expanded`. It takes an optional leading `icon` and a `button`, `plus` or `chevron` indicator.

parts.name: AccordionContent
parts.description: The panel under the trigger. It opens on a grid-row transition, and its text lines up with the trigger label.

items.text: Use an Accordion for a list of sections people read one at a time, such as an FAQ or grouped settings. For a single show-more panel, use Collapsible; for views of one object, use Tabs.
Keep one `variant` per list: `card` items for a stand-alone list, `divider` items inside a surface that already has a frame.
Set `multiple` on `Accordion` when people compare answers. By default, opening one item closes the one that was open.
Write the trigger as the question or the section name in sentence case: `How do refunds work?`. It is the button's accessible name.
Don't put buttons or links inside `AccordionTrigger`. The whole row is already a `<button>`, and a control nested in it is not reliably reachable by keyboard.

components.example:

<Avatar size="lg" variant="primary">

parts.name: Avatar
parts.description: The round or square frame in five sizes from `sm` to `xl`. Set `color` for tinted initials or `variant="primary"` for a filled one.

parts.name: AvatarImage
parts.description: The photo. It shows once it has loaded; until then, or when the URL fails, the fallback stays in its place.

parts.name: AvatarFallback
parts.description: Initials or an icon, shown while the image loads or when there is none. The text size follows the avatar size.

parts.name: AvatarBadge
parts.description: A status dot at the bottom corner: inside the edge of a circle, on the corner of a square. Its icon hides on the two smallest sizes.

items.text: Use an Avatar to show who a person or workspace is, next to their name. For several people in little space, use Avatar Group or Avatar Stack.
Always add an `AvatarFallback` with initials, also when there is an image. It covers the moment before the photo loads and a broken image URL.
Give `AvatarImage` the person's name as `alt` when the avatar stands alone, and `alt=""` when the name is printed right beside it.
Use `color` for initials avatars and keep the same hue per person. The tints are theme tokens, so the initials stay readable in dark mode.
Don't resize an avatar with classes like `size-12`. Pick `size` (`sm`, `xs`, `default`, `lg`, `xl`): initials, icon and badge scale with it.

components.title: Avatar Group
components.description: A stack of overlapping avatars, with an optional overflow count.
components.props: function AvatarGroup({ className, children, ...props }: React.ComponentProps<"div">): React.JSX.Element;

parts.name: AvatarGroup
parts.description: Overlaps its avatars and rings each one in the surface colour. Hovering one lifts it and nudges its neighbours, except with reduced motion.

parts.name: Avatar
parts.description: Each person, an Avatar with an image or initials. All avatars in one group share the same `size`.

parts.name: AvatarGroupCount
parts.description: The `+N` circle at the end for everyone not shown. It takes the size of the avatars in the group.

items.text: Use an Avatar Group to show who is on a project or document, composing each avatar yourself. For people passed as data with a built-in limit, use Avatar Stack.
Cut the list yourself and put the rest in `AvatarGroupCount` as `+12`. The group renders every child it gets; it does not count or hide anyone.
Place the group on a surface that sets `--surface`, such as a Card. The rings take that colour, so each avatar reads as cut out of the background.
Don't mix avatar sizes in one group. The overlap and the size of the count circle assume one `size` for every avatar.

components.title: Badge
components.description: A small status or category label in 12 colors and 6 styles.

props.name: render
props.description: Allows you to replace the component's HTML element with a different tag, or compose it with another component. Accepts a `ReactElement` or a function that returns the element to render.

parts.name: Badge
parts.description: A short label in one of 12 `color`s and 6 `badgeStyle`s. Rendered as a `<button>` or `<a>`, it gains hover, focus and press states.

parts.name: BadgeCell
parts.description: A Badge for a table cell, made from a `label` string, with the `light_border` style by default.

items.text: Use a Badge for a short status or category on a row or card: `Paid`, `Draft`, `Beta`. For a change in a number, use Trend Chip; for a message people need to read, use Alert.
Give each status one `color` and keep it wherever that status appears. Write the status in the label too, so colour is never the only cue.
Use `light` or `light_border` in tables and lists and keep the solid `plain` style for the one badge that should stand out. `BadgeCell` already uses `light_border`.
Pass `render={<button />}` when the badge does something, such as removing a filter. Only a `<button>` or `<a>` gets the pointer, the hover ring and the focus ring.
Don't recolour a badge with classes or hex values. Every `color` and `badgeStyle` pair is measured for AA contrast in light and dark mode.

components.title: Breadcrumb
components.description: Shows the user's location in a hierarchy, in the `plain`, `border` or `underline` style.

parts.name: Breadcrumb
parts.description: The `<nav>` landmark named `breadcrumb`. Its `variant` sets the look of every part: `plain`, `border` or `underline`.

parts.name: BreadcrumbList
parts.description: The ordered list `<ol>` of items and separators. It wraps onto a second line when the trail runs out of room.

parts.name: BreadcrumbItem
parts.description: One step of the trail, an `<li>` holding a link or, at the end, the current page.

parts.name: BreadcrumbLink
parts.description: A level above the current page, as a plain `<a>` that takes `href`. It can hold an icon before the text.

parts.name: BreadcrumbSeparator
parts.description: An `<li>` between two items, hidden from screen readers. It shows a chevron unless you pass your own icon as children.

parts.name: BreadcrumbPage
parts.description: The current page as text, not a link, marked with `aria-current="page"`.

items.text: Use a Breadcrumb on nested pages, such as one project's settings, so people see where they are and can step back up. For switching between sibling views, use Tabs.
End the trail with `BreadcrumbPage`, not a link. It carries `aria-current="page"`, so screen readers announce where the person is.
Put a `BreadcrumbSeparator` between items yourself; the list does not add them. Each one sits in its own `<li>` and is hidden from assistive technology.
Don't link the current page or set `aria-current` on a link by hand. `BreadcrumbPage` already marks the last step and is not clickable.

import { Button } from "@wunderui/react"
import { Plus } from "lucide-react"

parts.name: Button
parts.description: The clickable element: a native `<button>` with the label and an optional icon before or after it.

parts.name: ButtonCell
parts.description: A small `plain` button sized for a table cell, for a secondary action in a row.

items.text: Use a Button for an action on the current page: save, send, open a dialog. A move to another page is a link: pass `render={<a href=… />}` together with `nativeButton={false}`.
Give each view one `primary` button for its main action. Every other action is `plain` or a link.
Label it with a verb and its object: `Save changes`, `Invite member`. A destructive button repeats the action; the button next to it says `Cancel`.
Don't use `outline` for ordinary secondary actions. In WunderUI the secondary button is `plain`; `outline` is the indigo-rimmed accent for the rare case that needs one.
Don't set heights or paddings by hand (`h-9`, `px-6`). Pick a `size`: the sizes read the density tokens, so compact and comfortable both stay right.

parts.name: IconButton
parts.description: A native `<button>` that holds one icon. It has no visible text, so its name comes from `aria-label`.

parts.name: IconButtonTextCell
parts.description: A table cell with a small `plain` icon button beside a label. Its `label` prop becomes the button's name and falls back to `Action`.

items.text: Use an IconButton for a frequent action whose icon is unmistakable: close, edit, more options. When the icon alone could be misread, use a Button with a text label.
Give every IconButton an `aria-label` that names the action: `Delete invoice`, not `Trash`. A tooltip is extra help, not the name.
Set `variant="plain"` or `ghost` for secondary icon actions. The default is `primary`, and a view has one primary action.
Pass `label` to IconButtonTextCell. Without it every row's button is announced as `Action`.
Don't use `sm` or `md` as the only control on a touch screen. Pick `xl` or `2xl`, which reach the 44 px hit area the polish rules ask for on touch.

components.title: Button Group
components.description: A row of connected buttons sharing borders and outer corners, for view switchers or segmented actions.

props.name: orientation
props.description: "horizontal" puts the buttons in a row, "vertical" stacks them with shared edges.

parts.name: ButtonGroup
parts.description: A `role="group"` row or stack that joins its children: neighbours overlap by one border and only the two outer ends keep their corners.

parts.name: Button
parts.description: Each direct child, usually a plain Button or Icon Button. The focused one moves on top, so its focus ring is not covered.

items.text: Use a Button Group for a few related actions that belong together, such as zoom in and zoom out or previous and next. For one choice that stays selected, use a Radio Button Group.
Give the group an `aria-label` that names what the buttons do together, such as `Zoom`. It already has `role="group"`, but no name.
Use the same `variant` and `size` on every button inside. The shared borders only line up when the buttons have the same height and border.
Don't wrap the buttons in extra elements. Corners and overlaps are set on direct children only, so a wrapper breaks the joined edges.
Don't put a primary button into the group. A view has one primary action, and the joined edges present the buttons as equals.

components.title: Card
components.description: A bordered container for grouping related content.

parts.name: Card
parts.description: The surface in `default`, `elevated` or `outlined` style. It has 20 px padding on every side and 16 px between its parts (12 px in the small size), and it sets `--surface` for the parts inside.

parts.name: CardMedia
parts.description: An image area flush with the top edge. Put an `` inside to fill it; empty, it shows an image placeholder.

parts.name: CardHeader
parts.description: A grid for the title, the description and an optional action on the right.

parts.name: CardTitle
parts.description: The card's title. It renders a `<div>`, so put a heading element inside when the card opens a section.

parts.name: CardDescription
parts.description: Secondary text under the title.

parts.name: CardAction
parts.description: Sits top right in the header beside the title and description, for a menu or one small button.

parts.name: CardContent
parts.description: The body, with the card's side padding.

parts.name: CardFooter
parts.description: A right-aligned row of buttons with a line above it. The card drops its own bottom padding when a footer is present.

items.text: Use a Card to group content about one thing, such as a project, a plan or a settings section. For a row with icon, title and meta, use Item Card; when there is nothing to show yet, use Empty State.
Leave the padding to the card: the default size has the same 20 px inset as the chart, stat and metric cards. Use `size="sm"` for dense grids instead of overriding `p-*` classes.
Put a menu or one small button in `CardAction`. It stays top right however long the title runs.
Use plain buttons in `CardFooter` when cards repeat in a grid. A view has one primary action, and a primary button on every card leaves none.
Don't set `bg-white` or a hex background on a card. `bg-card` follows the theme and dark mode, and the parts inside read it through `--surface`.

components.title: Checkbox
components.description: A single choice that is on or off, with an indeterminate state for “some selected”.
components.props: function Checkbox({ className, ...props }: Checkbox.Root.Props): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: checked

props.name: className

items.text: Use a Checkbox for an on/off choice in a form or for picking several items from a list. For a settings row that toggles, use a Switch; for one choice out of several, use a Radio Group.
Give every checkbox a visible label through `Label` or `Field`. Clicking the label then toggles the box, and screen readers have a name to announce.
Set `indeterminate` on a select-all box when only some rows are selected. Screen readers hear `mixed`, and the box shows a dash instead of the check.
Mark an unchecked required box with `aria-invalid` and say what to do in the error text: `Accept the terms to continue.`
Don't build a checkbox from a styled `<div>`. The component already handles Space, the focus ring and the larger hit area around the small box.

items.text: Use a Switch for one setting that is on or off, such as email notifications. In a list of settings, pair it with SelectorItem; to pick several items from a list, use Checkboxes.
Give it a label through `Label`, `Field` or a wrapping `<label>`. The switch alone has no name, and screen readers would only say on or off.
Name the setting, not the state: `Email notifications`, not `On`. The `switch` role already tells screen readers whether it is on.
Use `size="sm"` in dense rows such as table cells, and the default size in forms and settings.
Don't use a Switch to choose between two named options such as Monthly and Yearly. That is a choice, not on or off; use a RadioGroup.

components.example:
<RadioGroup defaultValue="pro">
  <SelectorItemGroup>
    <SelectorItem title="Starter" description="1 project · community support" control={<RadioGroupItem value="starter" />} />
    <SelectorItem title="Pro" description="Unlimited projects · €12 per month" control={<RadioGroupItem value="pro" />} />
    <SelectorItem title="Team" description="Shared libraries · €49 per month" control={<RadioGroupItem value="team" />} />
  </SelectorItemGroup>
</RadioGroup>

parts.name: RadioGroup
parts.description: Holds the selected `value` as a `radiogroup` role. The arrow keys move between the options and select them.

parts.description: One round option with its own `value`. Its hit area reaches past the circle so a near miss still selects it.

parts.name: Dot
parts.description: The white dot shown while the option is selected. RadioGroupItem already renders it.

items.text: Use a RadioGroup when people pick exactly one option from a short list they should see at once. For a long list, use a Native Select; for options shown as buttons, use a Radio Button Group.
Name the group with a `FieldsetLegend` or an `aria-label`, and put each item and its text in one `<label>` so the text also selects it.
Preselect a sensible option with `defaultValue` when one exists. Once people pick an option they cannot clear the group again, so an empty start rarely helps.
Use SelectorItem with a RadioGroupItem as its `control` when each option needs a description, such as plans with their limits.
Don't use two radio options for on and off. A single setting that is on or off is a Switch or a Checkbox.

items.text: Use an Input for one line of free text: a name, an email address, a search term. Several lines go in a Textarea; a choice from a known list goes in a Native Select or a Combobox.
Give every Input a visible label through `Field` or `Label`. A placeholder disappears with the first keystroke and is not a name.
Mark a wrong value with `aria-invalid` and say in the error what to do: `Enter an email address like name@company.com`, not `Invalid input`.
Keep the label a noun (`Work email`) and put a rule in the help text below it as a full sentence.
Don't size a field with `h-*` classes. Use `size` (`sm`, `default`, `lg`): a field and a Button of the same size line up, in both densities.

parts.name: Character counter

items.text: Use a Textarea for free text over several lines: a message, a description, feedback. One line goes in an Input; formatted text goes in a Rich Text Editor.
Give it a visible label through `Field` or `Label`, or use TextareaField, which brings label and help text along.
Set `maxLength` together with `showCount` when there is a limit. The counter appears only when both are set.
Don't size it with `rows` or `h-*` classes. Pick `size` (`sm`, `default`, `lg`): the heights read the density tokens, so compact and comfortable both stay right.

items.text: Use Progress for a task that runs to completion: an upload, an import, onboarding steps. For a fixed value inside a range, such as storage used, use Meter.
Name the bar with `ProgressLabel` or `aria-label`, such as `Uploading report.pdf`. Screen readers then say what is progressing, not only the number.
Add `ProgressValue` when the number matters. It formats the value and uses tabular figures, so the text does not jump while it counts.
Don't animate the width of the fill yourself. The indicator already scales with a transform on the slow data-bar timing.

items.text: Use a Slider when the rough position matters more than the exact figure: volume, a price range, a zoom level. For an exact number, use a Number Field.
Name it with `aria-label` or `SliderLabel`. For a range the thumbs are announced as `Budget, minimum` and `Budget, maximum`.
Show the current value with `SliderValue`, and set `step` to the precision people need. Shift with an arrow key moves by `largeStep`.
Don't add SliderThumb children for a range. Pass an array such as `defaultValue={[20, 80]}`; Slider draws one thumb per value.

components.title: Pagination
components.description: Page navigation with Prev/Next and numbered pages, or a simple "Page X of Y" mode.
components.props: function Pagination({ page, pageCount, onPageChange, className }: PaginationProps): React.JSX.Element;

parts.name: Pagination
parts.description: A `<nav>` named `Pagination` with Prev and Next and numbered page buttons. Long ranges fold into an ellipsis around the current page.

parts.name: PaginationSimple
parts.description: The compact form: Previous and Next with a `Page X of Y` label between them, for narrow spaces.

items.text: Use Pagination to move through a long list or table one page at a time. Where only Previous and Next fit, use PaginationSimple.
Keep `page` in state and load the matching rows in `onPageChange`. Pages count from 1, and `pageCount` is the total number of pages.
Show the total near the pager when people need it, such as `124 invoices`. Pagination itself shows only page numbers.
Don't build page buttons by hand. Pagination already disables Prev on the first page and Next on the last, and marks the current page with `aria-current`.

items.text: Use a Separator to divide groups inside one surface, such as two sections of a card. For a line with text like `or`, use Divider with Label; inside a toolbar, use ToolbarSeparator.
Place a vertical Separator inside a flex row. It stretches to the row's height, so the row needs one.
Use `dashed` for a lighter break inside one section, such as the line above a total, and the solid line between sections.
Don't draw dividers with `border-t` or a hex colour. Separator uses the `--border` token, so it follows the theme and dark mode.

parts.name: DividerWithLabel

parts.name: Lines
parts.description: Two separators that stretch to fill the space on either side of the label.

parts.name: Label

items.text: Use a Divider with Label between two alternative ways to do the same thing, such as social sign-in and email. For a line without text, use Separator.
Keep the label to one or two words that say how the groups relate: `or`, `or continue with`. Longer text squeezes the lines away.
Place it only between two alternatives, such as sign-in buttons above and an email form below. The label reads as a choice between what is above and what is below.
Don't use it as a section heading. The label is small, muted text with no heading role; start a new section with a real heading.

items.text: Use a Skeleton while content with a known layout loads: a list, a card, a profile. For a short wait on an action, such as saving, use a Spinner.

items.text: Use a Dialog for a short task that needs the user's full attention and ends with a decision: rename a project, invite a member. A long form or a detail view belongs in a Sheet.
Always include a `DialogTitle`, also when the design shows none. Without it the dialog has no name for screen readers.
Put the main action last in `DialogFooter` and name it after what it does: `Invite member`, with `Cancel` before it.
Don't confirm a destructive action in a Dialog: a click outside closes it. An Alert Dialog closes only through a button or Escape.
Don't use a dialog to report that something worked. A saved state is a toast; a dialog that needs one click to dismiss only adds a step.

items.text: Use an Alert Dialog to confirm an action with consequences, such as deleting a project or revoking access. For a task with fields, use Dialog; to report that something worked, use a toast.
Name the object and the loss: `Delete “Q4 report”?` as the title and what goes with it in the description, not `Are you sure?`.
Repeat the action on the confirm button and set `variant="destructive"` for deletions: `Delete project` after `Cancel`, so it ends up on the right.
Control `open` yourself when the action is slow or can fail. `AlertDialogAction` closes the dialog on click, before any request has finished.
Don't confirm with `window.confirm`. It cannot be styled or tested, while an Alert Dialog keeps the product's look, its focus handling and its button labels.

items.text: Use a Collapsible for one optional block people open on demand, such as advanced options or a long description. For a list of several such sections, use Accordion.
Name the trigger after what is hidden: `Advanced options`, `Show 4 more fields`. Its text is the button's accessible name.
Keep fields a form needs outside the closed panel. A collapsed panel is easy to skip, and an error inside it stays out of sight.
Don't put buttons or links inside `CollapsibleTrigger`. It is a `<button>` itself, and the plus icon is added for you.
Don't add a height transition to `CollapsibleContent`. It already opens on `grid-template-rows` with motion tokens, and a second animation fights it.

items.text: Use Kbd to show a key or a shortcut in text, a menu or a search field. For a shortcut on a tooltip, set `shortcut` on TooltipContent instead.
Write a symbol shortcut in one Kbd, such as `⌘K`. For named keys, give each key its own Kbd in a KbdGroup with `+` between them: `Ctrl` + `Shift` + `P`.
Hide shortcut hints on small screens with `hidden sm:inline-flex`. A phone has no keyboard to press them on.

items.text: Use a Spinner for a short wait tied to an action: a button that saves, a panel that refreshes. When content with a known layout loads, use a Skeleton.
Pass a specific `aria-label`, such as `Saving changes`. The default `Loading` says nothing about what is happening.
Size it with a `size-*` class to match the icon or text beside it, such as `size-5` in a large button. It is as big as a small icon by default.
Don't swap a chart or a list for a Spinner while it loads. The area collapses and the layout jumps; use the `loading` prop or a Skeleton of the same size.

items.text: Use a Dropdown Menu for actions behind a button: an entry does something and the menu closes. To pick a value in a form, use Native Select or Combobox; for actions on right-click, use Context Menu.
Name destructive entries after the action and the object and set `variant="destructive"`: `Delete project`. The colour is a second cue, never the only one.
Disable an entry that does not apply right now instead of removing it. Arrow keys still reach it, so screen reader users learn that the action exists.
Show `DropdownMenuLoading` while entries load and `DropdownMenuEmpty` when there are none, with `aria-busy` on the content while loading. The menu never opens as an empty box.
Don't put links to pages in a Dropdown Menu. It is a menu of actions; navigation belongs in the Navbar menu or in plain links.
Don't write the shortcut into the label. Put it in `DropdownMenuShortcut` and `aria-keyshortcuts` on the entry, so the entry is read as `Copy`, not `Copy ⌘C`.

items.text: Use a Table for rows people read: the line items of an invoice, a short list of members. When they sort, search, select or page through the rows, use Data Grid or Data Table.
Name the table with a `TableCaption` or an `aria-label` on Table. When the table scrolls sideways, that name also labels the scroll region.

Give amounts and quantities their unit. `CurrencyCell` adds the currency; for other figures the column heading names the unit.

parts.name: ChartCard
parts.description: The card around a chart: title or small label with an optional headline `value` and trend chip, a period Segment on the right and legend chips above the plot.

items.text: Use ChartCard around any chart that needs a title, headline number or period switch. For a number without a chart use MetricCard.
Pass `value` and `delta` for a headline: the `title` then reads as a small label above the number. Use `good` on `delta` when a fall is the good direction.
Give `legend` the same colours as the series, in the same order. Entries default to `--chart-1` to `--chart-5`, so a custom `colors` array needs matching `color` values.
Handle the period with `period` and `onPeriodChange`, and reload the chart's data in that handler. `periods` alone only keeps its own selected state.
Don't add a second heading inside the chart. The card title is the heading; use `description` for the unit or range.
Don't put a ChartCard inside another card. It is already a bordered, shadowed surface at least 320 px wide on larger screens.

components.title: Agenda
components.description: A time-ordered list of scheduled events.
components.example: <Agenda items={[{ id, time, title, description, color }]} />

parts.name: Agenda
parts.description: The bordered list of `items`, one row each, in the order of the array. It does not sort by time.

parts.name: Row
parts.description: One entry: its `time`, a colour bar, the `title` and an optional `description`. Rows are text only, with no click or focus state.

parts.name: Time
parts.description: The `time` string as written, in a narrow fixed column on the left.

parts.name: Colour bar
parts.description: A thin bar in the item's `color`, set as an inline style; without one it takes the primary colour.

items.text: Use an Agenda for a short, read-only list of what happens when, such as a day's meetings. For past events in order, use Timeline; for rows with guests, a menu or a click action, use Agenda Event.
Sort `items` by time before passing them in. The list renders them in array order.
Write `time` in one short format across the list, such as `09:30`. The time column is narrow and fixed, so a long range wraps onto a second line.
Set `color` to a CSS variable such as `var(--primary)`, not a hex. The value goes straight into an inline style, and only a token follows the theme and dark mode.
Don't make the Agenda clickable by wrapping it in a link or button. Its rows have no hover or focus state; use Agenda Event with `onClick` when an entry opens something.

components.title: Action Bar
components.description: A pill-shaped bar of bulk actions for a selection. It sits where you place it, so fix it to the bottom of the page yourself if it should float.

parts.name: ActionBar
parts.description: The pill-shaped bar with a shadow. It does not position itself: place it fixed or sticky near the list it acts on.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The `label`, such as `3 selected`, followed by a vertical separator. Without a label the separator goes too.

parts.name: Actions
parts.description: The `children`, laid out in one row with a small gap; usually small plain buttons and icon buttons.

items.text: Use an Action Bar for bulk actions on rows someone has selected: export, archive, delete. For actions that are always available, use Toolbar.
Show the bar only while something is selected and put the count in `label`: `3 selected`. The count tells people what the buttons will act on.
Give icon-only buttons in the bar an `aria-label`. The bar has no role or name of its own, so each button has to carry its own name.
Place the bar yourself, for example fixed and centred near the bottom of the view. `ActionBar` draws the pill; it neither positions nor animates itself.
Don't run a destructive bulk action straight from the bar. Confirm it in an Alert Dialog that names how many items go: `Delete 3 invoices?`.

components.title: Carousel
components.description: A horizontally scrollable row of items with arrow controls.
components.props: function Carousel({ children, className, label, navigationShape, showArrows, slideSize, autoPlay, index, onIndexChange, drag, }: CarouselProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: autoPlay
props.description: Advances one slide every this many milliseconds and starts over after the last one. It stops while the pointer or the keyboard focus is inside, while the tab is hidden and with reduced motion. 0 or undefined turns it off.

props.name: drag
props.description: Drag the slides left or right with the mouse or a pen; touch already swipes. The row follows the pointer and, on release, springs to the nearest slide (a quick flick goes one slide further). Turn it off when the slides hold content that ne…

props.name: index
props.description: The slide the row shows, for dots and thumbnails that control it (controlled).

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name of the scrolling region.

props.name: navigationShape
props.description: Shape of the two arrow buttons: a rounded square or a circle.

props.name: onIndexChange
props.description: Called with the number of the slide the row now shows.

props.name: showArrows
props.description: Show the two arrow buttons. Turn them off when dots or thumbnails do the navigating.

props.name: slideSize
props.description: "auto" keeps every slide at its own width, "full" makes each slide as wide as the row.

parts.name: Carousel
parts.description: A row with a slide strip between two arrow buttons. It snaps to each slide and pauses `autoPlay` while hovered or focused.

parts.name: Previous and next buttons
parts.description: Plain icon buttons that step one slide. At either end they stay focusable but disabled; without overflow they are hidden.

parts.name: Slide strip
parts.description: The focusable region named by `label`. It scrolls with the arrow keys, drags with a mouse or pen, and announces `Items 2–4 of 6` after a scroll.

parts.name: Slide
parts.description: Each child, wrapped in a snap point. With `slideSize="full"` every slide is as wide as the strip.

items.text: Use a Carousel for a row of similar items that people browse, such as product images or template previews. When every item matters, show them all in a grid instead.
Set `label` to what the row holds: `Template previews`. It names the region, and the default `Carousel` tells nobody what is inside.
Drive dots or thumbnails through `index` and `onIndexChange` instead of scrolling the strip yourself. The carousel springs to the slide and reports the one in view.
Keep `autoPlay` for images, not text. It pauses on hover, focus, a hidden tab and reduced motion, but moving slides are hard to read.
Don't leave `drag` on when slides hold controls that need the mouse, such as a slider. Set `drag={false}`; touch still swipes natively.

components.title: Data Grid
components.description: A full-featured table: sort, search, select, resize columns, paginate.

props.name: pageSize
props.description: Rows per page. Default 5.

props.name: searchable
props.description: Search field above the grid (uses each column's filterValue). Default true.

props.name: selectable
props.description: Row checkboxes and the "n of m selected" footer. Default true; false shows the row count instead.

components.example:
<DataGrid
  columns={[{ key: "name", header: "Name", sortable: true, render: (r) => r.name }]}
  data={rows}
/>

parts.name: DataGrid
parts.description: A complete grid: search field, sortable and resizable columns, optional row checkboxes, and a footer with the page controls. Each column is a `DataGridColumn` with a `render` function.

items.text: Use a DataGrid for a compact list of records that needs search, sorting and paging in one component. If you need column filters, export or bulk actions on selected rows, use Data Table.
Give each `DataGridColumn` a `filterValue` that returns plain text. Search reads it, and sorting compares it with `localeCompare`, so a column without one is neither searched nor sorted by value.
Keep a stable `id` on every row. Selection and paging use it, and the rows are keyed by it.
Set `selectable={false}` for read-only lists. The footer then counts rows instead of showing `n of m selected`.
Don't sort number columns through the text alone. The comparison is textual, so `10` lands before `9`; return a zero-padded string from `filterValue`.
Don't expect to read the selection from outside. The grid keeps the selected rows to itself and has no callback for them.

components.title: Filter Menu
components.description: A filter button that opens a checklist of options with counts, an all-row and Clear filter — for table and list filters.
components.props: function FilterMenu({ label, options, value, onValueChange, allLabel, onClear, icon, size, align, className }: FilterMenuProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: value
props.description: The checked option values. Every option checked means "no filter".

props.name: allLabel
props.description: The row that checks or clears every option.

props.name: icon
props.description: Icon before the label; the lucide list-filter glyph by default (the one the blocks use).

props.name: label
props.description: Trigger text.

props.name: onClear
props.description: Called by Clear filter after the selection is reset to every option (e.g. to reset paging).

components.example:
import { FilterMenu } from "@wunderui/react"

const options = [
  { value: "paid", label: "Paid", count: 18 },
  { value: "pending", label: "Pending", count: 6 },
  { value: "overdue", label: "Overdue", count: 3 },
]

const [value, setValue] = React.useState(options.map((o) => o.value))

<FilterMenu label="Status" options={options} value={value} onValueChange={setValue} />

parts.name: FilterMenu
parts.description: A multi-select filter: a trigger button and a menu of checkbox rows. `value` lists the checked options, and every option checked means no filter.

parts.name: Trigger
parts.description: The plain button with the filter icon. It shows the count (`Filters · 2`) and takes the link colour while the list is filtered.

parts.name: All row
parts.description: The first row. It checks or clears every option and shows checked, mixed or empty, depending on how many options are on.

parts.name: Option row
parts.description: One option with a checkbox and an optional `count` on the right. Ticking it keeps the menu open.

parts.name: Checkbox square
parts.description: The visual checkbox at the start of a row. It is decorative; the row itself carries the checked state.

parts.name: Clear filter
parts.description: Resets to every option checked and then calls `onClear`. It is disabled while no filter is active.

items.text: Use a FilterMenu to narrow a list or table by one attribute with several values, such as status or owner. For choosing a single value, use a select.
Start with every option in `value`. Checked means shown, so the full list is the unfiltered state and the trigger stays in its plain look.
Pass `count` for each option when you have it. People see how many rows a choice leaves before they tick it.
Use `onClear` to reset the dependent state, such as the page number. `Clear filter` selects all options itself and then calls it.
Don't hold an empty `value` as the idle state. Nothing checked reads as a filter that shows nothing, and the trigger turns active.
Don't change the `label` per selection. The trigger adds the count itself, and its accessible name reads `Filters, 2 of 4 selected`.

components.title: Data Table
components.description: A data table on TanStack Table: sort on several columns, filter from the column definitions, select rows with a floating action bar, expand, pin, page and export to CSV — with controlled state for server-side data.
components.props: function DataTable<TData extends RowData>({ columns, data, getRowId, "aria-label": ariaLabel, className, selectable, searchable, searchPlaceholder, columnVisibilityMenu, pinnable, exportable, exportFileName, onExport, paginated, pageSizeOptions, renderSubRow, getRowCanExpand, bulkActions, toolbarActions, rowLabel, loading, loadingRows, error, onRetry, emptyState, sorting: sortingProp, onSortingChange, columnFilters: columnFiltersProp, onColumnFiltersChange, globalFilter: globalFilterProp, onGlobalFilterChange, columnVisibility: columnVisibilityProp, onColumnVisibilityChange, rowSelection: rowSelectionProp, onRowSelectionChange, pagination: paginationProp, onPaginationChange, columnPinning: columnPinningProp, onColumnPinningChange, expanded: expandedProp, onExpandedChange, initialState, onQueryChange, serverSide, rowCount, }: DataTableProps<TData>): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: data
props.description: Keep the reference stable (state, a memo, a module constant): a new array on every render makes the table recompute.

props.name: aria-label
props.description: Accessible name of the grid.

props.name: bulkActions
props.description: Buttons in the floating bar that appears when rows are selected.

props.name: columnVisibilityMenu
props.description: The View menu to show and hide columns. Default true.

props.name: emptyState
props.description: Replaces the default empty state (no filters active).

props.name: error
props.description: Shows the error state instead of the rows. `true` uses the default text.

props.name: exportable
props.description: The Export button (CSV). Default true.

props.name: getRowCanExpand
props.description: Which rows can open. Default: all.

props.name: getRowId
props.description: Stable row ids. Needed for selection to survive paging and sorting; defaults to the row index.

props.name: initialState
props.description: Starting values for the state you do not control.

props.name: loadingRows
props.description: Number of skeleton rows while loading. Default: the page size, at most 8.

props.name: onExport
props.description: Called instead of the default file download. Gets the CSV text and the rows it was made from.

props.name: onQueryChange
props.description: Called when the page, the order, a filter or the search changes (not on mount): the one callback to fetch from.

props.name: paginated
props.description: Rows in the footer pager. Default true; false shows every row.

props.name: pinnable
props.description: Pin to start / end in the column menus. Default true.

props.name: renderSubRow
props.description: A panel under the row when its chevron is opened. Setting it adds the expander column.

props.name: rowCount
props.description: Total rows on the server. Needed for the page count when the server pages.

props.name: rowLabel
props.description: Names a row for screen readers on its checkbox ("Select Alina Lorenz").

props.name: searchable
props.description: The search field over all text and number columns. Default true.

props.name: selectable
props.description: Row checkboxes, shift-click ranges and the floating action bar. Default true.

props.name: serverSide
props.description: The server pages, sorts and filters; `data` is then one page, already in order. `true` means all three.

props.name: toolbarActions
props.description: Extra buttons on the right of the toolbar.

parts.name: DataTable
parts.description: The whole table: a toolbar, the grid, pagination, and an action bar while rows are selected.

parts.name: Toolbar
parts.description: Search, filters, the view menu, export and your `toolbarActions` in one row above the grid. Each part can be switched off.

parts.name: Filters
parts.description: Opens the filter menu for the columns that define a filter; active filters show as chips beside it.

parts.name: View menu
parts.description: Shows and hides columns. Off with `columnVisibilityMenu={false}`.

parts.name: Export
parts.description: Downloads the rows as CSV. Off with `exportable={false}`; `onExport` replaces the download.

parts.name: Sort button
parts.description: The sort control in a column heading. Shift-click adds the column as a further sort.

parts.name: Column menu
parts.description: Per-column options: sort, then-by sort, pin and hide.

parts.name: Row details
parts.description: The expanded area under a row, drawn by `renderSubRow`.

parts.name: Action bar
parts.description: Appears while rows are selected and holds what `bulkActions` returns.

parts.name: Pagination
parts.description: Page size and page buttons under the grid. Off with `paginated={false}`.

items.text: Use a Data Table when people work with the rows: sort on several columns, filter, select rows for a bulk action, or page through data that lives on a server. For a short list people only read, a Table is lighter.
Name the grid with `aria-label` and each row with `rowLabel`, so a checkbox reads `Select Alina Lorenz` instead of `Select row 3`.
Pass `loading`, `error` with `onRetry`, and an `emptyState`. The table draws the skeleton rows, the alert and the empty message itself.
Keep the query in the address bar with `useDataTableUrlState`, so a reload or a shared link opens the same view.
Don't sort, filter or page the rows yourself before passing them in. Let the table do it, or set `serverSide` and answer `onQueryChange` with the matching page.

items.text: Use a List Item for a row people scan and act on in one place: a person, a payment, an app, a setting. To compare many columns across rows, use a Table or Data Table.
Give the row one primary action through `onSelect` or `href`. Buttons, switches and menus in the trailing slot stay separate tab stops.
Pick one leading type per list, so the titles line up and the eye can scan down one edge.
For crypto rows pass `leading: { type: "coin", coin: "btc" }`: the real mark is drawn and kept away from screen readers, because the coin name is already in the title.
Keep the trailing value short and tabular: an amount, a badge or a trend. Put the explanation in the description.
Don't put two buttons in the trailing slot; move secondary actions into the icon-button menu.
Don't use selected for hover or focus. It marks the chosen row, and the title turns link-coloured with it.

items.text: Use a List Group for a self-contained list in a settings page, a sidebar or next to a chart: a few rows under one heading. For a dashboard card with loading and empty states, use a List Panel.
Choose the group by what people do with the rows: pick (Selectable), switch (Toggle), reorder (Sortable), open (Expandable, Tree, Master–Detail) or run (Action).
Keep a group to about five to eight rows and link to the full list with the header action.
Name every group with a title or `aria-label`; the lists, trees and menus inside take their accessible name from it.
Don't mix dividers and no dividers in one group. Lists with figures and states get dividers; feeds, rankings and timelines go without.
Don't rely on drag alone. Sortable already offers Alt with the arrow keys and the row menu, so keep the handle visible.
