props.type: { icon?: React.ReactNode; title: React.ReactNode; description?: React.ReactNode; action?: React.ReactNode }

props.name: footer
props.description: Under the rows: a string renders a full-width plain button.

props.name: items
props.description: The rows. With a variant and no items, the variant's sample rows are shown.

props.name: loadingRows
props.description: Skeleton rows while loading. Defaults to the number of rows (the variant's), so the card keeps its height.

props.name: onEmptyAction
props.description: Runs from the empty state's button when `empty.action` is a string.

props.name: onItemSelect
props.description: Makes every row a button (rows that already have onSelect or href keep theirs).

props.name: onRetry
props.description: Adds the Try again button to the error state.

props.name: skeleton
props.description: Leading placeholder shape while loading.

props.name: timeline
props.description: Connector line behind step circles (the Timeline panels).

props.name: variant
props.description: One of the 31 Figma panels: sets title, description, action, dividers, the state copy and sample rows.

props.name: contentHeight
props.description: Height of the tallest part of a real row (text 38, value with badge 44, date tile 48, three lines 56).

parts.name: ListPanel
parts.description: The dashboard card: 400 px, 16 px radius, 24 px padding above and below and 12 px at the sides, a 16 px semibold title, a link action and the rows. `variant` picks one of the 31 Figma panels.

parts.name: ListPanelSkeleton
parts.description: Skeleton rows at the size of real rows while `state="loading"`: leading shape, two text lines, a value.

parts.name: Header
parts.description: Title, description and the link action ("View all").

parts.name: Footer
parts.description: An optional full-width plain button under the rows (Available Modules).

parts.name: State
parts.description: The empty and error message: a round icon tile, title, description and one button (Try again for the error).

items.text: Use a List Panel for a list card on a dashboard: recent transactions, orders, integrations, the team, an activity feed, a timeline or crypto holdings, next to charts and KPIs.
Start from a `variant` and pass your own `items`; the title, the dividers and the copy of the empty and error states come with it.
Pass `state="loading"`, `state="empty"` and `state="error"` with `onRetry`. The skeleton keeps the card's height, and the error is announced.
Link the header action to the full list, and give rows `onItemSelect` when they open a detail.
Don't show more than five or six rows in a panel; the card sits in a grid with charts and should line up with them.
Don't stretch a panel across a wide row on its own. It is designed at 400 px; let charts take the extra width.

components.title: Empty State
components.description: Placeholder shown when a list or search has no results.

props.name: variant
props.description: Frame style — mirrors the Figma Empty State "Style" variants.

parts.name: EmptyState
parts.description: A centred block of icon, title, description and action. The frame is `dashed` by default, or `default`, `outline` or `background`.

parts.name: Icon
parts.description: The `icon`, drawn in a muted circle above the title.

parts.name: Title
parts.description: The `title`, a short line on what is missing: `No invoices yet`. It renders as a paragraph, not a heading.

parts.name: Description
parts.description: The `description` under the title: why the place is empty or what will appear here.

parts.name: Action
parts.description: The `action` node below the text, usually one small Button that fills the empty place.

items.text: Use an Empty State where a list, table or search has nothing to show. While data is still loading, show a Skeleton; when loading failed, show an Alert that says what to do.
Say what will appear and why it is empty, then offer one action: `No invoices yet`, `They appear here as soon as the first one is sent.` and `New invoice`.
For a search without results, name the query and offer a way out: `No results for “invoice 2024”` with `Clear search`.
Use the frameless `default` look inside a card that already has a border, and the `dashed` default where the empty state stands on the page.
Don't show a bare `No results` line. Without a reason and a next step, an empty place looks broken and leaves people stuck.

components.title: File Tree
components.description: An indented list of folders and files: a tree with arrow-key navigation whose folders open and close, and onSelect reports the chosen file or folder.
components.props: function FileTree({ data, "aria-label": ariaLabel, onSelect, selectedId, className }: FileTreeProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: aria-label
props.description: Accessible name of the tree.

props.name: onSelect
props.description: Called when a file or folder is activated (click, Enter or Space).

props.name: selectedId
props.description: The selected node (controlled). Without it the tree keeps its own selection.

parts.name: FileTree
parts.description: A bordered panel with `role="tree"` (named by `aria-label`, default `Files`) that renders `data` as rows. Top-level folders start open, deeper ones closed. One row is the tab stop; arrow keys move between the visible rows.

parts.name: Folder row
parts.description: A `treeitem` with `aria-level`, `aria-expanded`, a chevron and a folder icon. A click, Enter or Space opens or closes its children with a slide and selects it; Right opens it or enters the first child, Left closes it.

parts.name: File row
parts.description: A `treeitem` with a file icon and the `name`, cut with an ellipsis when too long. A click, Enter or Space selects it and calls `onSelect`; the selected row has `aria-selected` and a muted fill.

parts.name: Children
parts.description: The nested rows in a `role="group"`, indented one step per level. While closed they are inert and the arrow keys skip them, so focus never lands inside a closed folder.

items.text: Use a File Tree to show a folder structure people look through, such as the files of a template or an export. For items people search, sort or select, use Table.
Give every node a unique, stable `id`. It is the React key, and a reused id mixes up which folders are open.
Mark a folder with a `children` array, even an empty one. A node without `children` is drawn as a file.
Use `onSelect` to react to the chosen file or folder (open it in a preview, show its details), and `selectedId` when the selection lives in your state; without it the tree keeps its own.

Give the tree a name with `aria-label` when the page has more than one, such as `Project files`. Keyboard: arrows move, Right and Left open, enter and close folders, Home and End jump, a typed letter goes to the next row with that initial.
Don't use it for multiple selection or drag and drop; it selects one row at a time.

components.title: Floating TOC
components.description: A table of contents for an article, with a marker that follows the section in view. It does not stick by itself: put it in a `sticky` container to keep it on screen.

props.name: scrollContainer
props.description: The element that scrolls the sections, if it is not the page.

parts.name: FloatingToc
parts.description: A `<nav>` named `On this page` with one link per section. It is not sticky itself; place it in a sticky column.

parts.name: Entry
parts.description: An `<a>` to `#id` for each item, indented by `depth`. The current one carries `aria-current="location"`.

parts.name: Active marker
parts.description: A bar on the left line that glides to the current entry; a fainter one previews the hovered entry.

items.text: Use a Floating TOC beside a long page with several headed sections, such as documentation or a policy. For switching between separate views, use Tabs.
Give every section an `id` that matches its item. The links and the scroll spy find sections by that `id`, and a missing one is never marked.
Pass `scrollContainer` when the sections scroll inside a panel rather than the page. Otherwise the spy watches the window and the marker stands still.
Put it in a sticky column yourself, for example with `sticky top-24`. The component draws the list and the marker, not its position.
Don't set `activeId` unless you track the section yourself. A set `activeId` turns the scroll spy off, and the marker stops following the reader.

components.title: Holo Card
components.description: A card with a mouse-tracking spotlight/gradient shine effect.

parts.name: HoloCard
parts.description: A bordered, padded card with a glow in the primary colour that follows the mouse while hovered.

parts.name: Glow
parts.description: A radial gradient that fades in on hover and tracks the pointer. It ignores pointer events and sits behind the content.

parts.name: Content
parts.description: The `children`, placed above the glow.

items.text: Use a Holo Card to make one or two showcase items stand out, such as a featured plan on a landing page. For everyday content and dashboard tiles, use Card.
Re-theme the glow by setting `--primary` on a wrapper, not with a gradient of your own. The glow mixes the primary colour, so it follows brand and dark mode.
Keep the card complete without the glow. It appears only on mouse hover, so touch and keyboard users never see it.
Don't rely on the glow to show that the card is clickable. It is decoration with no focus state; put a real link or Button inside for the action.

components.title: Kanban
components.description: A drag-and-drop board of columns and cards.

parts.name: Kanban
parts.description: The board, drawn from `columns`. Cards move by dragging or by keyboard, and every move is reported through `onColumnsChange`.

parts.name: Column
parts.description: One stage with its title and card count in the header. It is tinted while a card is dragged or carried over it.

parts.name: Card
parts.description: One item with its `title` and an optional `progress` bar, `tag` badge and `meta` text. It is a focusable, draggable element.

parts.name: Announcer
parts.description: A hidden live region that reads out each pick-up, move and drop with the column title and position.

items.text: Use a Kanban when people move items through stages, such as tasks from To do to Done. When they sort, filter or edit fields across many items, use Data Table.
Pass `onColumnsChange` and store the result. Without it the board keeps its own copy: moves are not reported and a new `columns` value is ignored.
Give columns short, distinct titles. Screen readers hear them in every move, for example `column Done, position 2 of 4`.
Switch to `layout="stacked"` on narrow screens. The `board` layout scrolls sideways, and columns past the edge are easy to miss.
Don't add your own key or drag handlers to the cards. Space or Enter picks a card up, the arrow keys move it, and Escape puts it back.

components.title: Item Card
components.description: A generic row card: icon, title, description, meta, action.

parts.name: ItemCard
parts.description: One framed row: an optional icon tile, a title and description that truncate to one line, then `meta` and `action` on the right.

parts.name: ItemCardGroup
parts.description: A bordered box that stacks several ItemCards with a small gap, for a set that belongs together.

items.text: Use an ItemCard for an object that stands on its own row: a file, a connected app, an integration, with one action. For many rows people compare by column, use a Table.
Put the action in `action` as a Button or a link. ItemCard takes no click handler of its own, so the row itself is not interactive.
Keep `title` and `description` short or give the full text another way. Both are cut to one line with an ellipsis.
Use `meta` for a short fact with its unit, such as `2.4 MB` or `Updated 3 min ago`.
Don't wrap each ItemCard in a Card. It draws its own border and padding; for a set, use ItemCardGroup.

components.title: KPI
components.description: A single metric with its change, as a card with a dot and delta, a plain card with a caption, or an inline value.
components.props: function StatCard({ label, value, prev, delta, trend, trendGood, dotColor, caption, variant, className, }: StatCardProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: caption
props.description: Figma KPI · Caption, shown by the `simple` style — "+12% vs last month".

props.name: variant
props.description: Figma KPI · Style: `trend` is the card with dot and delta, `simple` the card with label, value and caption, `inline` the bare value over its label.

parts.name: StatCard
parts.description: One metric with its label and value. `variant` picks the card with dot and delta (`trend`), the plain card with a caption (`simple`) or the bare value over its label (`inline`).

items.text: Use StatCard for a single number with its change. For a number with a sparkline, progress or breakdown use Metric Card, and for a number above a chart use ChartCard.
Pass `value` as the formatted string with its unit, such as `$84,250` or `2.4%`. Numbers are shown as given and carry no formatting.
Set `trendGood={false}` when a rise is bad, such as churn. The delta colour follows `trendGood`, while the arrow follows `trend`.
Place several cards in a row with KPIGroup. It draws one frame with hairlines, and the cards drop their own borders.
Don't add `prev` and a `caption` for the same comparison. `prev` belongs to the `trend` variant and `caption` to `simple`; use the one that matches the variant.

components.title: KPI Group
components.description: A row of KPIs sharing one bordered container.

parts.name: KPIGroup
parts.description: The shared frame for a row of KPIs, divided by hairlines. Cards inside drop their own border, radius and shadow. `columns` sets 2, 3 or 4 per row at larger widths.

items.text: Use KPIGroup for the KPI row at the top of a view when the cards belong together. For cards with sparklines or progress use MetricGroup.
Match `columns` to the number of children, 2, 3 or 4. The default is 4, which falls to 2 columns on medium widths and one on phones.
Use one card style inside, for example all `simple`. Mixed variants have different paddings and break the hairline rhythm.
Don't wrap each card in its own border or shadow. The group removes them, and your own wrapper puts a card in a card.

components.title: Metric Card
components.description: One number with its trend and, per variant, a sparkline, progress, breakdown, comparison, distribution, status, action or AI insight.

props.name: aside
props.description: Sits beside the value: a radial progress, a donut, or a chart (Figma Area right / Bar right).

props.name: asideAlign
props.description: Rings sit centred beside the value (`center`); charts sit on the trend chip's baseline (`end`), so the bottom of the chart and the bottom of the chip form one line. Defaults to `end` for a MetricSparkline, else `center`.

props.name: caption
props.description: Figma Caption, beside the chip — "vs last month".

props.name: children
props.description: The visualization under the value: MetricSparkline, MetricProgress, …

props.name: icon
props.description: Figma Show icon: a 32 px tile before the label.

props.name: iconVariant
props.description: Figma Type=Icon (muted tile) or Type=Icon Button (bordered button).

props.name: info
props.description: Text behind the (i) next to the label.

props.name: menu
props.description: Figma Show menu: `true` for the ⋯ menu (View details · Customize · Export data · Remove), or your own trigger.

props.name: onIconClick
props.description: Makes the icon button do something; without it the button is decorative.

props.name: onMenuSelect
props.description: Called with the chosen entry of the built-in ⋯ menu.

props.name: previous
props.description: Figma Comparison · Period: the previous value under the chip.

props.name: trend
props.description: Figma Show trend: the Trend Chip under the value.

props.name: series
props.type: { label: string; value: string; percent: number }[]

props.name: label
props.description: Under the bar, left — "$72K of $100K target".

props.name: segments
props.description: Segmented only.

props.name: color
props.description: Brand indigo, or the green tint of the Figma "Bar right" card.

props.name: formatValue
props.description: Bars only: formats a bar's value; with it, the hovered bar shows a small readout above the bars.

props.name: highlight
props.description: Bars only: the index drawn solid at rest; defaults to the last bar.

props.name: label
props.description: Screen-reader name of the chart.

props.name: labels
props.description: Bars only: a name per bar ("Mon", "Week 32") for the readout.

components.example:
<MetricCard label="Revenue" value="$85,250" icon={<Activity />} menu trend={{ value: "12.4%", direction: "up" }}>
  <MetricSparkline data={series} variant="area" />
</MetricCard>

parts.name: MetricCard
parts.description: The KPI card: label, large value and an optional trend chip, caption and previous value. Pass a visualization as `children`, or a ring or chart beside the value with `aside`.

parts.name: MetricBreakdown
parts.description: A list of label and value rows under a hairline that splits the total into parts. Pass it as a child.

parts.name: MetricComparison
parts.description: Two or more periods as horizontal bars with their values. The first bar is solid and the others lighter. Pass it as a child.

parts.name: MetricDistribution
parts.description: A stacked bar of shares with its legend, described to screen readers as a list of labels and percents. Pass it as a child.

parts.name: MetricDonut
parts.description: A small donut for the `aside` slot, drawn from the same `parts` as the legend. It reads as an image with the part names and percents.

parts.name: MetricInsight
parts.description: A short sentence on the indigo tint with an icon, for a generated note about the number. Pass it as a child.

parts.name: MetricLegend
parts.description: The dots-and-labels row with each part's percent. Use it beside a MetricDonut; MetricDistribution already includes it.

parts.name: MetricProgress
parts.description: Progress toward a target as a `linear`, `segmented` or `radial` bar with a label and percent. Radial goes into `aside`.

parts.name: MetricSparkline
parts.description: A trend as a `line`, `area` or `bar` variant. Bars can be focused and read with the arrow keys, and `label` names the chart for screen readers.

parts.name: MetricStatus
parts.description: A pill badge with a short note beside it, for the state of the metric. Pass it as a child.

parts.name: Header row
parts.description: The top row: optional icon tile or button, the label with an optional info tooltip, and the optional menu on the right.

parts.name: Value block
parts.description: The block with the large value and the trend chip and caption below. A MetricSparkline in `aside` ends on the chip's baseline.

parts.name: Sparkbars
parts.description: The bar form of the sparkline. It is a focusable group; arrow keys, Home and End move the readout between bars.

items.text: Use MetricCard for one number with context: a trend, a sparkline, progress or a breakdown. For a plain number use StatCard, and for a number above a full chart use ChartCard.
Give the number its unit in `value` and its comparison in `trend` with a `caption` such as `vs last month`. A change without its period is unclear.
Put a MetricSparkline beside the value through `aside`. It ends on the trend chip's baseline by default, so the chart and the chip form one line.
Name the visualization with `label` on MetricSparkline and `labels` for the bars, such as `Mon` or `Week 32`. The default label is the generic `Trend`.
Don't pass a radial `MetricProgress` or a `MetricDonut` as `children`. Rings are built for `aside`, where they sit centred beside the value.
Don't enable `menu` without `onMenuSelect`. The built-in menu offers View details, Customize, Export data and Remove, and reports the choice only through that callback.

components.title: Metric Group
components.description: Several Metric Cards in one frame, divided by hairlines — the KPI row at the top of a dashboard.
components.example:
import { MetricCard, MetricGroup } from "@wunderui/react"

<MetricGroup>
  <MetricCard label="Revenue" value="$85,250" trend={{ value: "12.4%", direction: "up" }} caption="vs last month" />
  <MetricCard label="New customers" value="1,204" trend={{ value: "8.1%", direction: "up" }} caption="vs last month" />
  <MetricCard label="Churn" value="2.1%" trend={{ value: "0.4%", direction: "down" }} caption="vs last month" />
  <MetricCard label="Avg. order" value="$70.80" trend={{ value: "0.0%", direction: "neutral" }} caption="vs last month" />
</MetricGroup>

parts.name: MetricGroup
parts.description: The shared frame for a row of Metric Cards, divided by hairlines. Cards drop their own border, radius and shadow. `columns` sets 2, 3 or 4 per row at larger widths.

items.text: Use MetricGroup for the KPI row at the top of a dashboard when the cards have trends or charts. For plain stat cards use KPIGroup.
Set `columns` to the card count (2, 3 or 4). At the default 4 it shows 2 columns on medium widths and a single column on phones.
Give every card the same structure: label, value, trend and caption. Cells with different rows leave uneven gaps in the frame.
Don't give the cards their own `className` borders or shadows. The group strips them, and the hairlines are the gaps showing the border colour.
Don't use it for a single metric. One card needs no frame, so use MetricCard.

components.title: List View
components.description: A simple bordered list of rows with leading/trailing content.

parts.name: ListView
parts.description: The bordered frame that stacks the rows. It adds no list role of its own.

parts.name: ListViewItem
parts.description: One row with optional `leading` and `trailing` content around a title and description, both cut to one line. Rows are divided by a line.

items.text: Use a ListView for a short set of similar rows in one frame: members, sessions, connected devices. Rows that stand alone get an ItemCard; rows people sort or filter go in a Data Table.
Put an Avatar or an icon in `leading` and one action or a Badge in `trailing`. More controls make the row hard to scan.
Keep `title` and `description` short or show the full text elsewhere. Both are cut to one line with an ellipsis.
Don't set row padding by hand. The rows read `--list-row-py`, so they follow the density setting.

components.title: Timeline
components.description: A vertical sequence of dated, dot-connected events.

props.name: compact
props.description: Smaller dots and text, for milestones and long lists.

props.name: orientation
props.description: "vertical" stacks the entries, "horizontal" lays them out in a row with the time above each dot.

parts.name: Timeline
parts.description: Draws the entries from `items`, stacked or in a row with `orientation`, and joins them with a line. `compact` makes dots and text smaller.

parts.name: Dot
parts.description: The marker of an entry, with an icon or a small point inside. `avatar` replaces it, and `color` sets its fill.

parts.name: Entry
parts.description: One item: its `title`, an optional `description` and a `timestamp`, which sits beside the title or above the dot in a row.

items.text: Use a Timeline for events in order, drawn from data: a shipment's stops, a project's milestones. For scheduled events use Agenda; for one rich entry with a person and a comment, use Timeline Event.
Pass dot colours as tokens, such as `color: "var(--success)"`. The icon colour inside is chosen to stay readable on that fill.
Set `compact` for long lists and milestones. Dots, text and gaps shrink so more entries fit.
Don't write times like `recently`. Give each `timestamp` a date or a time with its unit, such as `Oct 12, 14:30` or `3 min ago`.

components.title: Widget
components.description: A generic dashboard widget shell: header, body, footer.

parts.name: Widget
parts.description: A framed dashboard tile with a header from `title`, `description` and `action`, the body from `children`, and an optional `footer` under a line.

parts.name: Header
parts.description: The `title` as an `<h3>` with the `description` under it and the `action` on the right. It renders only when `title` or `action` is set.

parts.name: Footer
parts.description: The `footer` content below a divider line, for a link such as `View all` or a note on the data.

items.text: Use a Widget for one tile on a dashboard: a title, a list or chart in the body, and an optional footer link. For a content card with media or a custom header, use a Card.
Put widgets under a page heading of level two. The title renders as an `<h3>`, so the heading order stays intact.
Keep the header to one `action`, such as a plain `View all` button or an IconButton with an `aria-label`.
Don't set a `description` without a `title` or `action`. The header is then not rendered, and the description does not appear.

components.title: App Layout
components.description: The app shell: sticky navbar and sidebar over a scrolling page, aside, banner and footer, skip link, and a drawer below 64rem.
components.props: function AppLayout({ banner, navbar, sidebar, aside, asideLabel, asideOpen: asideOpenProp, onAsideOpenChange, footer, children, embedded, scroll, width, padding, skipLinkLabel, drawerBelow, className, }: AppLayoutProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: aside
props.description: Right-hand context panel: details, help, activity. A drawer below 64rem.

props.name: asideLabel
props.description: Name of the aside landmark — required, an unnamed aside loses its role.

props.name: asideOpen
props.description: Controlled open state of the aside (default: open).

props.name: banner
props.description: A bar above everything: offline, trial, impersonation. Its height is published.

props.name: drawerBelow
props.description: Below this width (of the layout, not the window) sidebar and aside become drawers. Default 64rem.

props.name: embedded
props.description: The shell is a demo inside another page: no skip link, and the content area is a plain element instead of a second <main> landmark.

props.name: navbar
props.description: The top bar, usually a Navbar. Rendered as a direct child so it can stick.

props.name: padding
props.description: comfortable — 24 px around the content. none — for canvases and edge-to-edge tables.

props.name: scroll
props.description: document — the page scrolls; navbar and panes are sticky. Keeps scroll restoration, printing, anchors and viewport-relative sticky. Default. pane — the shell fills the viewport and only the content scrolls. For editors, inboxes, canvases a…

props.name: sidebar
props.description: Primary navigation, usually a Sidebar. A drawer below 64rem.

props.name: skipLinkLabel
props.description: Label of the skip link, the first focusable element.

props.name: width
props.description: fluid — full width. contained — the content steps up 1280 → 1620 → 2160 px with the screen.

parts.name: AppLayout
parts.description: The app shell. It lays out banner, navbar, sidebar, main, aside and footer as landmarks, puts a skip link first, and turns sidebar and aside into drawers below `drawerBelow`.

parts.name: Skip link
parts.description: A link at the very start of the page for keyboard users. It stays out of sight until Tab reaches it, and activating it jumps past the navigation to the content area. `skipLinkLabel` sets its text, and `embedded` leaves it out.

parts.name: Banner
parts.description: The `banner` prop: a bar above everything for offline, trial or impersonation notices. In document scroll mode it sticks to the top, and its height is published as `--shell-banner-h`.

parts.name: Navbar
parts.description: The `navbar` prop, usually a Navbar. It must be a direct child of the layout so it can stick; the layout measures its height into `--shell-navbar-h`.

parts.name: Shell
parts.description: The grid below the navbar with three columns: sidebar, main and aside. In `pane` scroll mode it clips, so only the content scrolls.

parts.name: Sidebar
parts.description: The `sidebar` prop: primary navigation, sticky beside the content. Below the breakpoint it leaves the grid and opens in a left drawer.

parts.name: Main
parts.description: The content area, a `<main>` that can take focus (`tabIndex={-1}`) so the skip link lands there. With `embedded` it is a plain `div`.

parts.name: Aside
parts.description: The `aside` prop: a 20 rem context panel on the right, named by `asideLabel`. Closed, it is inert; below the breakpoint it opens as a right drawer.

parts.name: Footer
parts.description: The `footer` prop: a `<footer>` landmark under the shell, with a top border.

parts.name: Navigation drawer
parts.description: A left Sheet that shows the sidebar below the breakpoint. It is named `Navigation` for screen readers and opens from the navigation trigger.

parts.name: Aside drawer
parts.description: A right Sheet that shows the aside below the breakpoint, named by `asideLabel`. Closing it also closes the aside.

parts.name: AppLayoutNavigationTrigger
parts.description: An icon button that opens the sidebar drawer. It is visible only below the drawer breakpoint; place it in the navbar.

parts.name: AppLayoutAsideTrigger
parts.description: A square button for the aside. On a wide screen it shows or hides the pane, on a narrow one it opens the drawer, and `aria-pressed` tells assistive technology which state it is in.

items.text: Use AppLayout as the frame of a signed-in product page: navbar, sidebar, content and an optional detail panel. For a single centred page with no navigation, such as sign-in, skip the shell.
Pass the navbar as `navbar`, not as a child. It has to be a direct child of the layout to stick, and its height feeds the sticky sidebar and aside.
Choose `scroll="document"` for ordinary pages, which keeps anchors and print. Use `pane` only for editors, inboxes and canvases that must fill the viewport and scroll inside.
Always set `asideLabel` when you pass an `aside`. An unnamed aside loses its landmark role, and the drawer reuses the label as its title.
Put `AppLayoutNavigationTrigger` in the navbar. Below `drawerBelow` (64rem by default) the sidebar leaves the page, and this button is the only way back to it.
Don't add your own `<main>` inside the children. The layout renders the `main` landmark; use `embedded` only for a demo inside another page.

components.title: Sidebar
components.description: App navigation in six modes: docked, offcanvas, icon rail, rail with flyouts, double sidebar and overlay drawer.

props.name: collapsed
props.description: Icon-only rail (Figma: Sidebar Collapsed).

props.name: children
props.description: SidebarItems (without icons) for the group's pages.

props.name: active
props.description: One of the group's pages is the current page.

components.example:
<Sidebar logo={<Logo />} footer={<SidebarUser name="..." email="..." />}>
  <SidebarSection>
    <SidebarItem icon={<Home />} label="Dashboard" active />
  </SidebarSection>
</Sidebar>

parts.name: Sidebar
parts.description: The navigation column, an `<aside>` that is 16 rem wide, or a 3 rem icon rail with `collapsed`. It lays out `logo`, the scrolling children and `footer`.

parts.name: SidebarSearch
parts.description: A search-shaped button, not an input, that opens a command palette. It shows a shortcut hint and shrinks to an icon in the rail.

parts.name: SidebarCta
parts.description: A full-width primary button for one call to action, such as `Upgrade plan`. It is hidden in the collapsed rail.

parts.name: SidebarHeading
parts.description: A small caption above a run of links. It is hidden in the collapsed rail.

parts.name: SidebarSection
parts.description: A `<nav>` that holds a run of items and groups. Use one per block of links, and name it with `aria-label` when there are several.

parts.name: SidebarItem
parts.description: A navigation row, an `<a>`. `active` sets `aria-current="page"`. In the rail the label stays as hidden text, so the link keeps its name.

parts.name: SidebarGroup
parts.description: An expandable row that holds a set of links. It is a disclosure with `aria-expanded`, not a menu, and it hides in the collapsed rail.

parts.name: SidebarSwitchItem
parts.description: A row with a label and a switch, such as `Dark mode`. The switch hides in the rail.

parts.name: SidebarNotification
parts.description: A row with an avatar, a title, a time and an unread dot. It is a button; the text hides in the rail.

parts.name: Footer
parts.description: The `footer` prop: a block pinned to the bottom with a top border, usually a user or workspace row.

parts.name: SidebarUser
parts.description: The signed-in person: avatar, name and email, plus a `trailing` slot. It is a static block; only the avatar stays in the rail.

parts.name: SidebarWorkspace
parts.description: A button with an avatar, a name and a chevron for switching workspace or account.

parts.name: DoubleSidebar
parts.description: Two-level navigation: a collapsed rail for top-level areas next to a full sidebar for the pages of the chosen area. Pass the rail as `rail`.

items.text: Use a Sidebar for the primary navigation of an app with more than a few sections. For a handful of site links across the top, use a navbar. Place it in an app layout so it becomes a drawer on narrow screens.
Pass `icon` to every top-level `SidebarItem`. In the `collapsed` rail only the icon shows, and a row without one has nothing to click.
Mark the current page with `active` on its `SidebarItem`, and set `active` on the `SidebarGroup` that contains it. Both set the strong style, and the item sets `aria-current="page"`.
Give group children no icons. A `SidebarGroup` indents its links under its own icon and hides entirely in the rail.
Don't rely on `SidebarGroup` in the collapsed rail. It disappears there, so offer a flyout or a flat list of the top-level pages.
Don't use `SidebarItem` for commands. It renders an `<a>` with `href="#"` by default, so pass a real `href`; for actions use a button.

parts.name: Navbar
parts.description: The top bar. It renders a scroll marker and a `<header>`, moves links that do not fit into a `More` list, and below 36 rem collapses the links into a menu drawer.

parts.name: Bar

parts.name: Logo
parts.description: The `logo` prop, at the start of the bar. The menu drawer repeats it at the top.

parts.name: NavbarLink
parts.description: A top-level link. With `href` it is a real `<a>`; without one it is a button for client-side routing. `active` sets `aria-current="page"`.

parts.name: NavbarMenu
parts.description: A mega menu: a button that opens a full-width panel of links on click or after a short hover. It is a disclosure with `aria-expanded`, not a `menu`.

parts.name: NavbarMenuLink
parts.description: One entry in a mega menu panel: a `title`, an optional `description` and an `icon`. In the drawer it shrinks to the title.

parts.name: More list
parts.description: A popover named `More links` that takes the links which no longer fit the row. Links inside it close it when followed.

parts.name: NavbarSearchField
parts.description: Inline search: an icon button that widens into a field. Escape or leaving it empty collapses it. Pass it as `search`.

parts.name: NavbarSearch
parts.description: A search-shaped button, not an input, that opens a command palette; it shows a shortcut hint. Pass it as `command`; it hides in the narrow layout.

parts.name: Actions
parts.description: The `actions` prop: the icon cluster on the right for notifications, the theme and the account menu.

parts.name: NotificationBell
parts.description: An icon button with a bell. Its name includes the `count`, and the badge shows `99+` above 99. Place it in `actions`.

parts.name: Notification count
parts.description: The small badge on the bell. It appears only when `count` is above zero.

parts.name: ThemeToggle
parts.description: Switches light and dark. As `icons` it is a radio pair with names `Light mode` and `Dark mode`; as `switch` it is a labelled toggle for menus.

parts.name: UserMenu
parts.description: The account trigger with an avatar, an optional name and a chevron. Its name is `Account menu` plus the name. Pass it as the `render` of a dropdown trigger.

parts.name: Menu drawer
parts.description: A left Sheet below 36 rem, opened by the `Open menu` button. It lists all links, with mega menus as collapsible groups.

parts.name: MobileNav
parts.description: A separate 56 px top bar for phones with a menu button, a logo or `title`, and `actions`. Use it on its own, without Navbar, on small screens.

parts.name: BottomTabBar
parts.description: A `<nav>` of icon and label tabs at the bottom of a phone screen. The current one gets `aria-current="page"`.

items.text: Use Navbar for site-wide navigation across the top: a handful of links, optional mega menus, search and account controls. For a long list of app sections, use a Sidebar and keep the navbar for actions.
Pass `NavbarLink` and `NavbarMenu` as direct children of `Navbar`. The bar measures them to decide what moves into `More` or the drawer, and a wrapper component hides them.
Mark exactly one `NavbarLink` as `active`. It sets `aria-current="page"`, which is how screen readers tell where the user is.
Name the landmark with `label` when a page has a second navigation. The default `Main` is not enough next to a sidebar.
Use `hide-on-scroll` for long reading pages only. The bar stays while it holds focus or a menu is open, and under reduced motion it becomes plain sticky.
Don't put commands in `NavbarMenu`. It is a disclosure of links, not a `menu`; use a dropdown menu for actions such as `Sign out`.

components.title: Segment
components.description: A single-select toggle group, like a compact tab bar, with a pill or a rounded-corner track.

props.name: aria-label
props.description: Names the group for screen readers, e.g. "Version".

props.name: shape
props.description: `pill` (default) or `rounded` for the square-cornered version.

parts.name: Segment
parts.description: A switch between a few views or values, as a pill or, with `shape="rounded"`, with square-cornered 8 px corners. It is one `tablist` with a single tab stop; arrow keys, Home and End move and select, skipping disabled options.

items.text: Use a Segment to switch the view or the scope of one piece of content: day, week, month; list or grid. For separate panels of content, use Tabs. For on or off, use a switch.
Keep it to two to five options with one-word labels. The track hugs its content and does not scroll, so long labels crowd the control.
Pass `aria-label`, for example `Time range`. It names the tablist; the options only carry their own labels.

Pick the `size` by place: `xs` and `sm` inside a card or chart header, `md` and `lg` to line up with a Button. The `md` and `lg` heights follow the density tokens, so they stay level with buttons in compact and comfortable.
Don't pass a `value` that matches no option. The first enabled option becomes the tab stop, but none of them looks selected.

components.description: A horizontal multi-step progress indicator with connectors.

props.name: navigable

props.name: numbered

props.name: onStepClick

props.name: orientation

const [step, setStep] = useState(1)

<Stepper currentStep={step} steps={steps} navigable="all" onStepClick={setStep} />

parts.name: Stepper
parts.description: A progress indicator for a multi-step flow. `currentStep` is the zero-based index; earlier steps show a check and later ones their number. It is named `Progress`.

items.text: Use a Stepper for a flow with a known number of ordered steps: checkout, onboarding, setup. For switching between parallel views, use Tabs or a Segment.

Name each step with a short noun such as `Account` or `Payment`. Labels in the horizontal layout stay on one line, so long ones crowd their neighbours; the vertical layout has room for a `description` underneath.
Use `orientation="vertical"` with `description` in a sidebar, and the horizontal layout above a form. Only the vertical one has the `numbered` option.
Make finished steps clickable with `onStepClick`. By default only done steps can be revisited; set `navigable="all"` only when the steps do not depend on each other.
Don't use it for steps that can be done in any order. It marks one current step and the finished ones before it, which reads as a sequence.
Don't make the step buttons the only way forward. They go to the finished steps; the forward action is your own `Continue` button.

parts.name: CommandGroup

parts.name: CommandInput
parts.description: The search field, a `combobox` that keeps focus while arrow keys move the active option. It focuses itself on mount; pass `autoFocus={false}` for an inline palette.

parts.name: CommandItem

parts.name: CommandList

items.text: Use Command for a searchable list of actions and destinations, opened by a shortcut. For choosing one value in a form, use a select or combobox field. For a short fixed list of actions, use a dropdown menu.

Give every `CommandItem` a unique `value` made of the words people search for, such as `Invite member`. Filtering matches the `value`, not the visible children, and an item without a value is skipped by the arrow keys.
Put `CommandGroup` directly inside `CommandList` and the items directly inside the group. The filter and the keyboard order read only this structure, so a wrapper `div` hides items from both.

Use `CommandDialog` with a global shortcut such as ⌘K, and pair it with a visible trigger. It opens with no animation on purpose, since a palette that people open many times a day should not delay them.
Don't leave the field's name to a hint placeholder. The placeholder becomes the `aria-label`, so set `aria-label` yourself when the placeholder is an example such as `Try Invite`.
Don't use `Command` for a search against a server. It filters the items you render, so fetch the matches and render only those yourself.

items.text: Use NativeSelect to choose one option from a short fixed list in a form: country, role, plan. For a long list with search, use a Combobox; for a choice inside a sentence, use InlineSelect.

Use values that are stable keys (`de`) and labels that read well (`Germany`), and keep the list under about ten items.

items.text: Use InlineSelect to switch a value inside a sentence, a title or a toolbar: `Sort by Newest`. For a field with a border in a form, use NativeSelect.
Give the trigger an `aria-label` such as `Sort order`. It has no visible label, and the announced value alone does not say what is being chosen.
Keep option labels short, one or two words. The trigger is only as wide as the current label, so long labels push the surrounding text.
Don't use it as the only way to reach a primary setting in a form. The missing border does not look like an input; use NativeSelect inside a Field.

items.text: Use CheckboxButtonGroup for a few short options that can be combined: text styles, days of the week, filters. For exactly one choice, use RadioButtonGroup; for a long list, use Checkbox.
Keep `value` as `string[]` and update it in `onValueChange`. Wrapping on narrow screens is built in, so no custom breakpoints are needed.
Give every icon-only `ToggleButton` an `aria-label` such as `Bold`. The pressed state is announced, but the icon alone has no name.
Don't use it for options with a sentence of explanation. A button holds a word or two; use a Checkbox with a description instead.

items.text: Use RadioButtonGroup for a few short exclusive options: a size, a plan period, a layout. For several at once, use CheckboxButtonGroup; for options with explanations, use RadioGroup.
Keep the choices to a word or two each and no more than about five, so the row stays on one line.
Give icon-only `ToggleButton` elements an `aria-label` such as `Grid view`.
Don't assume a value is always set. Pressing the active button again clears the choice, so accept an empty `value` or restore your default in `onValueChange`.

components.description: A +/- increment control for a bounded numeric value.

props.name: format
props.description: Formats the displayed value, e.g. `(n) => `${n}%``

parts.description: A group of a minus button, the current value and a plus button. It is controlled: you pass `value` and `onValueChange`.

items.text: Use NumberStepper for small counts changed by step: guests, quantity in a cart. For typing, long ranges or decimals, use NumberField.
Set `min`, `max` and `step` so the buttons stop at real limits. The value is clamped, so it never leaves the range.
Use `format` to add the unit, for example `(n) => n + " seats"`, so the number is not read without it.
Don't use it for values the user may want to type, such as 250. There is no text entry, so a jump from 1 to 250 takes 249 clicks.

items.text: Use DropZone for uploads where drag and drop helps: images, documents, imports. For a single file in a tight form row, a Button that opens the file dialog is enough.
State the limit in `hint`, for example `PDF or PNG, up to 10 MB`. The zone does not enforce a size.
Receive files in `onFiles` and show them in a list with name, size and a remove action. The zone itself shows no uploaded files or progress.
Don't trust `accept` for dropped files. It filters the file dialog, but a drop passes every file to `onFiles`, so check the type there and report which file was refused.

Give it a visible label through `Field` or `Label`. The editing area has no label of its own.
Store the HTML from `onChange` and pass it back as `content`. `content` is the starting text, so later changes to the prop do not replace what the user typed.

Don't use it for text that must stay plain, such as names or titles. The output is HTML (`

parts.name: ColorPickerTrigger

items.text: Use ColorPicker for a free colour choice, with hex, RGB or HSL entry and opacity. For a short fixed palette in a table row, use CellColorPicker.
Use `ColorPickerTrigger` in forms and give it `label` (default `Colour`). Its accessible name becomes `Colour: <hex>`.
Treat `value` as `#RRGGBB` and keep opacity apart in `alpha` (0 to 1). Hide the opacity slider with `showAlpha={false}` where transparency makes no sense.
Pass `swatches` with `onSwatchesChange` to save the user's colours; the plus button adds the current colour.
Don't add a native colour input beside it as a fallback. The area and both tracks are sliders that already take the arrow keys, and Shift makes bigger steps.

items.text: Use CellColorPicker for a colour column in a table: a label colour, a tag colour. For a free colour with opacity and a hex field, use ColorPicker.
Keep `value` as a hex string as `#RRGGBB` and store it with `onValueChange`. The trigger names itself `Colour <hex>. Choose a colour`.
Don't expect colours outside the six swatches. A `value` that is not in the set still shows on the trigger, but the user can only pick from the six.
Don't use it outside a row. It is 24 px wide and has no label; in a form, use ColorPickerTrigger so the field has a visible label and the hex value.

parts.name: Number

items.text: Use CellSlider to show a level inside a table row: a score, a quota used. For a value the user changes, use Slider; for a task's completion, use Progress.
Set `max` to the real ceiling, such as `max={5}` for a 5-point score. The fill is clamped at 100 %, but the number still shows the raw value.
Put it in a column whose header names the measure, such as `Usage`. The bar and the number carry no label or role of their own.
Don't build a cell around it that is expected to be editable. It has no handler, no keyboard support and no ARIA role; use a Slider with an `aria-label` in the cell instead.

props.name: aria-label
props.description: Name for screen readers — a combobox is not named by its current value.

parts.name: CellSelect

parts.name: Trigger

parts.name: Options list

items.text: Use CellSelect to edit one value of a row in place: a status, an owner, a priority. For a select in a form with a label, use NativeSelect.
Set `aria-label` per column, for example `Priority`. A trigger that shows only its current value does not name itself to a screen reader.
Pass `options` as the exact strings you store, and keep `value` one of them. The value is the text, there is no separate label.
Don't use it for long lists or for options that need a description. It has no search and no groups; use a Combobox in a form instead.

components.title: Cell Switch

props.name: aria-label
props.description: Name for screen readers — a cell has no visible label of its own.

parts.name: CellSwitch
parts.description: A Switch with a default `aria-label` of `Toggle`, for a table cell that has no visible label of its own.

items.text: Use CellSwitch for an on/off column in a table: enabled, notify, public. Outside a table, use Switch with a visible label or a SelectorItem.
Set `aria-label` per row or column, for example `Email notifications for Alina Lorenz`. The default `Toggle` is identical for every row.
Keep `checked` in your own state and write it back in `onCheckedChange`. The cell does not keep any state of its own.
Don't ship the default label when a column has more than one switch. Screen-reader users hear `Toggle` repeated and cannot tell which row they are on.

parts.name: SelectorItemGroup

parts.name: Leading

parts.name: Control
parts.description: The `RadioGroupItem`, `Checkbox` or `Switch` passed as `control`. The row border turns primary while it is checked.

items.text: Use SelectorItem for choices that need a title and an explanation: payment methods, plans, a setting with a switch. For a short label next to a box, use CheckboxField.
Pass the matching control: `RadioGroupItem` inside a `RadioGroup`, or `Checkbox` or `Switch` alone. The border follows the control's checked state.
Keep `title` to one line and put the detail in `description`. Both are truncated, so long text is cut with an ellipsis.
Don't put a link or button in `title` or `description`. The row is one label, and a click on it toggles the control.

Match `htmlFor` to the control's `id`, or wrap the control in the Label. Clicking the text then focuses or toggles the control.
Write a noun in sentence case (`Work email`) and keep rules for the answer in the help text below the control.
Don't use a placeholder or a heading instead of a Label. A placeholder vanishes on typing and a heading is not linked to the input.

items.text: Use a Combobox to choose one or more items from a list too long to scan: people, countries, projects. For free text with suggestions, use Autocomplete; for fewer than ten fixed options, use NativeSelect.
Type the state as `useState<Value | null>`. In single mode `onValueChange` receives `null` when the selection is cleared.
Always render a `ComboboxEmpty` with a sentence such as `No people found. Try a different name.`
Pass `multiple` for several choices and keep `value` as an array. Group long lists with `{ items }` objects and a `ComboboxGroupLabel`.
Don't leave the input unlabelled. The placeholder disappears once the user types; label it with `Field` or `Label`.

<Autocomplete items={fruits}>
  <AutocompleteInputGroup>
    <AutocompleteInput placeholder="Type a fruit..." />
  </AutocompleteInputGroup>
  <AutocompletePopup>
    <AutocompleteEmpty>No matches.</AutocompleteEmpty>

parts.name: Autocomplete
parts.description: The root. It holds the typed text, the items and the filter; `value` is the string in the input, not a chosen item.

parts.name: AutocompleteEmpty
parts.description: Shown instead of the list when nothing matches. It is hidden while it has no content.

parts.name: AutocompleteInput
parts.description: The text input. It is the combobox: arrow keys move through the suggestions, Enter takes one, Esc closes the list.

parts.name: AutocompleteInputGroup
parts.description: The bordered frame around the input. It carries the height, border and focus ring so the input inside stays borderless.

parts.name: AutocompleteItem
parts.description: One suggestion. Its `value` is what fills the input when it is chosen.

parts.name: AutocompleteList
parts.description: Renders the items. Pass a render function as the child so the filtered list, not the full one, is mapped.

parts.name: AutocompletePopup
parts.description: The suggestion panel. It brings its own portal and positioner, matches the width of the input and scrolls when it runs out of room.

parts.name: AutocompletePortal
parts.description: Renders the list outside the DOM flow. `AutocompletePopup` already includes it, so mount it yourself only for a custom popup.

items.text: Use Autocomplete when the user may type anything and the list only suggests: a search box, a tag, a city. When the answer must be one of the items, use a Combobox.
Give the input a visible label through `Field` or `Label`. The placeholder is a hint such as `Type a fruit...`, not the name of the field.
Always include an `AutocompleteEmpty` with a sentence like `No matches. Check the spelling or try a shorter word.` so an empty list never looks like a broken one.
Control `value` as a string with `onValueChange` when the text drives something else, such as a server search. The value is the input text, never an item object.
Don't treat the value as validated. Typed text that matches no item still ends up in `value`, so check it on submit or use a Combobox.

components.title: Calendar
components.description: A month grid for picking one date or a range, with keyboard navigation and optional min, max and disabled days.
components.props: function Calendar({ mode, selected, onSelect, month, defaultMonth, onMonthChange, min, max, disabled, className }: CalendarProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: disabled
props.description: Days inside min–max that cannot be picked. They stay reachable with the arrow keys and are announced as unavailable.

props.name: max
props.description: Latest day that can be picked. Keyboard focus stops here and later months cannot be opened.

props.name: min
props.description: Earliest day that can be picked. Keyboard focus stops here and earlier months cannot be opened.

parts.name: Calendar
parts.description: An inline month grid, Monday first, in single or range `mode`. It has no popover, so place it in a card or use DatePicker for a field. `min`, `max` and `disabled` limit which days can be picked.

parts.name: Month bar
parts.description: The previous and next month buttons around the month name. Both carry an `aria-label`; the month is controlled with `month` and `onMonthChange`. A button is disabled when its month lies completely outside `min`–`max`. The month name labels the grid and is announced when it changes.

parts.name: Day button
parts.description: One `<button>` per day inside a `gridcell`, in `row`s under the weekday `columnheader`s of a `role="grid"`. The chosen day's cell has `aria-selected`, today has `aria-current="date"`, and days of neighbouring months are muted but still selectable. Days outside `min`–`max` or matched by `disabled` are `aria-disabled` and dimmed.

items.text: Use Calendar to show a month inline, for example next to a schedule or inside your own popover. To pick a date into a form field, use DatePicker.
Set `mode="range"` and keep `selected` as `{ from, to }`. The first click sets `from`, the second sets `to` (an earlier day swaps the two), and a third click starts a new range.
Open on the right month with `defaultMonth`, or control it with `month` and `onMonthChange` when two calendars must move together.

Limit the choice with `min` and `max`, and block single days with `disabled` (a list of dates or a test such as weekends). Blocked days stay reachable with the arrow keys and are announced as unavailable; still say near the calendar why a day is blocked.

Count on the date-grid keyboard: Tab enters the grid once (on the selected day, today or the first day), arrows move by day and week, Home and End go to the start and end of the week, Page Up and Page Down change the month (with Shift the year), Enter or Space picks the day.

components.title: Date Picker
components.description: A Calendar inside a Popover, with Cancel/Apply actions.
components.props: function DatePicker(props: DatePickerProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: disabled
props.description: Days that cannot be picked: a list of dates or a test (passed to Calendar).

props.name: max
props.description: Latest day that can be picked (passed to Calendar).

props.name: min
props.description: Earliest day that can be picked (passed to Calendar).

props.name: numberOfMonths
props.description: Months shown side by side. Defaults to 2 for range mode.

props.name: presets
props.description: Quick-select sidebar (Figma: Type=presets). `true` uses the built-in presets.

parts.name: DatePicker
parts.description: A button that opens a popover with one or two calendars. The value changes only when the user chooses Apply.

parts.name: Trigger
parts.description: The button the user clicks to open the picker. It carries a calendar icon and shows the chosen date or range, or the placeholder text (`Pick a date` or `Pick a date range`) while nothing is chosen.

parts.name: Presets
parts.description: A list of quick ranges (`Last 7 days`, `Month to date`) beside the calendars. It appears with `presets` in range mode.

parts.name: Calendar
parts.description: One month in single mode, two side by side in range mode (`numberOfMonths`). It is the Calendar component, with its keyboard grid; `min`, `max` and `disabled` are passed through to it.

parts.name: Footer
parts.description: Cancel and Apply. Cancel, Esc or a click outside closes the popover and discards the draft.

items.text: Use DatePicker to put one date or one range into a form field or filter bar. For an always-visible month, use Calendar.
Set `mode="range"` for periods and `presets` for reports: `true` brings seven quick ranges, or pass your own `{ label, range }` list.
Put a visible `Label` above the trigger. The button shows only the date or the placeholder, so the label says what the date is for.
Set `placeholder` to the action in the context, such as `Pick a start date`. The default texts are generic.
Pass `min`, `max` and `disabled` to keep impossible dates out of the calendar, such as past days or weekends. Say next to the field what is allowed, because blocked days only look dimmed.

components.title: Chat Message
components.description: A single message bubble on the indigo tint, aligned right for the user and left for the assistant.

parts.name: ChatMessage
parts.description: One turn of the chat: a tinted bubble up to 75% of the width. `role="user"` puts it on the right, `assistant` on the left, each with the corner next to the sender flattened.

parts.name: ChatConversation
parts.description: Stacks the messages of a chat with an even gap.

parts.name: Avatar
parts.description: The optional `avatar` before the bubble, an Avatar or Agent Avatar. For the user the row is reversed, so it sits on the right.

items.text: Use ChatMessage for one turn in a chat. Group several in a Chat Conversation. For a chat with several agents, add an Agent Avatar to each message.
Set `role` on every message. It flips the row and the flattened corner; both roles use the same tint, so give the assistant an `avatar` as well.
Wrap the messages in `ChatConversation` for an even rhythm instead of spacing them by hand.
Don't put wide content into the bubble. It wraps at 75% of the width, so show code in a Code Block and documents in an Artifact Panel.
Don't recolour the bubbles to tell sender from receiver. The library uses one tint for both on purpose; role and position do that.

components.title: Chat Message Actions
components.description: Copy / retry / thumbs up-down actions shown under an assistant message.

props.name: feedback
props.description: The rating already given; marks the matching thumb as pressed.

parts.name: ChatMessageActions
parts.description: A row of four icon buttons under an assistant message: Copy, Regenerate, Good response and Bad response. Each has an `aria-label` and a tooltip title.

items.text: Use ChatMessageActions under a finished assistant message: copy, regenerate and a thumbs rating. For actions on code or a document, use the controls of Code Block or Artifact Panel.
Show it once the answer is complete, not while it streams. Copy and Regenerate act on the whole message.
Pass the rating already given as `feedback`. The matching thumb stays pressed through `aria-pressed`, also after a reload.
Do the copying in `onCopy` and confirm it where the eye is, for example in a tooltip. The component writes nothing to the clipboard itself.
Don't pass `onFeedback` without storing the value and handing it back as `feedback`. The thumbs only mirror `feedback`; they do not toggle on their own.

components.title: Chat Loader
components.description: A bouncing-dots indicator shown while the assistant is composing a reply.

parts.name: ChatLoader
parts.description: Three bouncing dots with the hidden text `Assistant is typing`, announced through `role="status"`. The dots stand still under reduced motion.

items.text: Use ChatLoader at the end of a conversation while the assistant has not started its answer. For a running tool call, use Chat Tool with `status="running"`; for a whole run, use Agent Status.
Show it after the user sends and remove it with the first streamed text, so the loader and the growing reply never appear together.
Leave the built-in text alone. It tells screen readers that the assistant is typing, which the moving dots cannot do under reduced motion.
Don't leave it on after a failure or an abort. It has no timeout and no error state, so replace it with the failure message and a retry.

components.title: Chat Attachment
components.description: A file chip attached to a chat message, with an optional remove button.

parts.name: ChatAttachment
parts.description: A chip for a file attached to a message or prompt: file icon, truncated name and an optional size line.

parts.name: Remove button
parts.description: An icon button named `Remove <name>`, rendered only when `onRemove` is given. Its hit area is larger than the icon.

items.text: Use ChatAttachment for a file attached to a message or a prompt. For a reference to a person, channel or link inside a prompt, use Context Pill.
Pass `size` already formatted with its unit, such as `2.4 MB`. The chip shows it as given.
Pass `onRemove` only while the file can still be taken back, typically before sending.
Don't pass a path as `name`. The name truncates at the end, so the part that tells files apart should come first.

components.title: Chat Source
components.description: A citation chip linking to a source referenced in an answer.

parts.name: ChatSource
parts.description: A compact link card for one cited source: optional number, globe icon, truncated title and domain. With a real `href` it opens in a new tab with `rel="noreferrer"`.

items.text: Use ChatSource for one source cited in an answer. For a numbered, pinned list of all sources use Source List.
Give `index` the same number as the citation in the answer text, such as `[1]`, so a reader finds the source.
Pass the real `href`. With the default `#` the card does not navigate and only calls `onClick`.
Don't put a full URL into `domain`. Pass the host, such as `docs.example.com`, and the page name as `title`; both truncate to one line.

components.title: Chat Tool
components.description: A collapsible card showing a tool/function call's name, status, and result.

parts.name: ChatTool
parts.description: One tool call in a chat: wrench icon, tool name, a running spinner or a done check, and the arguments or result behind a disclosure.

parts.name: Details
parts.description: The `children`, shown below the header when expanded. Without children there is no chevron and no `aria-expanded`.

items.text: Use ChatTool for a tool call inside a chat message. For a file edit use Diff View; for a run with many steps use a run timeline.
Pass the arguments or result as `children` to make the row expandable. Keep them short and as text.
Set `status="running"` while the call is in flight. The spinner stops under reduced motion, and screen readers hear `Running` or `Done`.
Don't show a failed call with it. It knows only `running` and `done`, and done shows a green check. Use a run error for failures.

components.title: Chain of Thought
components.description: A collapsible list of the model's intermediate reasoning steps.

parts.name: ChainOfThought
parts.description: A collapsed block for the model's reasoning, folded away under an answer.

parts.name: Toggle
parts.description: A `button` with `aria-expanded` that opens and closes the list. Its label is fixed: `Thought for a few seconds`.

parts.name: Steps
parts.description: The `steps` strings as short lines with a bullet, rendered as text.

items.text: Use ChainOfThought to fold the model's reasoning away under an answer. For tool calls and their results use Chat Tool; for the steps an agent plans to take, use Agent Plan.
Keep it closed, which is the default, so the answer comes first. Set `defaultOpen` only where the reasoning is the content.
Pass `steps` as short plain strings, one thought per entry. They render as text lines, not markup.
Don't expect the header to show a duration. Its text is fixed; for measured times use Duration Bar or Agent Status.
Don't hide a failure in it. A failed step needs its own error state with the step and the cause, visible without opening anything.

components.title: Code Block
components.description: A syntax-styled code block with a language label and copy button.

props.name: onCopy
props.description: Called after the code landed on the clipboard. The block already confirms it with a tooltip.

parts.name: CodeBlock
parts.description: A bordered code snippet with a header and the code below.

parts.name: Header
parts.description: The `language` label (default `code`) and the Copy button, which confirms with `Copied` and a tooltip.

parts.name: Code region
parts.description: A scrollable `pre` with `role="region"`, named `<language> code`. Long lines scroll sideways and the region takes focus for the arrow keys.

items.text: Use CodeBlock for a snippet in a message or a doc: language label, copy button and sideways scrolling. For a file the agent made, with versions, use Artifact Panel; for a change, Diff View.
Pass `language`, such as `tsx` or `bash`. It labels the header and names the region for screen readers.
Use `onCopy` for side effects only. The block already confirms the copy itself, so add no toast.
Don't expect syntax highlighting. The block renders plain monospace text in the foreground colour.
Don't wrap long lines by hand. The region scrolls and is reachable by keyboard.

components.title: Markdown
components.description: Prose styling wrapper for rendered markdown/HTML assistant output.

parts.name: Markdown
parts.description: A styled text container for formatted agent answers. It styles headings, links, inline code and lists, and does not parse Markdown itself.

items.text: Use Markdown to give an agent answer consistent typography once it is parsed. For source code with copy and line numbers, use a Code Block.
Parse the string into React elements first and pass those as `children`. The component only styles `h1`, `h2`, `a`, `code`, `ul`, `ol` and `p`, so a raw string stays raw.
Render agent text through that parser, not through `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. Model output and tool results are data, and they can contain markup.
Don't expect tables, block code or deeper headings to be styled. Only the elements listed above have rules, so use Code Block or Table for the rest.
Don't override the link or paragraph colour with hex values. Links use `text-link` and paragraphs `text-secondary`, which follow light and dark.

components.title: Prompt Input
components.description: An auto-resizing chat input with attach and send buttons.

props.name: aria-label
props.description: Accessible name of the text field (the placeholder is not a name).

props.name: models
props.description: Models for the model chip; the chip opens a popover to switch between them.

props.name: onAttach
props.description: Called by the attach (paperclip) button — open your file picker here.

props.name: tools
props.description: Extra buttons after the attach button (link, web search …).

parts.name: PromptInput
parts.description: The message box of a chat: a growing textarea with Attach files, optional tools and model chip, and a round Send button.

parts.name: Text field
parts.description: The `<textarea>` named by `aria-label`, "Message" by default. It grows up to about 160 px and then scrolls.

parts.name: Attach button
parts.description: An icon button named "Attach files". It calls `onAttach`, where you open your file picker.

parts.name: Model chip
parts.description: A Model Picker shown only when `models` is passed.

parts.name: Send button
parts.description: A round primary icon button named "Send". It is disabled while the text is empty.

items.text: Use a Prompt Input for chat and agent prompts with a send button. For a short single-line field, use Input. For voice, use Voice Input.
Keep `value` in state and send in `onSubmit`. Enter sends, Shift+Enter adds a line, and an Enter that confirms IME input is not a send.
Give the field a name that fits the screen through `aria-label`, such as `Message to the planner`. The placeholder does not count as a name.
Pass `models` and `onModelChange` when the user may switch models. The chip appears only then.
Don't clear `value` before `onSubmit` has read it. The component skips empty prompts itself, but clearing the text after a send is your job.

components.title: Prompt Suggestion
components.description: A pill-shaped suggested-prompt chip shown above an empty chat input.

parts.name: PromptSuggestion
parts.description: A rounded chip with a ready-made prompt. It is a plain `<button>` that calls `onClick` and takes its text from `children`.

items.text: Use Prompt Suggestions on an empty chat to show what is possible. For a command list opened by typing "/", use Slash Command Menu.
Write each suggestion as the full request the click will use, such as `Summarise this week's failed runs`. Short labels hide what happens.
Fill the prompt box in `onClick` and let the person edit before sending. Sending directly would put words in their mouth.
Don't expect an icon or a description. The chip is text only; for commands with both, use Slash Command Menu.

components.title: Text Shimmer
components.description: A shimmering-gradient text effect for a 'thinking...' loading label.

parts.name: TextShimmer
parts.description: A line of text with a light that sweeps across it every two seconds, for a label that says the agent is working.

items.text: Use a Text Shimmer for a short status such as `Thinking` while work is open. For a measured value, use Usage Meter; for a step status, use Plan Step.
Pass a short string only. `children` is typed as a string, and the shimmer reads best on a few words.
Swap the shimmer for plain text as soon as the work ends. The loop means "in progress", so it must not outlive the work.
Say the same state in words next to it, such as `Reading 3 files`. With reduced motion the sweep stops, so the text carries the meaning.
Don't use more than one shimmer in a view. A running step may pulse, but nothing else should loop.

components.title: Chat List View
components.description: A sidebar list of past conversations with preview and timestamp.

props.name: onSelect
props.description: Called with the clicked item; the default "#" navigation is prevented.

components.example: <ChatListView items={[{ id, title, preview, timestamp, active }]} />

parts.name: ChatListView
parts.description: The list of past conversations. Each row is a link with title, timestamp and a one-line preview.

parts.name: Row
parts.description: One conversation. The open one carries `aria-current="page"` and a filled background.

items.text: Use ChatListView for the history of conversations in a sidebar or panel: title, preview and time per entry. For navigation between app sections use a sidebar.
Set `active` on the open conversation only. It gets `aria-current="page"` and a filled row.
Handle selection in `onSelect`. Rows are anchors whose `#` navigation is prevented, so Tab and Enter work like on links.
Pass `timestamp` already formatted, such as `2 min ago` or `Mon`. It renders as given next to the title.
Don't put a whole message into `preview`. It truncates to one line, so send the first words of the last message.

components.title: Agent Status
components.description: A pill showing what a run is doing right now, with a live elapsed counter.

props.name: endedAt
props.description: When a finished run ended. With `since`, the pill shows the final duration `endedAt − since`.

props.name: label
props.description: Overrides the default status label.

props.name: since
props.description: When the run entered this status (or started, together with `endedAt`). Drives the elapsed counter.

parts.name: AgentStatus
parts.description: The state of one run as a pill: icon, word and, when `since` is set, an elapsed time. The `running` icon spins only when motion is allowed; the word carries the state either way.

items.text: Use AgentStatus for the state of one run, with its elapsed time. For spend against a budget use Cost Meter; for the steps of a run use a run timeline.
Pass `since` for `running` and `waiting`; both tick every second. For a finished run pass `since` and `endedAt`, and the pill shows the fixed duration.
Use `waiting` when a person has to act (it reads `Waiting for you`) and `idle` when nothing is queued. A run blocked on an approval is `waiting`, not `running`.
Override `label` only for a more precise word such as `Retrying`, and keep the status that matches the run so icon and tint stay right.
Don't build the pill from a Badge and a spinner. AgentStatus has one icon, tint and word per state, and a stalled run still shows how long it has been there.

components.title: Approval Card
components.description: The human-in-the-loop gate: what the agent wants to do, how risky it is, approve or reject.

props.name: approveLabel
props.description: Defaults per kind: Approve / Allow once / Allow / Run anyway.

props.name: cost
props.type: { estimate: React.ReactNode; budget?: React.ReactNode; note?: React.ReactNode }
props.description: high-cost: the banner, e.g. { estimate: "$18.40", budget: "$10.00", note: "…" }.

props.name: expiresAt
props.description: After this moment the card resolves itself as `expired`.

props.name: onEdit
props.description: When given, an "Edit" action appears beside reject.

props.name: preview
props.description: The payload, diff or command behind the request. Renders in a disclosure.

props.name: ref
props.description: The card is focusable (tabIndex -1): call ref.current.focus() when a new request needs attention, instead of focusing Approve.

props.name: rejectLabel
props.description: Defaults per kind: Reject / Reject / Deny / Cancel.

props.name: requestedAt
props.description: Shown verbatim next to the title, e.g. "2 min ago".

props.name: secondaryAction
props.description: A second, softer way to say yes — e.g. "Always allow" or "Render 400 only". Resolves as approved.

props.name: state
props.description: Controlled state. Omit to let the card manage its own.

props.name: summary
props.description: One sentence: what happens if this is approved.

components.example: {request.payload}} onApprove={() => approve(request.id)} onReject={() => reject(request.id)} />

parts.name: ApprovalCard
parts.description: The human-in-the-loop gate. A focusable group named by its title; it resolves in place to `approved`, `rejected` or `expired`, or follows `state` when you control it.

parts.name: Risk badge
parts.description: The `low`, `medium` or `high` risk label next to the title, with a matching icon tint. Defaults to `medium`.

parts.name: Cost banner
parts.description: In `high-cost`, a yellow banner with `cost.estimate`, the run budget and a note.

parts.name: Details
parts.description: The `preview` payload. In `inline` and `high-cost` it sits behind a `Show what will run` toggle; in `dialog-diff` and `permission` it is shown directly.

parts.name: Actions
parts.description: Approve and Reject, plus an optional softer `secondaryAction` and an Edit button when `onEdit` is given. Labels default per `kind`.

items.text: Use ApprovalCard wherever an agent may not go on without a person's yes. `kind` picks the layout: `inline`, `dialog-diff`, `permission` or `high-cost`. For a lasting Allow, Ask or Deny setting per tool, use Tool Permission Row.
Write `summary` as one sentence about what happens on approval, set `risk` honestly and put the exact payload in `preview`, so the person can inspect it before deciding.
Set `expiresAt` where requests lapse. The card counts down, turns the time red under a minute and resolves itself as `expired` without running anything.
When a new request appears, move focus to the card with `ref.current.focus()`. Never focus Approve; the card is focusable for this reason.
Don't start with `state="approved"` or approve inside your own handler. A default yes removes the gate.
Don't hide Reject in a menu or add a louder Approve elsewhere. Use `secondaryAction` for a softer yes such as `Always allow`, and `onEdit` to change the request.

components.title: Run Timeline
components.description: Every step of a run in order, with duration, tokens and expandable input/output.

props.name: activeStepId
props.description: Highlights the row the run is currently on.

props.name: defaultExpandedId
props.description: Opens one step's detail on first render.

parts.name: RunTimeline
parts.description: The ordered list of what an agent did. Each step has a status marker and a label, and may expand to show input and output.

parts.name: Step
parts.description: One `<li>` with a marker for pending, running, done, failed or skipped. The state word is available to screen readers.

parts.name: Step meta
parts.description: Tokens, cost and duration at the right of the row. Pass the cost formatted with its currency.

parts.name: Step detail
parts.description: An Input and Output block that opens in place. Only steps with `input` or `output` get a button, and one step is open at a time.

items.text: Use a Run Timeline to show what a finished or running agent did, step by step. For a plan that has not run, use Plan Step. For raw timestamped lines, use Log Stream.
Set `activeStepId` to the step the run is on. The row is highlighted and carries `aria-current="step"`.
Put an approval request into the waiting step's `output` and open it with `defaultExpandedId`. The gate then sits where the run stopped.
Give `cost` with its currency, for example `€0.04`, and `durationMs` as measured. Don't estimate numbers that look like measurements.
Don't pass HTML from tools as `input` or `output`. Tool results are data, so render them as text nodes.

components.title: Cost Meter
components.description: Spend against budget for a run, a day or a month — amber at 80%, red when it is gone.

props.name: currency
props.description: ISO code, used when `unit` is "currency".

props.name: label
props.description: Overrides the default "Spend this run" heading.

props.name: warnAt
props.description: Fraction of the budget at which the meter turns amber.

parts.name: CostMeter
parts.description: What an agent has spent against what it may spend: heading, budget, amount, bar and a status line. Turns amber at `warnAt` and red once the budget is reached.

parts.name: Meter bar
