parts.description: A `role="meter"` bar showing the percentage of the budget used.

parts.name: Status line
parts.description: The percentage used, and `Nearly spent`, `Budget reached` or the remaining amount. The remainder hides with `showRemaining={false}`.

items.text: Use CostMeter for what an agent spent against its budget. For usage against a plan quota use Usage Meter; for the context window, Context Meter.
Set `unit`, `currency` (ISO code, default `EUR`) and `period` (`run`, `day`, `month`), so heading and numbers carry their unit.
Rely on the words as well as the colour. At `warnAt`, default `0.8`, the line says `Nearly spent`; at the budget it says `Budget reached`.
Pair it with an approval of kind `high-cost` where continuing would exceed the budget.
Don't pass `budget={0}` to mean unlimited. A zero budget counts as used up by any spend.

components.title: Run Error
components.description: A failed run: which step threw, how many attempts are left, retry or resume.

props.name: detail
props.description: Stack trace or raw error body, shown in a CodeBlock behind a disclosure.

props.name: failedStep
props.description: The step that threw, e.g. "fetch_invoices".

props.name: onRetry
props.description: Start the whole run over.

props.name: onRetryFrom
props.description: Resume from the failed step, keeping everything before it.

components.example:
<RunError
  message="The invoice API refused the request"
  failedStep="fetch_invoices"
  attempt={2}
  maxAttempts={3}
  detail={error.stack}
  onRetryFrom={() => resume(run.id)}
  onRetry={() => restart(run.id)}
  onCancel={() => cancel(run.id)}
/>

parts.name: RunError
parts.description: The failure card of a run: message, failed step, attempt count, optional error detail, and the buttons to resume, run again or cancel.

parts.name: Message
parts.description: The headline that says what went wrong. The whole card is a `role="alert"`, so it is announced when it appears.

parts.name: Failure line
parts.description: The failed step in monospace and, with `attempt` and `maxAttempts`, "Attempt n of m". At the last attempt it adds "no retries left".

parts.name: Error detail
parts.description: A disclosure that opens a Code Block with the stack trace or the raw error body. It is closed unless `defaultOpen` is set.

parts.name: Actions
parts.description: Resume from this step (primary), Run again and Cancel run. Each appears only when its handler is passed.

items.text: Use a Run Error when a whole run stops. For a failed command, use Terminal Output with its exit code. For a single failed row in a plan, use Plan Step.
Say what failed and what to do in `message`, such as `Couldn't read invoices. Check the connection and resume.` Name the step in `failedStep`.
Pass `onRetryFrom` when earlier steps are kept. Resume from this step then becomes the primary action and Run again turns plain.
Put the stack trace in `detail`. It sits behind a disclosure, so the headline stays short.
Don't pass `onRetry` once `attempt` reaches `maxAttempts`. The card marks "no retries left" but still renders any button you give it.

components.title: Agent Grid
components.description: The fleet view — every agent, its current status and how long it has been there.

parts.name: AgentGrid
parts.description: The fleet view: a grid of agent cards. `columns` sets the widest layout (1 to 4, default 3) and the grid drops to fewer columns on narrow screens.

parts.name: Agent card
parts.description: One agent: icon, name, a description clamped to two lines, a status pill with live counter and an optional meta line. With `onSelect` it becomes a `button` role card, reached with Tab and activated with Enter or Space.

parts.name: Action
parts.description: The trailing control of a card, such as a menu or a Run button. Clicks and keys on it never select the card.

items.text: Use AgentGrid for the fleet overview: every agent, what each is doing and for how long. For the steps of one run use a run timeline; for parallel workers inside one run, use Agent Lane.
Set `since` to the moment the agent entered its current status. The pill then counts from it, so nobody has to ask how long an agent has been stuck.
Pass `onSelect` together with `selectedId` when the grid drives a detail pane. The selected card gets a primary ring and `aria-pressed`.
Put short facts in `meta`, such as `14 runs today · €2.10`, and keep `description` to one sentence.
Don't expect a click on `action` to open the agent. It is stopped on purpose, so keep run, pause or menu controls there and use `onSelect` only for opening.

components.title: Plan Step
components.description: One step of an agent plan: number or status icon, title, status in words and how long it took.

props.name: action
props.description: A control on the right, e.g. a Retry button for a failed step.

props.name: detail
props.description: What the step is doing, shown below the title.

props.name: duration
props.description: Already formatted, e.g. "1m 12s" or "0:16". Shows "—" when empty.

props.name: index
props.description: Shown in the marker while the step is queued or blocked.

props.name: meta
props.description: Label and value pairs under the detail, e.g. Target and Estimate.

props.name: since
props.description: When the step started. A running step then counts up from it.

components.example:
<PlanStep
  status="running"
  title="Sync tokens from Figma"
  detail="Rewriting the variant map so legacy props keep resolving after the rename."
  meta={[
    { label: "Target", value: "packages/react/tabs.tsx" },
    { label: "Estimate", value: "4 min" },
  ]}
  since={step.startedAt}
/>

parts.name: PlanStep
parts.description: One row of an agent plan: a numbered or status marker, the title, the status in words, and the time the step took.

parts.name: Marker
parts.description: The round badge. It shows the step number while queued or blocked, and an icon for running, done, failed and skipped. It is hidden from screen readers.

parts.name: Status label
parts.description: The status as a word (Queued, Running, Done, Failed, Skipped, Blocked), with the duration after it. Without a duration it shows a dash.

parts.name: Detail
parts.description: Optional text under the title plus label and value pairs from `meta`. It is hidden in the `compact` density.

parts.name: Action
parts.description: A slot on the right for a control such as a Retry button on a failed step.

items.text: Use a Plan Step for the plan before and during a run, where steps are named in advance. For the log of what a run actually did, with input and output, use Run Timeline.
Set `status` for every step, and pass `since` for the running one. It then counts up by itself, and the count starts on the client, so it does not cause a hydration mismatch.
Add an `action` such as `Retry` to a failed step and explain the failure in `detail`. A failed step with no way forward is a dead end.
Use `density="compact"` in side panels. It drops the detail block, so keep what matters in the title.
Don't rely on the marker colour alone. The status word is always shown next to it, so keep it and don't hide it for space.

components.title: Agent Plan
components.description: The agent's plan as a checklist: follow it live, edit it before the run, or group it into phases.

props.name: groups
props.description: Phases for `tree`.

props.name: hint
props.default: "Drag to change the order. Skipped steps stay in the plan."
props.description: Footer hint in `editable`.

props.name: onStart
props.description: Shows the Start button in `editable`; receives the steps that will run.

props.name: onStepsChange
props.description: Called in `editable` after every reorder, skip or add.

props.name: onStop
props.description: Shows the Stop button in `live`.

props.name: steps
props.description: Steps for `live` and `editable`. In `editable` only `id`, `title` and a skipped status are used.

props.name: subtitle
props.description: Overrides the computed "2 of 7 done" / "4 to run · 1 skipped" line.

components.example: <AgentPlan mode="tree" title="Migrate icons to Lucide 1.4" groups={plan.phases} />

parts.name: AgentPlan
parts.description: The agent's plan as a card in one of three modes: `live` follows a run, `editable` lets a person change the plan before it starts, `tree` groups steps into phases. It is a `section` named by the title.

parts.name: Header
parts.description: Title and a computed line such as `2 of 7 done`. In `live` it also holds a progress bar and the Stop button when `onStop` is given.

parts.name: Plan step
parts.description: One step with number or status icon, title, status in words and duration. A running step counts up from `since`.

parts.name: Phase
parts.description: A group in `tree` mode: a toggle with `aria-expanded` and a count like `2 of 5`. It opens by default once any step has started.

parts.name: Add step form
parts.description: In `editable` mode, an input and Add button below the list. New steps get the next position.

items.text: Use AgentPlan to show what the agent intends to do: `live` to follow a run, `editable` to let a person reorder, skip and add steps before it starts, `tree` for plans in phases. For what actually ran, with tool output, use a run timeline.
Use `editable` before the run and start it from `onStart`. It receives only the steps that will run, and the button reads `Start 4 steps` and disables at zero.
Pass `onStop` in `live` mode so a run can always be stopped, and set `stopLabel` if `Stop` is not precise enough.
Give every step a status (`queued`, `running`, `done`, `failed`, `skipped`, `blocked`) and `since` on the running one. Failed and blocked steps stay visible.
Don't pass elements as `title` in `editable` mode. The list uses `id`, the title text and the skipped status only; non-string titles fall back to the `id`.

components.title: Plan Summary
components.description: A plan on one card before it runs: goal, steps, time, cost, tools and phases.

props.name: description
props.description: Where the plan came from, e.g. "Drafted 3 min ago from the release notes".

props.name: stats
props.description: Usually Steps, Est. time and Est. cost.

props.name: tools
props.description: Tool names, shown as chips.

components.example:
<PlanSummary
  goal="Ship the Tabs v2 release"
  description="Drafted 3 min ago from the release notes"
  stats={[
    { label: "Steps", value: 7 },
    { label: "Est. time", value: "18 min" },
    { label: "Est. cost", value: "$0.42" },
  ]}
  tools={["Figma API", "GitHub", "npm"]}
  phases={[
    { title: "Map the old icons", steps: 3 },
    { title: "Swap the components", steps: 4 },
    { title: "Publish and announce", steps: 3 },
  ]}
  onEdit={openEditor}
  onRun={() => run(plan.id)}
/>

parts.name: PlanSummary
parts.description: The plan on one card before anything runs: goal, stats, tools, phases and the Edit plan and Run plan buttons.

parts.name: Stats
parts.description: A definition list of label and large value pairs, usually Steps, Est. time and Est. cost.

parts.name: Tools
parts.description: The tool names as indigo pills in a list.

parts.name: Phases
parts.description: An ordered list of phase titles. A numeric `steps` value reads "1 step" or "n steps"; text is shown as given.

parts.name: Actions
parts.description: Edit plan as a plain button and Run plan as the primary one. Each appears only when its handler is passed.

items.text: Use a Plan Summary to ask for a go before a run starts. For the steps of a running plan, use Plan Step. For a gate in the middle of a run, use Approval Card.
Put units in the stat values, such as `12 min` and `€0.40`, and say where the plan came from in `description`. Cost and time are what people decide on.
List every tool the plan will touch in `tools`. A plan that hides a tool hides what it may change.
Pass `onRun` only when the plan may start. The primary Run plan button disappears without it, so there is no half-working card.
Don't start the run before a click on Run plan. Nothing here auto-starts, and a plan that starts itself is a pre-approved plan.

components.title: Activity Item
components.description: One line in a live activity stream: status, action, tool and elapsed time.

props.name: elapsed
props.description: Already formatted, e.g. "6.3s". Shows "—" when empty.

props.name: since
props.description: When the action started. A running item then counts up from it.

props.name: tool
props.description: Tool or file name, shown as a chip.

props.name: wrap
props.description: Lets a long label break onto a second line instead of truncating.

components.example:
<ActivityItem status="running" label="Comparing Figma and code tokens" tool="tokens.diff" since={action.startedAt} />
<ActivityItem status="done" label="Read 214 variables from Figma" tool="figma.read" elapsed="3.6s" />

parts.name: ActivityItem
parts.description: One line of a live activity stream: status dot, label, optional tool chip and elapsed time. The dot pulses while `running`, and screen readers hear the status word before the label.

parts.name: Tool chip
parts.description: A pill with the tool or file name, shown when `tool` is set. It truncates at a fixed width.

items.text: Use ActivityItem for one line in a live activity stream: what the agent is doing, with which tool and for how long. For a step with output and detail, use a run timeline step; for a plan as a checklist, use Agent Plan.
Pass `since` on a `running` item so it counts up by itself. Pass a formatted `elapsed` such as `6.3s` once the action ended, so the final time stays fixed.
Keep `label` to the action in plain words, such as `Reading 14 files`, and put the tool or file name in `tool`. Set `wrap` only where a second line is worth the height; otherwise the label truncates.
Set `status` to `failed` or `waiting` instead of dropping the line. The status word is part of the accessible name, the dot colour is not.
Don't let the dot colour explain a failure. Put the cause into `label`, for example `Write failed: file is read-only`.

components.title: Log Stream
components.description: A run's log with an All or Errors filter and auto-scroll.

props.name: autoScroll
props.description: Controlled auto-scroll.

props.name: emptyLabel
props.description: Shown when the filter leaves no lines.

props.name: level
props.description: Controlled filter.

props.name: maxHeight
props.description: Height in px after which the log scrolls.

components.example:
<LogStream
  lines={[
    { time: "0:05.2", level: "warn", message: "Figma API busy, retrying in 2s" },
    { time: "0:12.0", level: "error", message: "Push to docs-preview timed out" },
  ]}
/>

parts.name: LogStream
parts.description: The card around a run log: title, an All or Errors filter, the scrolling log and the Auto-scroll toggle.

parts.name: Level filter
parts.description: Two toggle buttons, All and Errors, with `aria-pressed`. Controlled through `level`, or uncontrolled with `defaultLevel`.

parts.name: Log
parts.description: The scrolling `role="log"` region. It is a polite live region, takes keyboard focus for scrolling and stops growing at `maxHeight`.

parts.name: Log line
parts.description: Time, level dot and level word, then the message. Info lines show no level word on screen but keep it for screen readers.

parts.name: Auto-scroll toggle
parts.description: A pressed-state button that keeps the newest line in view. It is on by default and can be controlled through `autoScroll`.

items.text: Use a Log Stream for the timestamped lines a run writes while it works. For one command with its exit code and output streams, use Terminal Output. For the steps of a run, use Run Timeline.
Pass `time` already formatted, such as `0:02.9`, and give each line a stable `id`. The log uses `id` as the row key.
Set `level` to `error` on failing lines. The Errors filter shows only those, and the empty text then reads "No errors so far." instead of "Nothing logged yet."
Keep Auto-scroll on for a live run and let the reader turn it off. Control it with `autoScroll` and `onAutoScrollChange` if the page needs to know.
Don't pass HTML strings or untrusted markup as `message`. Log lines come from tools and files, so render them as plain text nodes.

components.title: Agent Lane
components.description: One parallel worker: its status, queue, throughput and the tasks it holds.

props.name: queue
props.description: Tasks waiting in this lane.

props.name: emptyLabel
props.description: Shown when the lane holds no tasks.

props.name: more
props.description: Tasks not shown as chips, rendered as "+16 more waiting".

props.name: throughput
props.description: Tasks per minute. Shows "—" when empty.

components.example:
<AgentLane
  name="Figma sync"
  status="saturated"
  queue={18}
  throughput={96}
  tasks={[
    { title: "Binding 214 variables", state: "Running" },
    { title: "Rebuild the icon sets", state: "Queued" },
  ]}
  more={16}
/>

parts.name: AgentLane
parts.description: One worker of a run that fans out: name, status word, queue length, throughput and the tasks it holds. It is a `section` named by the lane name.

parts.name: Task
parts.description: One entry of `tasks`: a truncated title with a short `state` underneath, such as `Running` or `Queued`.

items.text: Use AgentLane for one worker of a run that fans out. Put several side by side to see where work piles up. For a fleet of independent agents, use Agent Grid.
Set `status` to `saturated` when the queue grows faster than the lane works. The dot and the word `Saturated` turn yellow, so the state is readable without colour.
Pass `throughput` in tasks per minute. Leave it out when it is unknown: the lane shows `—` instead of a wrong `0/min`.
List only the tasks running now in `tasks` and pass the rest as `more`; it renders `+16 more waiting`.
Don't leave an idle lane unexplained. `emptyLabel` says why, default `Waiting for a free slot`; change it when the reason is another one, such as `No tasks assigned`.

components.title: Duration Bar
components.description: A step's share of the run as a bar, with a tick at the estimate and red when it runs over.

props.name: max
props.description: The longest step or the whole run — the full width of the bar.

props.name: value
props.description: How long the step took, in seconds unless you pass `formatValue`.

props.name: fill
props.description: Lets the bar take the free width; the label and the time keep their own width.

props.name: planned
props.description: The estimate. Draws a tick and turns the bar red when `value` is past it.

props.name: tone
props.description: Overrides the tone derived from `planned`.

props.name: valueLabel
props.description: Replaces the visible time on the right, e.g. "6 min actual · planned 4 min". Screen readers still hear the value text.

components.example:
<DurationBar label="Build the docs" value={8.3} max={12.4} />
<DurationBar label="Check the stroke widths" value={12.4} max={12.4} planned={9.6} />

parts.name: DurationBar
parts.description: One step's time as a share of `max`: label, a bar and the time. A `role="meter"` whose value text includes the estimate and the overrun.

parts.name: Planned tick
parts.description: A thin mark on the bar at the `planned` value. The bar and the time turn red once `value` is past it.

items.text: Use DurationBar for the time of one step against the longest step or the whole run, stacked in a list. For the state of a run use Agent Status.
Pass the same `max` to every row of a list, the longest step or the total, so the bars can be compared.
Pass `planned` where an estimate exists. Past it, the bar and the time turn red, and screen readers hear how far over it is.
Use `valueLabel` for wording such as `6 min actual · planned 4 min`. Screen readers still hear the computed text.
Don't pass milliseconds without `formatValue`. `value` is read as seconds.
Don't set `tone="over"` to mean failed. Over means slower than planned; a failure needs its own state.

components.title: Diff View
components.description: The result of an edit tool call: file, added and removed lines, and the changed code.

props.name: additions
props.description: Defaults to the number of added lines.

props.name: deletions
props.description: Defaults to the number of removed lines.

components.example:
<DiffView
  file="packages/react/src/components/ui/tabs.tsx"
  hunks={[{ header: "@@ -41,3 +41,6 @@ TabsList", lines: [
    { type: "del", old: 42, content: '  return <div role="tablist" {...props} />' },
    { type: "add", new: 42, content: "  const ref = useRovingFocus()" },
  ] }]}
/>

parts.name: DiffView
parts.description: The result of an edit: file name, counts of added and removed lines and the changed lines. Colour is backed by a `+` or `−` sign and by hidden `Added` and `Removed` text.

parts.name: Header
parts.description: A button with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` that folds the diff, showing the file and the counts.

parts.name: Hunk header
parts.description: The `header` text of a hunk, such as `@@ -41,3 +41,6 @@`. Shown only in `unified`.

parts.name: Lines
parts.description: The rows of a hunk in a horizontally scrollable region that takes keyboard focus. `unified` adds two line-number columns.

items.text: Use DiffView for the result of an edit tool call or the payload of an approval. For a plain snippet use Code Block; for a whole file the agent wrote, Artifact Panel.
Use `unified` where reviewers need context, with line numbers and hunk headers. Use `compact` for summaries; it keeps only the changed lines.
Put it in `preview` of an ApprovalCard with `kind="dialog-diff"`, so the person sees the exact change before deciding.
Pass `additions` and `deletions` when the hunks are trimmed. Otherwise they are counted from the lines.
Don't set `defaultOpen={false}` when the diff is what someone has to approve. It is open by default for that reason.

components.title: Terminal Output
components.description: The result of a code-execution tool call: command, exit code, run time, stdout and stderr.

props.name: duration
props.description: Already formatted, e.g. "3.8 s".

props.name: maxHeight
props.description: Height in px after which the output scrolls.

components.example:
<TerminalOutput
  command="pnpm vitest run tabs"
  exitCode={0}
  duration="3.8 s"
  stdout={run.stdout}
  stderr={run.stderr}
/>

parts.name: TerminalOutput
parts.description: The result of a command: the command line with exit-code badge and duration, a stdout and stderr tab pair, and the scrolling output.

parts.name: Command line
parts.description: The command in monospace after a dollar sign, the exit badge (green for 0, red otherwise), the duration and the copy button.

parts.name: Stream tabs
parts.description: A stdout and stderr tab list. Arrow keys switch and Home and End jump; a red count shows lines on stderr.

parts.name: Output panel
parts.description: The focusable tab panel that scrolls after `maxHeight`. Lines are plain text, in tones for muted, success and error.

items.text: Use Terminal Output for what a code-execution tool call returned. For a running stream of timestamped lines, use Log Stream. For a code listing, use Code Block.
Pass `exitCode` when the command is done and leave it out while it runs. Without it the card has no badge and reports a running status.
Split output into `stdout` and `stderr` and mark single lines with `tone`, such as `error`. Copy takes the visible stream.
Pass `duration` already formatted with its unit, such as `3.8 s`.
Don't send output through HTML. Lines render as text, which is how command output from an agent should stay.

components.title: Search Result Card
components.description: One ranked result of a web-search tool call: source, relevance, title and snippet.

props.name: relevance
props.description: 0–1 or 0–100. Shown as "94% match".

components.example:
<SearchResultCard
  rank={1}
  title="Tabs pattern — keyboard interaction"
  url="https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/tabs/"
  snippet="Arrow keys move focus between tabs; …"
  relevance={0.94}
/>

parts.name: SearchResultCard
parts.description: One ranked web-search result: rank, host and path, relevance badge, the linked title and a snippet.

parts.name: Rank
parts.description: A numbered circle shown when `rank` is set.

parts.name: Source line
parts.description: The host without `www.` and the path, taken from `url`. A value that is not a full URL is shown as given.

parts.name: Relevance badge
parts.description: "n% match". It accepts 0 to 1 or 0 to 100. It turns indigo on a selected result.

parts.name: Title link
parts.description: The title as a link that opens in a new tab with `rel="noreferrer"`.

items.text: Use a Search Result Card to show what a search tool call returned. For the pinned sources of a final answer, use Source List.
Mark the result the agent used with `selected`. The ring and the indigo badge show the difference without reading the snippet.
Pass the full `url`, with the scheme. The card shows the host and path from it, so the person can judge the source before clicking.
Keep the snippet to the text the tool returned. It is data from the web, so render it as text.
Don't invent a relevance score. Pass `relevance` only when the tool provides one, or the badge claims a precision that does not exist.

components.title: Tool Permission Row
components.description: Whether an agent may call a tool: Allow, Ask or Deny, with the scope it covers.

props.name: tool
props.description: The tool id, shown in monospace, e.g. "figma.write_variables".

components.example:
<ToolPermissionRow
  tool="figma.write_variables"
  description="Create and update variables in the WunderUI Figma file"
  defaultValue="ask"
  scope="Asks before each write · current file only"
  onValueChange={(value) => save("figma.write_variables", value)}
/>

parts.name: ToolPermissionRow
parts.description: One tool an agent may call, with an Allow, Ask or Deny switch, and a scope line that can fold out into more detail.

parts.name: Tool name
parts.description: The tool id in monospace with an optional description. Pass a string, so the switch gets the name "Permission for" plus the id.

parts.name: Permission switch
parts.description: A three-way segment. Allow runs the tool without asking, Ask pauses for a person and Deny blocks it. It defaults to Ask.

parts.name: Scope line
parts.description: Text that says what the setting covers. With `scopeDetail` it becomes a button with `aria-expanded` that folds out the detail.

items.text: Use a Tool Permission Row in a list of tools to set what runs on its own. For the access one request asks for, use Scope List.
Leave the default at Ask. A tool that is allowed without asking is a decision the person has to make on purpose.
Fill `scope` with what Allow would cover, such as `Any file under apps/docs`, and fold longer lists into `scopeDetail`.
Use the tool's real id, such as `figma.write_variables`, and a one-line description of the effect, so the person knows what they allow.
Don't set `defaultValue="allow"` for tools that write, delete or spend. Reserve it for read-only tools the person has already seen.

components.title: Expiry Timer
components.description: Countdown until an approval or permission request lapses — amber at the end, red once expired.

props.name: warnAt
props.description: Milliseconds left at which the timer turns amber.

parts.name: ExpiryTimer
parts.description: A pill counting down to `expiresAt`: `Expires in 04:32`. Amber under `warnAt`, red as `Expired` once it ran out. A `role="timer"` that stays silent every second.

items.text: Use ExpiryTimer for the countdown on a request that lapses, such as a permission request. An ApprovalCard counts down by itself when you pass it `expiresAt`.
Pass `expiresAt` as a Date, an ISO string or a timestamp. A new deadline resets the one-time `onExpire`.
Handle `onExpire` by changing the request itself, for example by marking it expired and disabling Approve. The timer only shows the time and calls it once.
Leave the announcement to the component. It says `Expiring soon` and `Expired` once and does not read out every second.
Don't pass `warnAt` in seconds. It is in milliseconds, default `60_000`.
Don't treat the pill as the lock. It uses the visitor's clock, so check the deadline on the server as well.

components.title: Scope List
components.description: What an agent asks to access, one scope per row, with a countdown until the request lapses.

props.name: bare
props.description: Drop the card frame, e.g. inside an Approval Card.

components.example:
<ScopeList
  scopes={[
    { title: "Read the docs site", detail: "apps/docs · 412 files" },
    { title: "Open a pull request", detail: "wunder-ui/wunderui · branch tokens-sync" },
  ]}
  expiresAt={request.expiresAt}
/>

parts.name: ScopeList
parts.description: The list of access an agent asks for, one scope per row with icon, title and monospace target, and an optional expiry countdown.

parts.name: Expiry timer
parts.description: An Expiry Timer in the header, shown when `expiresAt` is set. `warnAt` sets when it warns and `onExpire` fires at zero.

parts.name: Scope row
parts.description: An icon (a shield by default), the scope title and an optional `detail`, such as the path or count it covers.

items.text: Use a Scope List to show what a tool or agent may touch. For the Allow, Ask or Deny choice per tool, use Tool Permission Row.
Write each `title` as the permission in plain words and put the target in `detail`, such as `Read files` and `apps/docs · 412 files`.
Set `bare` when the list sits inside an Approval Card, so the frame does not double up.
Set `expiresAt` for requests that lapse and handle `onExpire`. Show the expired state; an expired request must not stay approvable.
Don't list a broad scope without a target. A row that only says `Files` hides how much the agent can reach.

components.title: Usage Meter
components.description: One limit as a row: what is used, what is allowed, and a warning before it runs out.

props.name: format
props.description: Formats `used`, `limit` and the overage. Defaults to 420k / 1M.

props.name: sub
props.description: Small print under the bar, e.g. "Resets at 00:00 UTC".

props.name: unit
props.description: Word after the overage, e.g. "tokens" → "Over by 20k tokens".

props.name: warnAt
props.description: Fraction of the limit at which the meter turns amber.

components.example: <UsageMeter label="Tokens today" used={420_000} limit={1_000_000} unit="tokens" sub="Resets at 00:00 UTC" />

parts.name: UsageMeter
parts.description: One limit as a row: label, used and allowed values, a meter bar and a status line that warns before the limit and reports an overage.

parts.name: Meter bar
parts.description: A `role="meter"` with the status text as its value text. It is primary below `warnAt`, amber from there and red above the limit.

parts.name: Status line
parts.description: "n% used", "n% · nearly at the limit" or "Over by" the overage with `unit`. The small print in `sub` sits beside it.

items.text: Use a Usage Meter for limits that can be passed, such as quotas and rate limits. For the cost of a run, use Cost Meter; for context fill, use Context Meter.
Set `unit` to the word that follows the overage, such as `tokens`, and put reset times in `sub`, such as `Resets at 00:00 UTC`.
Change `warnAt` from the default 0.8 only when the limit has a longer lead time. The meter turns amber at that share, before it runs out.
Pass `format` for money or bytes. The default shortens numbers to `420k` and `1M`, which suits tokens only.
Don't hide the status text and rely on the bar colour. The word is there for people who cannot tell amber from red.

components.title: Context Meter
components.description: How full the model's context window is: a ring for the prompt toolbar or a bar with a breakdown.

props.name: breakdown
props.description: What fills the window, e.g. system prompt, files, conversation.

props.name: warning
props.default: "Nearly full — older messages get summarised next."
props.description: Shown under the bar once `warnAt` is reached.

parts.name: ContextMeter
parts.description: How full the model's context window is. `ring` is compact for a prompt toolbar; `bar` shows label, token count, bar and legend.

parts.name: Breakdown
parts.description: The `breakdown` parts. In `ring` they open in a tooltip on a button; in `bar` they are segments of the bar plus a legend.

parts.name: Warning text
parts.description: In `bar`, the `warning` line shown once `warnAt` is reached. The `ring` only turns amber.

items.text: Use ContextMeter for the context window: `ring` in a prompt toolbar, `bar` where the breakdown deserves room. For money or request budgets use Cost Meter; for plan quotas, Usage Meter.
Pass `breakdown` with token counts per part, such as system prompt, files and conversation. In `ring` they appear in a tooltip that is also reachable by keyboard.
Write `warning` as the consequence and the next step. The default says that older messages get summarised next. Change `warnAt`, a fraction with default `0.8`, to fit the model.
Don't let the `breakdown` tokens exceed `limit`. Segment widths are `tokens / limit`, so the bar and the legend would disagree.

components.title: Slash Command Menu
components.description: The popover that opens when someone types / in the prompt: commands with a short description, filtered as they type.

props.name: query
props.description: Text typed after "/", e.g. "t".

components.example:
const menu = useMenuKeys(list.length, { open, onEnter: (i) => run(list[i]) })

<SlashCommandMenu commands={commands} query={query} activeIndex={menu.index} onSelect={run} />

parts.name: SlashCommandMenu
parts.description: The "/" popover: a listbox of commands that filters by what is typed after the slash and shows the keys at the bottom.

parts.name: Heading
parts.description: "Commands", or the matching text when `query` is set.

parts.name: Command row
parts.description: A `role="option"` with icon tile, the name with a leading slash and an optional description. The active row is filled.

parts.name: Key hint
parts.description: A footer line for the arrow keys, Enter and Escape.

items.text: Use a Slash Command Menu for actions that start with "/" in a prompt. For references to files and people, use Mention Picker.
Pass the text after "/" as `query`. The list matches names that start with it and shows "No command matches" when none do.
Use `useMenuKeys` on the textarea for the arrow keys, Enter and Escape, and point `aria-activedescendant` at `${id}-${index}`. Focus stays in the prompt.
Write each description as the effect of the command, such as `Clear the conversation`. Run the command in `onSelect`.
Don't run a command on hover. Hover only moves the active row; Enter or a click runs it.

components.title: Mention Picker
components.description: The @ picker for adding context to a prompt: files, people and channels in groups.

parts.name: MentionPicker
parts.description: The "@" popover: a listbox of grouped files, people, channels and links that filters itself by the text typed after "@".

parts.name: Group
parts.description: A `role="group"` section with a small heading. Groups with no matching item disappear from the list.

parts.name: Mention row
parts.description: One `role="option"`: an avatar for people or an icon for other kinds, the label and an optional description. Hover moves the active item.

parts.name: Empty message
parts.description: "Nothing matches" with the typed query, shown when no group has a match.

items.text: Use a Mention Picker for "@" references to things in the workspace. For commands that start with "/", use Slash Command Menu. For the chip that remains after picking, use Context Pill.
Pass the text after "@" as `query` and drive `activeId` from the prompt's arrow keys. Point `aria-activedescendant` at the option id `${id}-${item.id}`, so focus stays in the textarea.
Give every item a unique `id` and a `kind`. The id builds the option id, and the kind decides between avatar and icon.
Set `initials` and `color` for people, so the avatar matches the one used elsewhere in the screen.
Don't move focus into the list. The rows cancel `mousedown`, so clicking a row never blurs the prompt, and the picker is built for that.

components.title: Context Pill
components.description: A removable chip for what the prompt refers to: a file, a person, a channel or a link.

parts.name: ContextPill
parts.description: A removable chip for what the prompt refers to. `person` shows an avatar, `file`, `channel` and `link` an icon.

parts.name: Remove button
parts.description: An icon button named `Remove <label>`, rendered only when `onRemove` is given.

items.text: Use ContextPill for what a prompt refers to: a file, person, channel or link. For a file with name and size use Chat Attachment.
Set `kind` to what is referenced. A `person` shows `initials` (default: the first two letters of `label`) in the given `color`.
Pass `onRemove` for chips the user added. Leave it out for context the system added and the user may not remove.
Don't put a path or sentence into `label`. It truncates on one line, so use the file or channel name.

components.title: Prompt Mode Switch
components.description: What the agent may do with the next prompt — answer, act or edit — with the send keys underneath.

parts.name: PromptModeSwitch
parts.description: A segmented Ask, Agent and Edit control with a live hint of what the next prompt may do and the keys for sending.

parts.name: Mode segment
parts.description: Three options named "Prompt mode": Ask, Agent and Edit. It defaults to Ask and can be controlled through `value`.

parts.name: Mode hint
parts.description: One line that explains the chosen mode. It is a polite live region, so the change is announced.

parts.name: Key hint
parts.description: "Enter to send, Shift+Enter for a new line". Turn it off with `showKeys={false}`.

items.text: Use a Prompt Mode Switch to decide what the agent may do before the person sends. For the choice between models, use Model Picker.
Keep Ask as the default. Ask only answers and changes nothing, so a first prompt can never do more than the person expects.
Rewrite `hints` when your modes behave differently. The text must describe what the mode can change, not how it is named.
Show the mode next to the prompt, not in a settings page. The person decides per prompt, so the switch has to be in view when they type.
Don't soften what Agent does in the hint. The default says "Asks before risky steps", so back that with an approval gate for every risky step.

components.title: Model Picker
components.description: The model chip in a prompt box: always clickable, it opens a popover to switch models.

props.name: label
props.description: Heading above the list.

parts.name: ModelPicker
parts.description: The model chip for a prompt box: a button with the model name that opens a popover list with a check on the current one.

parts.name: Model chip
parts.description: The trigger button. Its name reads "Model: " plus the current model, and the chevron turns while the popover is open.

parts.name: Model list
parts.description: The popover with a `role="listbox"` of options: mark, name, optional tag, description and a check on the selected model.

items.text: Use a Model Picker as a small chip inside a prompt box. For a full card with specs and reasoning effort, use Model Select.
Give each model a short `description` or `meta` line and, for the default, a `tag` such as `Recommended`. The row shows `description` first and falls back to `meta`.
Leave `side="top"` when the prompt sits at the bottom of the screen, and use `bottom` when it sits near the top. The popover then never opens off screen.
Handle `onValueChange` and store the id. Picking a model closes the popover, so no extra close step is needed.
Don't fill it with a long list. The popover has no search field, so keep it to the few models a person really chooses between.

components.title: Model Select
components.description: Pick the model and how hard it should think, with context size and price at a glance.

parts.name: ModelSelect
parts.description: A card that shows the model list beside the details of the chosen model: description, specs and a reasoning-effort switch.

parts.name: Model list
parts.description: A `role="listbox"` of models with name and meta. The selected row has `aria-selected` and a subtle fill.

parts.name: Model details
parts.description: Name, description and the `specs` as label and value pairs for the selected model.

parts.name: Reasoning effort
parts.description: A Low, Medium or High segment with a one-line hint of the cost. It defaults to Medium and can be controlled with `effort`.

items.text: Use a Model Select on a settings or onboarding screen where people compare models. For the compact chip in a prompt box, use Model Picker.
Fill `specs` with comparable pairs such as context size and price per million tokens, and write units into the value. The details change with every selection.
Handle `onEffortChange` together with `onValueChange` and save both. The High hint says it "costs more", so show the effect where the person decides.
Don't leave `meta` empty on the models. The list rows show only the name and `meta`, so the models are hard to tell apart without it.
Don't squeeze it into a narrow column. It is capped at 560 px wide and stacks the list over the details below the `sm` breakpoint.

components.title: Voice Input
components.description: Talk instead of typing: idle, listening with a live waveform and transcript, then transcribing.

props.name: transcript
props.description: The words heard so far (listening).

parts.name: VoiceInput
parts.description: A pill for dictation with three states: tap to talk, listening with waveform, clock and transcript, and transcribing.

parts.name: Record button
parts.description: A round button named "Start recording" or "Stop recording". It calls `onStart` and `onStop`.

parts.name: Waveform and transcript
parts.description: Shown while listening. The bars are decorative; the transcript is a polite live region.

parts.name: Status text
parts.description: "Tap to talk" with a hint, or "Transcribing…" with the length of audio in seconds. The elapsed clock shows while listening.

items.text: Use a Voice Input when speaking is an option next to typing. For typed prompts, use Prompt Input.
Control it with `state` and do the recording in your code. The component only shows state; it never opens the microphone.
Feed `transcript` while listening and `seconds` from a measured timer. The live region reads the transcript, so people who cannot see the bars still follow along.
Replace the default `hint` with your product's own line. The built-in text names an assistant.
Don't send the transcript without letting the person read it. Put the text into the prompt box after `transcribing`.

components.title: Artifact Panel
components.description: The side panel for what the agent made — code or a document — with versions, copy and download.

props.name: code
props.description: Renders the code view with line numbers. Omit and pass `children` for a document.

components.example: <ArtifactPanel title="tabs.tsx" versions={["v1", "v2", "v3"]} version={v} onVersionChange={setV} code={source} onCopy={copy} onClose={close} />

parts.name: ArtifactPanel
parts.description: The side panel for what the agent made, code or a document. A `section` with a header and a body.

parts.name: Header
parts.description: Title, optional `meta` line, version switch and the Copy, Download and Close buttons.

parts.name: Version switch
parts.description: A segmented control that appears from two `versions`. It starts on the last version and keeps its own selection unless you pass `version`.

parts.name: Code view
parts.description: Shown when `code` is set: numbered lines in a scrollable `pre` that takes keyboard focus for the arrow keys.

parts.name: Document view
parts.description: Shown when `code` is omitted: `children` as padded body text.

items.text: Use ArtifactPanel for what the agent made, shown beside the chat: code or a document with versions, copy, download and close. For a change to a file use Diff View; for a snippet inside a message use Code Block.
Pass `code` for code and `children` for a document. When both are given, `code` wins.
List `versions` oldest first. The panel opens on the last one, and the switch only appears with two or more.
Pass `onCopy`, `onDownload` and `onClose` only for actions that exist. Each button renders only when its handler is given.
Don't use the panel for the transcript of tool calls. It shows a result; steps and tool output belong in a run timeline or terminal output.
Don't turn model output into markup. `code` renders as text in a `code` element, and `children` should be text too.

components.title: Source List
components.description: Numbered sources pinned to a chat; citations like [1] in answers point here.
components.example: <SourceList sources={[{ title: "Tabs pattern — WAI-ARIA", meta: "w3.org · web page", kind: "web" }]} />

parts.name: SourceList
parts.description: A card with the numbered sources of an answer: kind icon, title, meta line and an optional link, with a count of pinned items.

parts.name: Header
parts.description: The title ("Sources" by default) and the count of pinned items.

parts.name: Source row
parts.description: The number, a kind icon for web, file, doc or channel, the title and the meta. With `href` the row is a link to a new tab.

items.text: Use a Source List for the references behind an answer. For the results of one search call, use Search Result Card.
Keep the order stable. Citations such as [1] in the answer point to the same number here, so renumbering breaks them.
Pass `id` and link citations to `#id-1`. Each row gets the id `${id}-${n}`, so an anchor can jump to it.
Set `kind` and a `meta` line such as the host or file path. The icon and the line tell the person what they open before they click.
Don't add a source the agent did not use. The list reads as proof, so unused entries make the answer look better than it is.

components.title: Agent Avatar
components.description: Who is talking in a multi-agent chat: tint colour, name and role.
components.example: <AgentAvatar name="Planner" role="Breaks the task into steps" initials="PL" color="indigo" />

parts.name: AgentAvatar
parts.description: Who is speaking in a multi-agent chat: a tinted avatar with the agent's initials, its name and an optional role underneath.

items.text: Use AgentAvatar to say which agent speaks in a multi-agent chat: tint, name and role. For a single assistant or a person, a plain Avatar is enough. To mark the change of speaker, add a Handoff Divider.
Give each agent its own `color` and keep it for the whole conversation, so people learn who is who from the tint.
Add a short `role` such as `Researcher` or `Reviewer`. It renders under the name and tells people what the agent is responsible for.
Pass the two-letter `initials` yourself. The avatar shows them as given and does not derive them from `name`.
Don't reuse a tint for two agents in one conversation. Name and role always render, but the tint is what people scan first.

components.title: Handoff Divider
components.description: Marks the moment one agent passes the conversation to another.

parts.name: HandoffDivider
parts.description: A separator with the text "{from} handed off to {to}" between two hairlines, marking the turn where one agent passes the conversation on.

parts.name: Handoff label
parts.description: The centred text with the lightning icon. `from` and `to` are the only content, so pass short agent names.

items.text: Use a Handoff Divider in a multi-agent chat at the point where the speaker changes. To show who speaks, use an avatar with name and role on the message itself.
Pass the same agent names that the messages show, such as `Planner` and `Reviewer`, so the label reads as a sentence: "Planner handed off to Reviewer".
Place one divider per handoff, between the last message of the first agent and the first message of the next. The divider already has `role="separator"`.
Don't put long text or a reason into `from` or `to`. The label is one line between two hairlines; put the reason in a message.
Don't use it as a general section break. It always reads "handed off to", so it only fits a change between agents.

components.title: Alert
components.description: An inline banner in 5 colors and 2 sizes, with an optional close button and action.

props.name: icon
props.description: Replaces the leading icon (default: a check circle, a warning triangle for negative and warning). `null` hides it.

parts.name: Alert
parts.description: The banner. It renders with `role="alert"`, picks its icon from the `variant`, and shows a close button only when you pass `onClose`.

parts.name: Icon
parts.description: The leading icon: a check circle, or a warning triangle for `negative` and `warning`. Replace it with `icon`, hide it with `icon={null}`.

parts.name: AlertTitle
parts.description: The bold first line. In the `small` size it stays on one line and truncates only when the banner is very narrow.

parts.name: AlertDescription
parts.description: The message text. In the `small` size it takes the remaining width of the line and truncates; in `large` it wraps under the title.

parts.name: Close button
parts.description: A `<button>` labelled `Dismiss` that calls `onClose`. It is rendered only when `onClose` is set.

items.text: Use an Alert for a message that stays on the page until the cause is gone: a failed payment, a limit reached, a read-only workspace. For feedback on a finished action, use a toast.

Pick the `variant` by meaning: `negative` for what blocks the user, `warning` for what needs attention soon, `positive` for a confirmed state, `primary` for neutral news. `plain` is for notes without urgency.
Put the next step in the text or as one action button inside `Alert`: `Update payment method`. An alert that only states a problem leaves the user to find the fix.
Use `size="small"` for a one-line notice with a short title and description. Longer text belongs in `large`, where it wraps instead of truncating.
Don't pass `onClose` on an alert that reports a blocking problem. A dismissed error leaves the page looking healthy while the cause is still there.
Don't rely on the colour alone. The title or description has to say what is wrong, since the variants differ only by tint and icon.

components.title: Toast
components.description: A temporary notification that appears in the corner of the screen, with success/error/warning/info types.

props.name: position
props.description: Corner the stack lives in.

props.name: limit
props.description: The maximum number of toasts that can be displayed at once. When the limit is exceeded, the oldest toasts are marked as `limited` (via the `data-limited` attribute) rather than removed, so they can be hidden or animated out.

props.name: timeout
props.description: The default amount of time (in ms) before a toast is auto dismissed. A value of `0` will prevent the toast from being dismissed automatically.

props.name: toastManager
props.description: A global manager for toasts to use outside of a React component.

props.name: className
props.description: CSS class applied to the element, or a function that returns a class based on the component's state.

props.name: render
props.description: Allows you to replace the component's HTML element with a different tag, or compose it with another component. Accepts a `ReactElement` or a function that returns the element to render.

props.name: style
props.description: Style applied to the element, or a function that returns a style object based on the component's state.

parts.name: Toaster
parts.description: The one-line setup: it wraps your app in a provider, renders the viewport and draws every toast. `position` picks the corner.

parts.name: ToastProvider
parts.description: The provider on its own, with a default `timeout` of 5000 ms. Toaster already includes it.

parts.name: ToastViewport
parts.description: The fixed container in the top-right or bottom-right corner that holds the stack. Toaster already renders it.

parts.name: Toast
parts.description: One notification. Older toasts sit smaller and fainter behind the newest, and hovering the viewport spreads the stack into a list.

parts.name: Content
parts.description: The row inside a toast: the type dot, the text block and the close button.

parts.name: Title
parts.description: The bold line that names the outcome, such as `Changes saved`. Set it with `title` in `add`.

parts.name: Description
parts.description: A secondary line, drawn only when `description` is passed to `add`.

parts.name: Action
parts.description: An inline text link such as `Undo`, drawn only when `actionProps` is passed to `add`.

parts.name: Close button
parts.description: A button labelled `Close` that dismisses the toast. It can be reached with Tab; toasts never take focus themselves.

items.text: Use a toast for short feedback on an action the user took: saved, copied, sent. For a message that has to stay until the cause is fixed, use an Alert.
Mount `Toaster` once around the app and call `useToast().add({ title, type })` anywhere below it. `useToast` only works inside the provider.
Name the outcome in `title` and set `type` (`success`, `error`, `warning`, `info`) to match. Add `actionProps` with `Undo` when the action can be reversed.

Don’t make a toast the only place an error appears. It disappears by itself after 5000 ms and never takes focus, so anyone looking elsewhere will not see it. Keep the message where the user is working, for example in an inline alert.
Don't fire several toasts for one action. The stack shows four at most; older ones fade out.

components.title: Pull to Refresh
components.description: Drag down from the top of any content past a threshold to trigger an async refresh, with a rotating spinner and a rubber-band release.
components.props: function PullToRefresh({ onRefresh, threshold, maxPull, children, className, }: PullToRefreshProps): React.JSX.Element;

parts.name: PullToRefresh
parts.description: Wraps your content and turns a downward drag from the top into a refresh. The pull starts only when everything above is scrolled to the top.

parts.name: Indicator
parts.description: The spinner above the content. It fades and rotates while you pull, then spins until `onRefresh` resolves.

items.text: Use PullToRefresh for a touch-first list or feed that the user reloads by hand. For data that updates itself, show the new state and skip the gesture.
Return the promise from `onRefresh`. The spinner and the lock stay until it settles, also when it fails, so a slow request never looks finished.
Keep `threshold` at or below `maxPull` (defaults 70 and 110). The pull moves at half the finger speed, so the user drags about twice the threshold.
Don't make the gesture the only way to refresh. It is pointer-based with no keyboard route, so give keyboard and screen reader users a visible `Refresh` button.
Don't expect a tap to work right after a pull. The click that ends a drag is swallowed on purpose, so the item under the finger is not opened.

components.title: Rating
components.description: An interactive star rating input.

props.name: aria-label
props.description: Names the group ("Rating" by default); read-only, it replaces "Rated 3.5 out of 5".

props.name: aria-labelledby
props.description: Id of a visible label that names the group, instead of `aria-label`.

parts.name: Rating
parts.description: The group of options. Interactive it is a `radiogroup` with one Tab stop; with `readOnly` it is a single image that reads `Rated 3.5 out of 5`.

parts.name: RatingCell
parts.description: A read-only star row with the value on the right, made for table cells. Takes `value` and `max`.

items.text: Use Rating to collect or show a score: stars or hearts for opinions, emojis for sentiment, `scale` for a 0 to 10 survey answer. In a table column, use `RatingCell`.
Name the group with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`, for example `Rate this article`. The default name is only `Rating`.
Set `readOnly` when you display an average. A fractional `value` such as 3.5 fills rounded stars and keeps the exact number in the accessible name.
Turn on `label="right"` when the number matters. Without it, a score of 4.5 is only a row of icons.
Don't expect hover to select. It previews the fill, but only a click or an arrow key calls `onValueChange`; arrows move and select in one step.
Don't use the `emojis` type for a required answer. Clicking the chosen face again clears it and sends `0`.

components.title: Number Value
components.description: A large number with its change beside it: caret up or down, green or red.

parts.name: NumberValue
parts.description: A bold 24 px figure with an optional change beside it. The caret and the label appear only when both `delta` and `trend` are set.

items.text: Use NumberValue for one headline figure with its change, inside your own layout. For a pill that shows only a percentage change, use a trend chip.
Pass `value` as a finished string with its unit: `$48,200`, `1,284 users`. The component does not format numbers, so the unit has to come with it.

Set `trendGood={false}` when the change is bad, and keep `trend` for the caret direction. Colour follows `trendGood`, direction follows `trend`: a falling churn rate is `trend="down"` with the default `trendGood`.
Give `delta` its sign and unit: `+4.2%`. The caret is decorative (`aria-hidden`), so the text must carry the direction.
Don't pass `delta` without `trend`. The change is hidden unless both are set.

components.title: Trend Chip
components.description: A small pill showing a change, up or down, in seven icon styles.

props.name: direction
props.description: Figma Trend Chip · Trend; `flat` is the old name for `neutral`.

props.name: icon
props.description: Figma Trend Chip · Icon; the same glyph turns for `down`.

parts.name: TrendChip
parts.description: The pill. `direction` colours it green, red or neutral grey, and `icon` chooses which of seven glyphs shows the direction.

parts.name: TrendCaret
parts.description: The filled triangle used by the `triangle` icon and by the change label of a number value. It is decorative and hidden from screen readers.

items.text: Use a TrendChip for a percentage change next to a figure: in a table cell, a card header, a list row. For the figure and its change as one unit, use a number value.
Write the sign and unit into `value`: `+12.4%`, `-3 pts`. The glyph is `aria-hidden`, so the text is the only thing a screen reader gets.
Choose one `icon` style per screen and keep it. The chip's padding adapts to the glyph, so mixed styles in a column do not line up.
Don't use `direction` to mean good or bad. `up` is always green and `down` always red, so a falling error rate shows red. Show such a metric with a number value and `trendGood`.
Don't use `direction="flat"` in new code. It is the old name for `neutral`.

components.title: Pressable Feedback
components.description: Wraps any content with a scale-down press animation.

props.name: asChild
props.description: Apply the press effect to the child element instead of wrapping it.

parts.name: PressableFeedback
parts.description: Scales its content down to 95% while pressed. Alone it renders a `<button>`; with `asChild` it lends the effect to its single child.

items.text: Use PressableFeedback to give press feedback to something that is not a button yet, such as a card or a tile. Buttons and icon buttons already react to a press.
Pass `asChild` when the child is already a button or a link. Without it you nest a `<button>` inside a `<button>`, which is invalid HTML.
Handle the action with `onPress`. With `asChild` the child's own `onClick` still runs first, then `onPress`.
Don't put links or other buttons inside it without `asChild`. The content then sits inside a `<button>`, so nested interactive elements break.

components.title: Emoji Reaction Button
components.description: A toggleable emoji reaction with a count, like a Slack reaction.

parts.name: EmojiReactionButton
parts.description: A pill `<button>` with an emoji and its count. `active` marks your own reaction and is exposed as `aria-pressed`; `onToggle` fires on every click.

items.text: Use EmojiReactionButton for one reaction under a message or comment, with its count. To let the user add a new reaction, offer an emoji picker next to the row.
Update `count` and `active` together in `onToggle`. The component keeps no state, so toggling without changing `active` leaves the pill unchanged.
Set `active` for the reactions the current user made, so the tint and `aria-pressed` show which ones they can take back.
Don't keep a reaction with a count of 0 in the row. Remove it until someone reacts again.

components.title: Emoji Picker
components.description: A grid of selectable emoji, typically shown inside a Popover.

parts.name: EmojiPicker
parts.description: A six-column grid of emoji buttons in a `role="group"` named `Emoji`. Each button's name is its emoji, and `onSelect` receives the one clicked.

items.text: Use EmojiPicker for a short, curated set of emoji to react or label with. It shows only the emojis you pass, so it is not a searchable emoji keyboard.
Place it inside a popover that opens from an icon button, and close the popover in `onSelect`. The picker has its own card styling and does not close anything itself.
Pass a short `emojis` array in a fixed order, 12 by default. The grid has six columns, so multiples of six fill the rows.
Don't use an emoji as the only information in a control. The buttons are named by the emoji alone, so keep visible text where the meaning matters.

parts.name: Sheet
parts.description: Holds the open state and links trigger, panel and close buttons. Renders nothing itself.

parts.name: SheetClose
parts.description: Closes the sheet. Wrap a Cancel or Done button in it.

parts.name: SheetContent
parts.description: The panel. It brings its own portal and backdrop, slides in from `side` (`right` by default) and shows a close button unless `showCloseButton={false}`.

parts.name: SheetDescription
parts.description: One or two sentences on what the sheet is for, read out after the title.

parts.name: SheetHeader
parts.description: Stacks the title and the description at the top of the panel.

parts.name: SheetTitle
parts.description: Names the sheet; screen readers announce it when the sheet opens.

parts.name: SheetTrigger
parts.description: The element that opens the sheet. Focus returns to it when the sheet closes.

items.text: Use a Sheet for detail views, edit forms and filters that should keep the page visible behind them. For a short decision, use a Dialog. For a confirmation with consequences, use an Alert Dialog.
Always include a `SheetTitle`, also when the design shows none. It is the only name the sheet has for screen readers.
Choose `side="bottom"` for phones and `right` for desktop detail views. The bottom sheet is capped at 80vh, the side sheets at `max-w-sm`.
Put a primary action and a `Cancel` button inside the content, the Cancel wrapped in `SheetClose`. The corner × alone is easy to miss on a form.
Don't set `showCloseButton={false}` without another way out. Add a `SheetClose` button, since Escape is the only other route for keyboard users.

components.title: Resizable
components.description: A two-pane layout with a draggable divider between them.

props.name: handleLabel
props.description: Accessible name of the handle, e.g. "Resize sidebar".

parts.name: Resizable
parts.description: Two panels split by a draggable handle. `side` picks the panel that has the pixel size (`defaultSize`, between `min` and `max`); the other takes the rest.

parts.name: Panel
parts.description: One of the two children. The sized panel has a fixed width or height, the other one fills the remaining space; both scroll on their own.

parts.name: Handle
parts.description: The divider. It is a focusable `separator`: arrow keys move it by 16 px (64 with Shift), Home and End jump to the limits.

items.text: Use Resizable when the user decides how much room a side panel gets: a file tree next to an editor, a list next to a detail view. For a fixed split, plain layout is simpler.
Pass exactly two children. The first is the start panel (left or top) and the second is the end panel, and the `side` prop says which one has the set size.
Set `handleLabel` to name the panel, such as `Resize sidebar`. The default `Resize panels` does not say which split it moves.
Persist the size from `onSizeChange` if it should survive a reload. The component keeps its size in memory and starts from `defaultSize` again.
Don't expect `min` and `max` to beat the container. The size is also capped to leave 48 px for the other panel, so a large `min` is ignored.

parts.name: ScrollArea
parts.description: A scrolling region with a styled scrollbar. Give it a fixed height or width; it adds the viewport, content wrapper, vertical bar and corner.

parts.name: Viewport
parts.description: The element that scrolls. It shows a focus ring when focused, follows the root's corner radius and stops scroll chaining with `overscroll-contain`.

parts.name: Content
parts.description: The wrapper around your children. It grows with them and is measured to size the thumb.

parts.name: ScrollBar
parts.description: The scrollbar track, vertical by default. The root renders one for you; `orientation` switches a bar to horizontal.

parts.name: Thumb
parts.description: The draggable handle inside the scrollbar. Its length shows how much of the content is visible.

items.text: Use a ScrollArea for a panel with its own scrolling inside a fixed layout, when the scrollbar must look the same on every platform: a long list in a popover, a log, a side panel. For ordinary overflow, `overflow-y-auto` is enough.
Give the root a height, such as `h-72`. The viewport fills the root, so without a bounded size the content only grows and nothing scrolls.
Put the border and radius on the root. The viewport inherits the radius, so the content is clipped at the rounded corners.
Don't nest scroll areas in each other. Two scrolling regions compete for the wheel and the keyboard, so cut the inner one down to a plain list.
Don't expect sideways scrolling out of the box. The root renders only the vertical bar.
