props.description: Text link on the trailing edge (Figma Action=link).

components.example:
<PageHeader
  title="Audit log"
  description="Every security event in your workspace, newest first."
  actions={
    <>
      <Button variant="plain" size="sm">Export</Button>
      <Button variant="primary" size="sm">New rule</Button>
    </>
  }
/>

<PageHeader level="section" title="Recent orders" description="Last 5 transactions" link="View all" href="/orders" />

parts.name: PageHeader
parts.description: The title of a page or section with an optional description and, on the trailing edge, `actions` or a text `link`.

items.text: Use Page Header at the top of an app page or above a section. For the title of a sign-in form, use Auth Heading.
Keep `level="page"` (an `h1`) once per view and use `level="section"` (an `h2`) for sections below it.
Put at most one primary button in `actions`; other actions stay plain. Use `link` for a single text action such as `View all`.
Don't use `level="page"` for a section title. It renders a second `h1` and a display-size title.

components.title: Keyboard Hint
components.description: One or more key caps with a short label, for the shortcut legend at the bottom of a command menu.
components.example:
<KeyboardHint keys={["↑", "↓"]} label="Navigate" />
<KeyboardHint keys={["↵"]} label="Open" />
<KeyboardHint keys={["esc"]} label="Close" />

parts.name: KeyboardHint
parts.description: A row of key caps followed by a short label, for example the arrow keys and `to navigate`.

items.text: Use Keyboard Hint in the footer of a palette or search overlay to explain keys. For a single shortcut inside a sentence, use Kbd.
Pass one entry per key in `keys` (`["↑", "↓"]`) and describe the action in `label`, starting with `to`.
Show only the keys that work in the current view.
Don't put a combined shortcut in one string such as `Ctrl+K`. Each entry becomes one key cap, so split it into `["Ctrl", "K"]`.

components.title: Command Item Row
components.description: One row in a command menu: an icon, a label, optional context and its shortcut keys.
components.props: function CommandItemRow({ icon, label, meta, keys, active, onSelect, className }: CommandItemRowProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: keys
props.description: Shortcut keys → rendered as key caps. Omit to show a chevron instead.

props.name: meta
props.description: Secondary label after the title (Figma "Project").

parts.name: CommandItemRow
parts.description: One selectable row of a command palette, with an icon, a label, optional `meta` and either shortcut keys or a chevron.

items.text: Use Command Item Row for actions and destinations in a command palette. For search hits with a description and a link, use Search Result.
Set `active` on the highlighted row from your own arrow-key handling. The row is a button with a hover state but does not move a selection itself.
Pass `keys` for rows that have a shortcut (`["G", "I"]`). Omit it for rows that open a deeper level, which then show a chevron.
Don't put the shortcut in `label` or `meta`. `keys` renders real key caps and keeps the label short enough to truncate cleanly.

components.title: Search Result
components.description: A search hit with an icon, a title, a short excerpt and where it lives.
components.props: function SearchResult({ icon, title, description, meta, href, onSelect, className }: SearchResultProps): React.JSX.Element;
components.example:
<SearchResult
  icon={<FileText />}
  title="Onboarding checklist"
  description="Five steps every new teammate completes in their first week."
  meta="Docs · Updated 2 days ago"
  href="/docs/onboarding"
/>

parts.name: SearchResult
parts.description: One hit of a search page: an icon tile, title, a description limited to two lines, a meta line and a chevron.

items.text: Use Search Result in a results list with descriptions. For actions in a command palette, use Command Item Row.
Pass `href` for results that go to a page. Without `href` the row acts as a button, and the click never jumps to `#`.
Keep `description` to a sentence or two, and use `meta` for path, date or type.
Don't rely on the default icon for every kind of result. Pass an `icon` that tells types apart.

components.title: Notification Item
components.description: One entry in a notification list, with an avatar or icon, the message, optional actions and an unread dot.
components.props: function NotificationItem({ icon, avatar, children, quote, actions, time, unread, onClick, className }: NotificationItemProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: children
props.description: Message; wrap the actor in <strong> for emphasis.

props.name: avatar
props.type: { src?: string; initials?: string; color?: AvatarColor }

props.name: icon
props.description: Icon in a round muted box (Type=icon). Ignored when an avatar is given.

props.name: quote
props.description: Quoted excerpt (Type=avatar quote).

components.example: markRead(id)} > Sarah Lindqvist commented on Q3 roadmap } > Lucas Meyer invited you to WunderUI Design } time="Yesterday"> Deploy finished for main in 42 seconds

parts.name: NotificationItem
parts.description: One entry of a notification list: icon or avatar, message, optional quote and actions, the time and an unread marker.

items.text: Use Notification Item in the notification centre or a popover list. For a history of changes on one object, use Timeline Event.
Wrap the actor in `<strong>` inside `children`. The row styles it, in the unread tint as well.
Set `unread` for new entries: the row is tinted and shows a dot with the label `Unread`.
Don't pass `icon` together with `avatar`. The icon is ignored when an avatar is set.

components.title: Checklist Task
components.description: One step of an onboarding checklist that can be ticked off, with the next step to do highlighted.

props.name: action
props.description: A button shown on the current step, e.g. "Start".

props.name: current
props.description: The step to do next — tinted, with room for `meta` and an `action`.

props.name: onClick
props.description: Toggle the step.

components.example:
• toggle("profile")}>Complete your profile
  • Start} onClick={() => toggle("invite")} > Invite your team
  • toggle("project")}>Create your first project

parts.name: ChecklistTask
parts.description: One step of an onboarding checklist in one of three states: `done`, `current` (tinted, with `meta` and an `action`) or open.

items.text: Use Checklist Task for the steps of an onboarding or setup checklist. For a plain list of items without a next step, use Checkbox Field.
Mark exactly one step `current` and give it an `action` such as `Start`. Only the current step shows the action; its circle becomes its own checkbox button labelled `Mark as done`.
Handle `onClick` as a toggle: it fires for done and open steps alike, so a step can be ticked and unticked again.
Don't pass `action` to steps that are not `current`. It is not rendered there.

components.title: Project Card
components.description: A clickable project tile with a colored cover, a name and a short line of detail.
components.example:
<ProjectCard
  name="Website redesign"
  meta="Edited 2 hours ago"
  color="indigo"
  cover={<LayoutDashboard className="size-8" />}
  onClick={() => openProject("website")}
/>

parts.name: ProjectCard
parts.description: A button tile with a tinted cover area, the project name and a meta line.

items.text: Use Project Card for projects or workspaces in a grid. For files with previews and selection, use File Card.
Pick `color` from the tint set to tell projects apart, and put an icon or image in `cover`.
Pass `onClick`; the whole card is the button.
Don't put buttons or links in `cover`. The whole card is a `<button>`, and nested controls are invalid.

components.title: File Card
components.description: A file tile with a preview, a name and details, plus optional selection, a menu and a deleted state.
components.props: function FileCard({ name, meta, icon, color, thumbnail, selected, onSelectedChange, deletedAt, onMenu, onOpen, className }: FileCardProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: deletedAt
props.description: Type=trash — deletion line shown in red, no menu/checkbox.

props.name: thumbnail
props.description: Image preview instead of the icon tile.

parts.name: FileCard
parts.description: A tile for a file or folder with a preview area, name and meta line. Optional checkbox, open area and menu button sit on or beside the preview.

items.text: Use File Card in a grid of files and folders. For a flat list with columns, use Table. For projects with a cover, use Project Card.
Pass `onOpen` so the preview becomes a real button. The checkbox sits next to it, not inside, so no control is nested in another.
Pass `onSelectedChange` for bulk selection: the checkbox shows on hover and focus, and stays visible once `selected` is true.
Don't set `onMenu` on a trashed file and expect a menu. With `deletedAt` the card shows the deletion line in the error colour and hides the menu button.

components.title: Status Bar
components.description: The phone status bar with the time, for the top of a mobile screen mockup.
components.example: {/* screen content */}

parts.name: StatusBar
parts.description: A decorative phone status bar with a time and a device icon, for mobile frames in mockups.

items.text: Use Status Bar at the top of phone frames in previews and documentation. A real app doesn't need it: the device draws its own.
Pass `time` as a string to match the screenshot; the default is `9:41`.
Place it above the screen content, inside the phone frame.
Don't ship it in a production screen. It shows no battery or network state.

components.title: Tab Item
components.description: A single underlined tab that shows a count while it is active, used inside a Tab Bar.
components.props: function TabItem({ active, count, children, onClick, className, ...props }: TabItemProps): React.JSX.Element;
components.example:
const [tab, setTab] = useState("All")

<TabBar>
  <TabItem active={tab === "All"} count={24} onClick={() => setTab("All")}>All</TabItem>
  <TabItem active={tab === "Unread"} count={3} onClick={() => setTab("Unread")}>Unread</TabItem>
  <TabItem active={tab === "Mentions"} count={5} onClick={() => setTab("Mentions")}>Mentions</TabItem>
</TabBar>

parts.name: TabItem
parts.description: One underline tab. The active tab is coloured, has `aria-selected`, and shows a `count` badge when one is given.

items.text: Use Tab Item inside a Tab Bar. For tabs with content panels, use Tabs.
Set `active` on the tab that matches the open view.
Use `count` for items in a view, such as unread messages. It shows only on the active tab.
Don't use tabs for actions. A tab switches a view and does not run a command.

components.title: Tab Bar
components.description: A horizontal row of underlined tabs on a bottom border that scrolls sideways when space runs out.

parts.name: TabBar
parts.description: The tab list of the underline tabs. One tab stop, arrow keys move and activate, Home and End jump, and it scrolls sideways when tabs don't fit.

items.text: Use Tab Bar with Tab Item for the underline tabs in blocks such as inboxes and tables. In your own screens, Tabs is the full component with panels.
Give the bar an `aria-label` that names what it switches.
Link each Tab Item to its panel with `id` and `aria-controls`, and set `aria-labelledby` on the panel.
Don't put non-tab elements in it. It has the role `tablist` and arrow keys move between tabs.

components.title: Timeline Event
components.description: One entry in an activity feed or history, with an avatar or status dot and a line to the next entry.
components.props: function TimelineEvent({ avatar, status, title, time, object, badge, badgeColor, meta, children, last, className }: TimelineEventProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: avatar
props.type: { src?: string; initials?: string; color?: AvatarColor }
props.description: Actor avatar (Type=event).

props.name: badge
props.description: Trailing badge/label on the title row (Type=step).

props.name: children
props.description: Extra content below the title (comment excerpt, reactions, attachments …).

props.name: last
props.description: Draw the connector line to the next entry.

props.name: object
props.description: Small object chip under the title (Type=event) — e.g. project name.

props.name: status
props.description: Status dot (Type=step): tone + icon.

components.example:
Alina Lorenz created a project} time="9:12" object={{ label: "Checkout redesign" }} /> Lucas Meyer commented} time="10:30">

Looks great. Can we ship the new cart before Friday?

 }} title="Merged into main" badge="v2.4.0" badgeColor="green" meta="Sep 17, 2026 · 14:25" last />

parts.name: TimelineEvent
parts.description: One entry of an activity feed: an avatar or a status dot on the left, a line down to the next entry, and the text on the right.

parts.name: Avatar or status
parts.description: An Avatar from `avatar`, or a round status mark from `status` with a tone and an icon, a check by default.

parts.name: Connector line
parts.description: The line to the next entry. It turns green under a `success` status and is left out when `last` is set.

parts.name: Title row
parts.description: The `title` with `time` or a `badge` on the right. Text in `<strong>` stands out from the rest of the sentence.

parts.name: Object chip
parts.description: A small chip under the title from `object`, naming what the event concerns, with a folder icon by default.

items.text: Use a Timeline Event for one rich entry in an activity feed: who did what, to which object, with a comment or attachment below. For a simple sequence drawn from data, use a Timeline.
Write the title as a sentence and wrap the names in ``: `Alina Lorenz moved Q4 report to Done`.
Name the person in the title. The avatar image is decorative and has an empty `alt`, so the title is all screen readers get.
Don't leave `last` off the final entry. Without it the connector line runs on into empty space below the feed.

components.title: Price
components.description: A price with an optional billing period, a crossed-out old price and a savings badge.
components.props: function Price({ amount, period, compareAt, badge, size, className }: PriceProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: badge
props.description: Savings badge, e.g. "Save 19%".

props.name: compareAt
props.description: Compare-at (struck through) for sale prices.

props.name: period
props.description: Billing period for plan prices, e.g. "/ month".

components.example:
<Price amount="$39" period="/ seat / month" size="lg" />
<Price amount="$489" compareAt="$599" badge="Save 18%" size="md" />
<Price amount="$24.00" size="sm" />

parts.name: Price
parts.description: A price with optional billing `period`, struck-through `compareAt` and a savings `badge`.

items.text: Use Price for plan prices, sale prices and product prices. Don't build price text by hand in cards.
Pass `period` (`/ month`) for plans. The size then defaults to `lg`; without a period it defaults to `sm`.
For a sale, pass `compareAt` for the old price and `badge` for the saving, such as `Save 19%`.
Don't rely on the default size inside a dense list. Set `size` explicitly so a plan card and a product row stay aligned.

components.title: Text Link Row
components.description: A line of text followed by a link, like “Don't have an account? Sign up”, or a back link with an arrow.
components.props: function TextLinkRow({ text, link, href, onLinkClick, variant, className, }: TextLinkRowProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: text
props.description: Leading copy, e.g. "Don't have an account?"

props.name: link
props.description: Link label, e.g. "Sign up". Omitted for Type=back.

props.name: variant
props.description: inline (14px) · small (12px) · stacked (two lines, centered) · icon (help icon + small) · back (arrow, no link)

components.example:
<TextLinkRow text="Don't have an account?" link="Sign up" href="/sign-up" />
<TextLinkRow variant="small" text="Didn't get the email?" link="Resend" />
<TextLinkRow variant="icon" text="Need help?" link="Contact support" />
<TextLinkRow variant="back" text="Use a different method" href="/sign-in" />

parts.name: TextLinkRow
parts.description: A line of text with a link, such as `Already have an account? Sign in`. `variant` picks inline, small, stacked, icon or back.

items.text: Use Text Link Row below auth forms to move to the other form. For a back link, use `variant="back"`.
Write `text` as the question and `link` as the action (`Sign up`).
Use `small` or `icon` for secondary help lines (`icon` adds a help icon) and `stacked` for two centred lines.
Don't pass `link` with `variant="back"`. The back variant shows an arrow and `text` only.

components.title: Social Sign In Buttons
components.description: Sign-in buttons for Google, Apple, GitHub and Microsoft, side by side or stacked.
components.props: function SocialSignInButtons({ providers, layout, prefix, onSelect, className, }: SocialSignInButtonsProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: layout
props.description: horizontal = one row, vertical = stacked full-width buttons

props.name: prefix
props.description: "Continue with" / "Sign in with" prefix; pass "" for icon + name only.

components.example:
<SocialSignInButtons
  providers={["google", "apple", "github"]}
  layout="vertical"
  onSelect={(provider) => signIn(provider)}
/>

{/* Icon and name only */}
<SocialSignInButtons providers={["google", "github"]} prefix="" />

parts.name: SocialSignInButtons
parts.description: Provider buttons for Google, Apple, GitHub or Microsoft. `layout` sets one row or a stack; each press calls `onSelect` with the provider.

items.text: Use Social Sign In Buttons above or below the email form on sign-in and sign-up. For the email submit, use a Button.
Pass only the `providers` you have wired. The default is Google and GitHub.
Keep the `prefix` the same on sign-in and sign-up (`Continue with`), or pass `""` for logo and name only.
Don't turn them into the primary action. They are plain buttons, so the email submit stays the only primary one.

components.title: Option Row
components.description: A selectable card with a radio button or checkbox, a title and a short description.
components.props: function OptionRow({ title, description, icon, badge, badgeColor, selected, variant, value, disabled, onSelect, href, className, }: OptionRowProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: badge
props.description: Small badge next to the title, e.g. "Recommended"

props.name: icon
props.description: Leading icon (rendered in a 36px box for variant="icon")

props.name: value
props.description: Required for radio/checkbox variants — the RadioGroupItem / Checkbox value.

props.name: variant
props.description: radio (default) · checkbox · link (chevron, no control) · icon (icon box + trailing radio)

components.example:
const [picked, setPicked] = useState(["dashboards"])
const toggle = (id: string) =>
  setPicked((list) => (list.includes(id) ? list.filter((x) => x !== id) : [...list, id]))

<OptionRow
  variant="checkbox"
  value="dashboards"
  title="Dashboards"
  description="Analytics, admin panels and internal tools"
  selected={picked.includes("dashboards")}
  onSelect={() => toggle("dashboards")}
/>

parts.name: OptionRow
parts.description: A selectable card with a title, description and optional badge. `variant` picks `radio`, `checkbox`, `link` (chevron, no control) or `icon`.

items.text: Use Option Row to choose between a few described options, such as a verification method or a role. For on-off settings, use Settings Row.
Wrap the `radio` and `icon` variants in Option Row Group and give each row a unique `value`.
Set `selected` from the group's value (`selected={value === "email"}`). It only draws the tinted frame; the selection itself lives in the group.
Don't use `variant="link"` for a choice. It is a navigation row that renders a link and calls `onSelect` without storing a selection.

components.title: Option Row Group
components.description: Wraps radio Option Rows so that exactly one of them is selected.
components.example:
const [method, setMethod] = useState("app")

<OptionRowGroup value={method} onValueChange={setMethod}>
  <OptionRow variant="icon" value="app" icon={<ShieldCheck />} title="Authenticator app"
    description="Use a code from an app like 1Password" badge="Recommended" selected={method === "app"} />
  <OptionRow variant="icon" value="sms" icon={<Smartphone />} title="Text message"
    description="We send a code to your phone" selected={method === "sms"} />
  <OptionRow variant="icon" value="key" icon={<KeyRound />} title="Security key"
    description="Use a hardware key or passkey" selected={method === "key"} />
</OptionRowGroup>

parts.name: OptionRowGroup
parts.description: The radio group around Option Rows. It keeps one row selected and stacks them with a gap.

items.text: Use Option Row Group around radio-style Option Rows. For a group of plain radio buttons, use Radio Group.
Control it with `value` and `onValueChange`; the handler gets the `value` string of the chosen row.
Give every row inside a distinct `value`, and set each row's `selected` from the group value so the frames follow.
Don't put `checkbox` or `link` variants inside. They have no radio control and don't take part in the group.

components.title: User Info
components.description: An avatar with a name and a second line, for account menus, sidebars and quotes.
components.props: function UserInfo({ name, subtext, src, initials, color, variant, onMenu, className }: UserInfoProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: variant
props.description: person (42px avatar, 14px name) · sidebar (40px, 12px, padded) · menu (adds a ⋮ button)

components.example:
<UserInfo name="Sarah Lindqvist" subtext="Head of Product, WunderUI" src="/avatars/05.png" />
<UserInfo name="Alina Lorenz" subtext="Free plan" initials="AL" color="indigo" variant="sidebar" />
<UserInfo name="Lucas Meyer" subtext="lucas@initech.dev" src="/avatars/02.png" variant="menu" onMenu={openMenu} />

parts.name: UserInfo
parts.description: An avatar with a name and a secondary line. `variant` picks person, sidebar or menu (adds a button).

items.text: Use User Info for the signed-in account in a sidebar, a menu or an account chooser. For people in table rows, use Person Cell.
Pass `src` for a photo. Otherwise initials come from `name` unless `initials` is set, tinted with `color`.
Use `subtext` for the email or role.
Don't use `variant="menu"` without `onMenu`. The button would do nothing.

components.title: Password Requirement
components.description: One password rule in a checklist that turns green once the password meets it.

parts.name: PasswordRequirement
parts.description: One rule of a password policy as a `<li>`: a green check when `met`, an empty circle otherwise.

items.text: Use Password Requirement for a visible checklist of password rules below a new-password field. For a single strength rating, use Password Strength.
Render the items inside a `<ul>`; the component is a list item.
Compute `met` from the same rules your validation uses, so the checklist can't show a green check for a password that gets rejected.
Don't list rules you don't enforce. Show only the rules your validation checks.

components.title: Password Strength
components.description: A four-step meter with a label that shows how strong a password is.

parts.name: PasswordStrength
parts.description: A four-segment meter with a label. The level (`weak`, `fair`, `good`, `strong`) sets the filled segments and the colour; changes are announced politely.

items.text: Use Password Strength under a new-password field for quick feedback. For rule-by-rule feedback, use Password Requirement.
Derive `strength` with `getPasswordStrength(password)` and render the meter only when it returns a level. It returns `null` for an empty password.
Pass `label` to replace the default text, for example to localise it.
Don't treat the helper as your password policy. It scores length and character classes only, so enforce your real rules on the server.

components.title: OTP Code Input
components.description: Large boxes for typing a 4- or 6-digit verification code.
components.props: function OtpCodeInput({ length, value, onValueChange, onComplete, invalid, disabled, autoFocus, "aria-label": ariaLabel, className, }: OtpCodeInputProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: aria-label
props.description: Names the group for screen readers; each digit is announced as "Digit n of N".

components.example:
const [code, setCode] = useState("")

<OtpCodeInput length={6} value={code} onValueChange={setCode} onComplete={(value) => verify(value)} autoFocus />

parts.name: OtpCodeInput
parts.description: A one-time code field of four or six separate digit boxes. Each box is labelled `Digit n of N` for screen readers.

items.text: Use OTP Code Input to enter a code sent by email, SMS or an authenticator app. For other short text, use Input.
Submit from `onComplete`. It fires once all digits are filled, so the person doesn't need a separate confirm step.
Set `invalid` after a wrong code, and give the group a clear `aria-label` such as `Verification code` if the default `One-time code` doesn't fit.
Don't use any length but 4 or 6. `length` accepts only those two values.

components.title: Backup Code
components.description: A recovery code that copies itself when clicked and is crossed out once it has been used.
components.example: notify(`Copied ${code}`)} />

parts.name: BackupCode
parts.description: One recovery code as a button. A click copies the code to the clipboard; with `used` it is disabled and struck through.

items.text: Use Backup Code to list recovery codes after two-factor setup, in a grid with one code per button. For a single long value with a copy action, such as an invite URL, use Invite Link Row.
Set `used` on codes that were already redeemed, so the list shows which ones are left.
Confirm the copy in `onCopy`, for example with a toast. It fires only after the clipboard accepted the text.
Don't show your own "Copied" message on click. When the clipboard is blocked (iframe, http, permission denied), `onCopy` does not fire, and a message of your own would be wrong.

components.title: Invite Row
components.description: An email field and a role picker for inviting one person, with a button to remove the row.
components.props: function InviteRow({ email, role, roles, onEmailChange, onRoleChange, onRemove, stacked, className, }: InviteRowProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: stacked
props.description: Stack email over role on small screens (Figma Type=email role stacked).

parts.name: InviteRow
parts.description: One invitee: an email field, a role select and, when `onRemove` is set, a remove button. It is fully controlled.

items.text: Use Invite Row for each person in a team invite list, one row per invitee. For one shareable link instead, use Invite Link Row.
Keep it controlled: pass `email` and `role` with `onEmailChange` and `onRoleChange`. Without the handlers the fields do not change.

Pass your own `roles` when the defaults (`Admin`, `Editor`, `Viewer`) don't match the product. Use `stacked` in narrow containers; otherwise the select moves next to the field from the small breakpoint.
Don't pass `onRemove` to a row you must keep. The remove button only renders when the handler exists.

components.title: Invite Link Row
components.description: A read-only invite link with a copy button that confirms when the link is copied.

parts.name: InviteLinkRow
parts.description: A read-only field with the invite link and a button that copies it. The button reads `Copied` for a moment after a successful copy.

items.text: Use Invite Link Row when people join through a shareable link. To invite by email address and role, use Invite Row.
Use `onCopy` for side effects such as a toast or tracking. It fires only after the clipboard accepted the link.
Pass the full URL in `link`; the field is read-only and truncates long values.
Don't add your own copied state. The row already switches the button label and resets it, and it stays unchanged if the clipboard is blocked.

components.title: Settings Row
components.description: A setting's title and description with a switch, or any other control, on the right.
components.props: function SettingsRow({ title, description, control, checked, onCheckedChange, className }: SettingsRowProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: control
props.description: Trailing control: a Button, Switch, Badge … Pass `switch` props instead for the toggle variant.

parts.name: SettingsRow
parts.description: A setting with a title, a description and a trailing control, or a switch when `checked` or `onCheckedChange` is set.

items.text: Use Settings Row for lists of preferences. For choices between described options, use Option Row.
Pass `checked` and `onCheckedChange` for a switch. It is labelled by the title.
Pass a `control` (a Button, a Badge) for settings that open something or show a state.
Don't pass both a switch and `control`. When `checked` or `onCheckedChange` is set, `control` is ignored.

components.title: Inline Note
components.description: A small line of supporting text with an icon, either neutral or as a warning.
components.example:
<InlineNote>14-day free trial of Pro included. No credit card required.</InlineNote>
<InlineNote tone="warning">Billing stops immediately. Unused credit of $184.00 is not refunded.</InlineNote>
<InlineNote icon={<Bell />}>Links expire after 15 minutes and can only be used once.</InlineNote>

parts.name: InlineNote
parts.description: A small hint line with an icon. `tone="neutral"` shows a shield, `tone="warning"` a triangle in the warning colour.

items.text: Use Inline Note for a one-line reassurance or caution below a form or action, such as how a code is used. For a message that needs attention on its own, use Alert.
Use `tone="warning"` when the note states a consequence, and keep the neutral tone for reassurance.
Pass an `icon` only when the default does not fit; it is shown at a small fixed size.
Don't use it for a field error. Put that in the `error` of the field so it is announced with the input.

components.title: Auth Heading
components.description: The title and subtitle at the top of a sign-in, sign-up or onboarding form.

props.name: as
props.description: The heading element: h1 on an auth page, a lower level when the heading sits inside a larger page. Looks the same either way.

components.example:
<AuthHeading title="Create your workspace" subtitle="A workspace is where your team designs and ships together." />
<AuthHeading align="center" title="You're all set, Alina!" subtitle="Your workspace is ready. Here's what you've set up." />

parts.name: AuthHeading
parts.description: The title and optional subtitle at the top of an auth form. It renders an `h1` by default; `as` changes the heading level without changing the look.

items.text: Use Auth Heading at the top of sign-in, sign-up, verification and onboarding forms. For the title of an app page with actions, use Page Header.
Keep the default `h1` when the form is the whole page. Set `as="h2"` or `as="h3"` when the heading sits inside a larger page, so the document outline stays correct.
Write the title as the task (`Welcome back`) and put the reassurance or hint in `subtitle`. Use `align="center"` when the card content is centred.
Don't pick `as` to change the size. The look is the same for every level, so the choice is only about structure.

components.title: Avatar Stack
components.description: Overlapping avatars with a “+N” count for everyone past the limit.
components.example:
const team = [
  { name: "Alina Lorenz", src: "/avatars/01.png" },
  { name: "Lucas Meyer", src: "/avatars/02.png" },
  { name: "Jonas Berg", initials: "JB", color: "purple" },
  // …
]

<AvatarStack people={team} size="default" max={4} />

parts.name: AvatarStack
parts.description: Shows the first `max` people, three by default, as overlapping avatars, with a `+N` avatar for the rest.

parts.name: Person
parts.description: One entry of `people`: the photo from `src`, or initials from `initials` or `name`, tinted in `color`, indigo by default.

parts.name: Count
parts.description: A `+N` avatar of the same size, shown only when `people` holds more than `max`.

items.text: Use an Avatar Stack for a compact row of assignees or guests passed as data, such as on a task or a schedule row. To compose avatars by hand, with a hover effect, use Avatar Group.
Pass the full `people` list and let `max` cut it. The `+N` count is worked out from what is left over.
Give every person a `name`. It is the avatar's hover title and the source of the initials when there is no `src` or `initials`.
Don't place the stack on a tinted or muted background without checking it. The rings that separate the faces are drawn in the card colour, not in the colour behind.

components.title: Kanban Card Item
components.description: A task card for a Kanban board, with labels, due date, comments, checklist progress and assignees.
components.props: function KanbanCardItem({ title, labels, due, comments, checklist, assignees, selected, onClick, className }: KanbanCardProps): React.JSX.Element;
components.example:
<KanbanCardItem
  title="Redesign the onboarding checklist"
  labels={[
    { label: "Design", color: "purple" },
    { label: "High", color: "red" },
  ]}
  due="Oct 4"
  comments={6}
  checklist={{ done: 3, total: 5 }}
  assignees={team}
  selected={selected}
  onClick={() => setSelected((s) => !s)}
/>

parts.name: KanbanCardItem
parts.description: A card on a board with labels, a title, due date, comment and checklist counts and assignees. With `onClick` it becomes a keyboard-operable button.

parts.name: Avatar stack
parts.description: The assignees, three faces at most, with a `+N` count for the rest.

items.text: Use Kanban Card Item for work items in a board column, under a Column Header. For a record in a table on small screens, use Record Card.
Pass `onClick` to open the item. The card then gets `role="button"`, a tab stop and Enter and Space handling.
Send only the meta you have. `due`, `comments` and `checklist` each render only when set; `checklist` takes `{ done, total }`.
Don't add many long labels. Each label is a pill that wraps onto further lines and pushes the title down.

components.title: Column Header
components.description: The top of a Kanban column, with a colored dot, a card count and buttons to add a card or open a menu.
components.props: function ColumnHeader({ title, count, dotClassName, onAdd, onMenu, className }: ColumnHeaderProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: count
props.description: Card count, or e.g. "3 / 3" when the column has a WIP limit.

props.name: dotClassName
props.description: Dot colour — any Tailwind bg class, defaults to muted.

components.example:
<ColumnHeader title="In progress" count={4} dotClassName="bg-primary" onAdd={addCard} onMenu={openMenu} />

{/* With a work-in-progress limit */}
<ColumnHeader title="Review" count="3 / 3" dotClassName="bg-brand-quaternary" />

parts.name: ColumnHeader
parts.description: The header of a board column: a coloured dot, the title, a count and optional add and menu buttons.

items.text: Use Column Header above the cards of a Kanban column. For the title row of a page or section, use Page Header.
Pass `onAdd` and `onMenu` only when the column supports them. The `Add card` and `Column menu` buttons render only when the handlers exist.
Use `count` for the number of cards, or text like `3 / 3` when the column has a work-in-progress limit. Colour the dot with a background token class in `dotClassName`, for example `bg-success`.
Don't use a hex colour for the dot. `dotClassName` takes a class, and tokens keep the dot right in light and dark.

components.title: Event Chip
components.description: A small colored event label that fits in a calendar day cell.
components.example:
<EventChip color="indigo" onClick={() => open("standup")}>Standup</EventChip>
<EventChip color="purple">Design review</EventChip>

{/* As a popover trigger */}
<PopoverTrigger render={<EventChip color="green" />}>Lunch with Mira</PopoverTrigger>

parts.name: EventChip
parts.description: A one-line, colour-coded event label for a calendar cell. It is a `<button>` that forwards its props and truncates long titles.

items.text: Use Event Chip inside calendar day cells, where space is tight. For a time-based list of events, use Agenda Event.
Give the chip an `onClick`, or render it as the trigger of a popover or menu. It forwards button props, so you don't need a second interactive element around it.
Choose `color` by meaning, such as one colour per calendar, and keep it consistent across the month. There are eight colours.
Don't put more than a short title in `children`. The text sits on one line and is cut off with an ellipsis.

components.title: Agenda Event
components.description: One event in an agenda list, with its start and end time, a color bar, details and guests.
components.props: function AgendaEvent({ start, end, title, meta, color, guests, onMenu, onClick, className }: AgendaEventProps): React.JSX.Element;
components.example:
<AgendaEvent
  start="9:00"
  end="9:15"
  title="Daily standup"
  meta="Zoom"
  color="indigo"
  guests={team}
  onClick={() => openEvent("standup")}
  onMenu={openMenu}
/>

parts.name: AgendaEvent
parts.description: One row of a schedule with a line below it. With `onClick`, the title becomes a `<button>` stretched over the whole row.

parts.name: Time
parts.description: The `start` time above an optional `end` time, in a narrow fixed column.

parts.name: Colour bar
parts.description: A short bar in the event `color`, one of eight hues, `purple` by default.

parts.name: Title
parts.description: The `title` on one truncated line, with `meta` below it in smaller text, such as the room or the call link.

parts.name: Guests
parts.description: The `guests` as overlapping avatars: the first three, then a `+N` count for the rest.

parts.name: Menu button
parts.description: A small ghost icon button named `Event menu`, shown when `onMenu` is set. It sits above the stretched title, so its click does not open the event.

items.text: Use an Agenda Event for a schedule row with guests, a menu or a detail view to open. For a plain read-only list of times and titles, use Agenda.
Pass `onClick` instead of wrapping the row in a link or button. The title turns into a real button over the whole row, and the menu button stays reachable on its own.
Keep `title` short and put the place or the call details in `meta`. Both lines are cut to one line with an ellipsis.
Give every guest a `name`. It becomes the avatar's hover title and the source of the initials when there is no `src`.
Don't let the colour bar carry the meaning alone. The bar has no text, so name the kind of event in `title` or `meta` as well.

components.title: Conversation Item
components.description: One conversation in an inbox list, with sender, subject, preview, tags and an unread state.
components.props: function ConversationItem({ person, time, subject, preview, tags, unread, active, onClick, className }: ConversationItemProps): React.JSX.Element;
components.example:
<ConversationItem
  person={{ name: "Sarah Lindqvist", src: "/avatars/05.png" }}
  time="10:42"
  subject="Q3 roadmap review"
  preview="I left a few notes on the launch dates, can you take a look before Thursday?"
  tags={[{ label: "Urgent", color: "red" }]}
  unread
  active={selectedId === 1}
  onClick={() => select(1)}
/>

parts.name: ConversationItem
parts.description: One thread in an inbox list: sender avatar, name, time, subject, a one-line preview and optional tags.

items.text: Use Conversation Item for the thread list of an inbox or support view. For a multi-column list, use Table.
Set `unread` for new threads: the row gets a tint, a dot next to the time and a bold subject.
Set `active` on the thread that is open in the reading pane. It sets `aria-current` and a muted background.
Don't count on `active` to change the background of an unread thread. The muted background applies only to read threads, so mark a thread read once it opens.

components.title: Person Cell
components.description: An avatar with a name and role for tables and lists, with an optional capacity bar.
components.props: function PersonCell({ person, role, capacity, className }: PersonCellProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: capacity
props.description: Size=lg adds a capacity bar: value 0–100 and a label like "32h".

components.example:
<PersonCell person={{ name: "Sarah Lindqvist", src: "/avatars/05.png" }} role="sarah@wunderui.dev" />
<PersonCell person={{ name: "Jonas Berg", color: "purple" }} role="Product designer" capacity={{ value: 80, label: "32h" }} />

parts.name: PersonCell
parts.description: An avatar with a name, an optional role line and, with `capacity`, a workload bar and label.

items.text: Use Person Cell in tables, leaderboards and team lists where a row needs a person. For an account block in a sidebar or menu, use User Info.
Pass `capacity` as `{ value, label }` with a unit in the label, such as `32h`. The bar is clamped to 0 to 100.
Pass `src` in the person for a photo; otherwise initials are derived from the name and tinted with `color`.
Don't add a long `role`. The name and role truncate on one line each.

components.title: Task Row
components.description: A row in a Gantt task list: either a task with its color, assignee and dates, or a group header that folds open and closed.
components.props: function TaskRow({ name, group, open, onToggle, barClassName, assignee, dates, className }: TaskRowProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: group
props.description: Group header row (collapsible) instead of a task.

parts.name: TaskRow
parts.description: One line of a Gantt task list: a status bar, name, assignee and dates, or with `group` a collapsible group header.

items.text: Use Task Row in the left list of a timeline or Gantt view. For a step in an onboarding checklist, use Checklist Task.
Use `group` rows with `open` and `onToggle` for collapsible sections. They set `aria-expanded`.
Set `barClassName` to a background token class such as `bg-success` to show the status.
Don't pass `assignee` or `dates` to a group row. It shows only the title.

components.title: Record Card
components.description: A card that stands in for a table row on small screens: who it is, a status and a few key fields.
components.props: function RecordCard({ person, title, subtitle, badge, fields, onClick, className }: RecordCardProps): React.JSX.Element;
components.example:
<RecordCard
  person={{ name: "Sarah Lindqvist", src: "/avatars/05.png" }}
  title="Sarah Lindqvist"
  subtitle="sarah@wunderui.dev"
  badge={{ label: "Active", color: "green" }}
  fields={[
    { label: "Plan", value: "Pro" },
    { label: "Seats", value: "12" },
    { label: "MRR", value: "$468" },
  ]}
  onClick={() => openCustomer("sarah")}
/>

parts.name: RecordCard
parts.description: A card that stands in for a table row on small screens: person, title, subtitle, status badge and a grid of labelled fields.

items.text: Use Record Card as the mobile version of a Table or Data Table row. On wide screens keep the table.
Pass up to three `fields`. They fill a grid of three columns and the values truncate.
Pass `onClick` for the row action. The title becomes a button stretched over the card.
Don't pass long field values. Each sits in a third of the card width and is cut off on one line.

components.title: Stars
components.description: A small, read-only row of stars that shows a rating.

parts.name: Stars
parts.description: A read-only row of stars. It is an image with the label `n of N stars`.

items.text: Use Stars to show a rating. To let people give a rating, use Rating.
Show the number next to the stars (`4.6`) and the count of reviews where it matters.
Pass `max` for scales other than five.
Don't expect partial stars. `value` is rounded to whole stars, so `4.5` fills five.

components.title: Product Image
components.description: A product photo, or a colored placeholder with an icon when there is no photo yet.

parts.name: ProductImage
parts.description: A product picture that fills its box. With no `src` it falls back to a tinted tile with an icon.

items.text: Use Product Image for thumbnails and photos in commerce parts. For a person, use Avatar.
Set the size with `className` (`size-12 rounded-md`). The component has no size of its own.
Pass a descriptive `alt` when the image carries information. The default is an empty `alt`, which marks it as decorative.
Don't rely on the fallback as final content. The `icon` and `tint` only hold the place until an image exists.

components.title: Product Card
components.description: A shop tile with image, name, price and rating, plus optional wishlist and add-to-cart buttons.
components.props: function ProductCard({ name, price, compareAt, rating, reviews, availability, badge, image, tint, wishlisted, onWishlist, onAddToCart, addToCartLabel, onClick, className }: ProductCardProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: availability
props.description: Replaces the rating line, e.g. "In stock" (Type=wishlist).

components.example:
<ProductCard
  name="Standing desk Pro"
  price="$489"
  compareAt="$599"
  rating={4.8}
  reviews={312}
  badge={{ label: "Sale" }}
  tint="indigo"
  wishlisted={wishlisted}
  onWishlist={() => setWishlisted((w) => !w)}
  onAddToCart={() => cart.add("desk-pro")}
/>

<ProductCard name="Ergonomic chair" price="$329" availability="In stock" tint="green" onAddToCart={() => cart.add("chair")} />

parts.name: ProductCard
parts.description: A shop tile with image, badge, wishlist toggle, name, price, rating or availability and an add-to-cart button. Only the name and price are required.

parts.name: Product image
parts.description: The image area. It shows `image`, or a tinted tile when none is given.

items.text: Use Product Card in product grids, wishlists and recommendations. For a compact row with quick add, use Product Mini Card.
Pass `onClick` to make the image open the product and `onWishlist` with `wishlisted` for the heart toggle (`aria-pressed`).
Use `availability` (`In stock`) in wishlists. It replaces the rating line, so pass either one.
Don't pass a non-text `name` together with `onClick`. The image button takes its label from `name` only when it is a string, otherwise it reads `Open product`.

components.title: Line Item
components.description: One product line in a cart or order summary, with image, variant, quantity and price.
components.props: function LineItem({ name, variant, price, quantity, image, tint, size, trailing, className }: LineItemProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: size
props.description: compact = 40px image, no padding · regular = 48px, padded

components.example:
<LineItem name="Standing desk Pro" variant="Oak · 160 × 80 cm" price="$489.00" tint="indigo" />
<LineItem name="Monitor arm" variant="Black" quantity={2} price="$258.00" tint="blue" />

{/* Tighter, for an order summary */}
<LineItem size="compact" name="Cable tray" variant="White" price="$39.00" />

parts.name: LineItem
parts.description: One line of a cart, order or invoice: a thumbnail, name, optional variant, a `× n` quantity and the price.

parts.name: Product image
parts.description: The thumbnail. It shows `image`, or a tinted tile with an icon when there is none.

items.text: Use Line Item for the lines of a cart, checkout summary, order confirmation or invoice. For a product to browse, use Product Card.
Pass `price` already formatted with currency. The row doesn't format numbers.
Use `size="compact"` inside summary panels that bring their own padding; `regular` pads the row itself. Put a stepper or remove button in `trailing`.
Don't pass `quantity={1}` expecting `× 1`. The quantity is shown only above one.

components.title: Product Mini Card
components.description: A compact product row with a quick add button, for recommendations next to a cart.
components.example:
<ProductMiniCard name="Cable tray" price="$39" tint="yellow" onAdd={() => cart.add("cable-tray")} />
<ProductMiniCard name="Monitor arm" price="$129" tint="blue" onAdd={() => cart.add("monitor-arm")} />

parts.name: ProductMiniCard
parts.description: A compact bordered row with a thumbnail, name, price and an optional round add button.

parts.name: Product image
parts.description: The thumbnail. It shows `image`, or a tinted tile when none is given.

items.text: Use Product Mini Card for recommendations beside a cart or product page. For a full grid tile, use Product Card.
Pass `onAdd` for the quick add. It renders an icon button labelled `Add to cart`.
Pass `onClick` to open the product. It is attached to the name and price, not to the thumbnail.
Don't use it for items already in the cart. Use Line Item there.

components.title: Checkout Steps
components.description: The numbered steps of a checkout, where finished steps can be clicked to go back.
components.example:
const [step, setStep] = useState(1)

<CheckoutSteps steps={["Information", "Shipping", "Payment", "Review"]} current={step} onStepClick={setStep} />

parts.name: CheckoutSteps
parts.description: The numbered step trail of a checkout, for example Information, Shipping, Payment, Review. The current step carries `aria-current="step"`.

items.text: Use Checkout Steps to show where the buyer is in a fixed, linear flow such as checkout or order tracking. To switch between sibling views, use Tab Bar.
Pass `onStepClick` so finished steps can be revisited. Without it every step is disabled.
Keep step names to one word each (`steps` is a list of strings), so the trail stays short on small screens.
Don't expect to jump ahead. Upcoming steps are always disabled; the buyer reaches them through the form's own continue button.

components.title: Histogram Bar
components.description: One row of a rating breakdown: the star level, a filled bar and its share.
components.example:
<HistogramBar label={5} value={78} />
<HistogramBar label={4} value={14} />
<HistogramBar label={3} value={5} count="16" />

parts.name: HistogramBar
parts.description: One row of a rating distribution: a star label, a filled track and a count or percentage.

items.text: Use Histogram Bar for the star breakdown next to a rating summary. For a single progress value, use Progress.
Pass `value` as a percentage from 0 to 100. Values outside the range are clamped.
Stack one bar per rating, from 5 to 1, with `label` as the number. Pass `count` for the absolute number; without it the row shows the rounded percentage.
Don't pass a fraction such as `0.8`. It draws a bar of under one percent.

components.title: Review Card
components.description: A customer review with author, rating, text, photos, a reply from the store and a helpful button.
components.props: function ReviewCard({ author, verified, rating, date, title, children, photos, reply, helpfulCount, helpful, onHelpful, onReport, onMenu, flagged, className }: ReviewCardProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: flagged
props.description: Type=flagged — moderation note

props.name: reply
props.type: { from: React.ReactNode; date?: React.ReactNode; text: React.ReactNode; logo?: React.ReactNode }

components.example:
<ReviewCard
  author={{ name: "Mira K.", color: "green" }}
  verified
  rating={5}
  date="Sep 12, 2026"
  title="Rock solid at standing height"
  reply={{ from: "WunderUI Store", date: "Sep 13", text: "Thanks, Mira! Glad the desk fits your setup." }}
  helpfulCount={24}
  helpful={helpful}
  onHelpful={() => setHelpful((h) => !h)}
  onReport={report}
>
  No wobble at all, even fully raised. Setup took about 30 minutes and the motor is quiet.
</ReviewCard>

parts.name: ReviewCard
parts.description: A customer review with author, stars, date, optional title, text, photos, shop reply and helpful and report actions.

parts.name: Product image
parts.description: The thumbnails of the attached `photos`.

items.text: Use Review Card in review lists on product pages. For the star breakdown above the list, use Histogram Bar.
Set `verified` only for confirmed purchases; it adds a `Verified purchase` badge.
Pass `onHelpful` with `helpful` to toggle the button (`aria-pressed`) and `helpfulCount` for the count text.

Don't put block elements in `children`. The text is wrapped in a `

`, so pass plain text or inline markup.

components.title: Payment Methods
components.description: A row of small labels for the payment methods a shop accepts.

parts.name: PaymentMethods
parts.description: A wrapping row of small text chips for the accepted payment methods. The chips show names, not brand logos.

items.text: Use Payment Methods in a cart or checkout footer to show which methods are accepted. It is a display only.
Pass only the methods you accept in `methods`. The default list is `VISA`, `MC`, `AMEX`, `PayPal`, `Apple Pay` and `Klarna`.
Keep names short, as in the defaults; each chip is a small box with a minimum width.
Don't expect logos or an interactive choice. The chips are plain text and not selectable.

components.title: Text Field
components.description: A text input with a label, helper or error text, and optional icons or add-ons on either side.
components.props: function TextField({ label, labelTrailing, optional, helper, error, leading, trailing, size, id: idProp, className, wrapperClassName, ...props }: TextFieldProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: labelTrailing
props.description: "Optional" tag or a trailing link next to the label (e.g. "Forgot password?")

components.example:
<TextField
  label="Work email"
  type="email"
  placeholder="name@example.com"
  leading={<Mail className="size-4" />}
  value={email}
  onChange={(e) => setEmail(e.target.value)}
  helper="We'll send a sign-in link to this address."
  error={valid ? undefined : "Enter a full email address, like alina@wunderui.dev."}
/>
<TextField label="Company" optional placeholder="WunderUI" leading={<Building2 className="size-4" />} />

parts.name: TextField
parts.description: An Input with a label, optional tag, helper or error text and optional leading and trailing add-ons. It wires `id`, `aria-invalid` and `aria-describedby` for you.

items.text: Use Text Field for labelled fields in forms. For a bare input in a toolbar or table, use Input.
Pass `error` with a message that says what to do. It replaces `helper` and sets `aria-invalid`.
Use `optional` to mark optional fields and `labelTrailing` for a link such as `Forgot password?`.
Don't replace `label` with a placeholder. The label stays visible while typing.

components.title: Password Field
components.description: A password input with a button to show or hide what was typed.
components.props: function PasswordField({ trailing, ...props }: TextFieldProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: labelTrailing
props.description: "Optional" tag or a trailing link next to the label (e.g. "Forgot password?")

components.example: Forgot password?} />

parts.name: PasswordField
parts.description: A text field with a show-and-hide toggle for the password. The toggle button has `aria-pressed` and a label that follows its state.

parts.name: Text field
parts.description: The labelled field underneath. It supplies `label`, `helper`, `error` and the `size` options.

items.text: Use Password Field for every password input. For other text with a label and hint, use Text Field.
Set `autoComplete="new-password"` on sign-up and password-change forms. The default is `current-password`, which suits sign-in.
Pass `labelTrailing` with a `Forgot password?` link on sign-in, and show what is wrong in `error`.
Don't pass `type`. Props are applied after the field's own type, so it would override the show-and-hide toggle.

components.title: Textarea Field
components.description: A multi-line text input with a label and helper or error text.
components.props: function TextareaField({ label, helper, error, optional, id: idProp, wrapperClassName, ...props }: TextareaFieldProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: showCount
props.description: Show a "n/maxLength" character counter in the bottom-right corner. Requires maxLength.

parts.name: TextareaField
parts.description: A Textarea with its label, helper text and error wired together. It accepts every Textarea prop, such as `size`, `maxLength` and `showCount`.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The `label` text linked to the textarea with an auto-generated `id`. `optional` adds a muted `(optional)` after it.

parts.name: Helper and error
parts.description: One line under the box. An `error` replaces `helper`, turns the box invalid and is linked with `aria-describedby`.

items.text: Use TextareaField for a multi-line answer with a label in a form: a message, a bio. For a single line, use a Field with Input; for formatting, use RichTextEditor.
Set `showCount` together with `maxLength` to show `n/max`. The counter needs both.
Write `error` as an instruction, for example `Add at least 20 characters so we can help.`, and keep `helper` for the rule.
Don't pass both expecting two lines. `error` replaces `helper` while it is set.

components.title: Checkbox Field
components.description: A checkbox with a clickable label and an optional description below it.
components.props: function CheckboxField({ label, description, id: idProp, wrapperClassName, className, ...props }: CheckboxFieldProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: checked
props.description: Whether the checkbox is currently ticked. To render an uncontrolled checkbox, use the `defaultChecked` prop instead.

props.name: className
props.description: CSS class applied to the element, or a function that returns a class based on the component's state.

props.name: defaultChecked
props.description: Whether the checkbox is initially ticked. To render a controlled checkbox, use the `checked` prop instead.

props.name: disabled

parts.name: CheckboxField
parts.description: A Checkbox with its label and an optional description in one clickable row. Anything in the row toggles the box.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The text next to the box. Links inside it are styled as links, so consent text such as `I agree to the Terms` works.

parts.name: Description
parts.description: A second line in smaller text under the label. Use it for a consequence or a rule, not for the label itself.

items.text: Use CheckboxField for one yes/no in a form: consent, a newsletter, a remember-me. For a group of related boxes, use a Fieldset; for a setting that takes effect at once, use a Switch.
Write the label as the statement that is true when the box is checked: `Send me product updates`. Put the detail, such as how often, in `description`.
Pass `checked` with `onCheckedChange` or `defaultChecked`; all props of Checkbox work here as well.
Don't wrap it in another `<label>`. The row already is one and links the text to the box with an auto-generated `id`.

components.title: Form Actions
components.description: The row of buttons at the end of a form, aligned right, left or spread to both edges.
components.example:
<FormActions>
  <Button variant="plain" size="sm">Cancel</Button>
  <Button variant="primary" size="sm" type="submit">Save changes</Button>
</FormActions>

<FormActions align="between">
  <Button variant="ghost" size="sm">Delete workspace</Button>
  <Button variant="primary" size="sm">Save</Button>
</FormActions>

parts.name: FormActions
parts.description: The button row at the end of a form. It wraps on narrow screens and aligns its children to `start`, `end` (default) or `between`.

items.text: Use FormActions at the bottom of a Form or dialog body to hold its buttons. For a bar that sticks to a selection, use an action bar instead.
Put the cancel action first and the primary one last, so the primary button sits at the right edge with the default `align="end"`.
Name the buttons for their effect: `Save changes` and `Cancel`, not `Submit` and `OK`.
Use `align="between"` when one action sits on its own, such as `Delete project` on the left and `Save changes` on the right.
Don't show more than one primary button. A row has one filled button; the others are plain.

otherExports.summary: Shows, updates and closes toasts from anywhere below a Toaster.
otherExports.guide: Returns the toast manager of the nearest `Toaster`. Call `add` with a title, an optional description and a type, and the toast slides into the corner the Toaster was given. `add` returns the toast's id, which `update` and `close` take.

properties.name: update
properties.type: <T extends Data = Data>(toastId: string, options: ToastManagerUpdateOptions<T> | ((prevToast: ToastObject<T>) => ToastManagerUpdateOptions<T>)) => void

properties.name: promise
properties.type: <Value, T extends Data = Data>(promise: Promise<Value>, options: ToastManagerPromiseOptions<Value, T>) => Promise<Value>

notes: Mount `Toaster` once, high in the tree (the root layout). Without it, `add` has nowhere to render.
`type` sets the colour of the dot: `success`, `error`, `warning` or `info` (the default).
Toasts close after 5 seconds. Pass `timeout` to keep one longer, or `0` to keep it until it is closed.
Use a toast to confirm something that already happened. A decision the user still has to make belongs in a Dialog.

skills.name: wunderui-screen
skills.description: Builds a complete React screen with WunderUI from a one-sentence request, within the user's plan (Free uses only the free components) — picks the components and a matching block layout, fills props from design.json, adds the empty, loading and error states that generated screens usually forget, uses motion tokens instead of raw milliseconds, and finishes with a typecheck and a build. Use when the user asks for a page, screen, view, dashboard, settings page, table view, form or similar in a project that uses WunderUI (@wunderui/react).

skills.name: wunderui-setup
skills.description: Sets up WunderUI in a React project from scratch to the first rendered screen — detects the framework, Tailwind version and existing tokens, puts DESIGN.md and design.json into the project, registers the WunderUI MCP server, wires styles.css and the @source path, renders a probe component and writes a setup report. Use when the user wants to install, add, set up or connect WunderUI (or "@wunderui/react") in a project, or asks why WunderUI components render unstyled.

skills.name: wunderui-theme
skills.description: Generates a complete WunderUI brand theme from one brand colour (hex) — optionally an accent colour, a radius preference and a font — the eleven-step brand scale (--brand-50 … --brand-1000), the brand tokens derived from it (primary, primary-foreground, text-link, ring, tint and tint text, chart 1) for light and dark, a WCAG AA check of every key pair with shades moved automatically until they pass, and one CSS file to import after @wunderui/react/styles.css (globally or for one subtree), plus a report. Use when the user wants to rebrand, theme or white-label WunderUI, use their own brand / primary / accent colour, change the radius or font of the library, asks for a "design system from my colour", or wants to check an existing WunderUI theme file for contrast.

skills.name: wunderui-token-check
skills.description: Finds hard-coded colours, spacing and radii that bypass the WunderUI design tokens, maps each literal to the nearest token with a measured distance (ΔE for colour, px for spacing and radius), separates safe swaps from values too far from any token, replaces the safe ones and reports how much the look changed. Use when the user asks to check or clean up tokens, remove hardcoded colours/hex values, make a codebase use the design system, or before a theming or dark-mode change in a WunderUI project.

skills.name: wunderui-a11y
skills.description: Accessibility check per component or screen in a WunderUI project — renders every variant, walks the focus order and checks that focus is visible, measures WCAG AA contrast of every text in light and dark, verifies the reduced-motion fallback, and delivers each finding with a patch instead of just a report. Use when the user asks for an accessibility or a11y check, WCAG contrast, keyboard or focus review, or a reduced-motion check of a component, page or pull request.

skills.name: wunderui-agent-ui
skills.description: Builds the interface of an AI agent with WunderUI's agent components — describes the run (steps, tools, costs, approvals), picks RunTimeline, ApprovalCard, CostMeter, AgentStatus, RunError and their relatives, plays through every state including failure and abort, applies the agent motion tokens and checks the approval moment separately. Use when the user asks for an agent run view, an agent dashboard, a tool-call transcript, a human-in-the-loop approval, a cost or usage view, or any UI that shows what an AI agent is doing, in a project that uses @wunderui/react.

skills.name: wunderui-compose
skills.description: Composes WunderUI blocks into a complete page — clarifies the page's goal and audience, proposes a block order that follows the visitor's questions, inserts the blocks and fills them with real content, checks the rhythm (one notable effect per section) and protects the LCP element from entrance animation. Use when the user asks for a landing page, marketing page, pricing page, product page, about page or any multi-section page assembled from WunderUI blocks or sections.

skills.name: wunderui-figma-screen
skills.description: Builds a screen in Figma from the WunderUI library — real component instances instead of drawn rectangles, every fill and text bound to the theme variables and text styles, auto layout throughout, a light frame first, then the dark frame as a clone with the Dark mode and a 390 px mobile frame — and checks the result with screenshots and an audit (unbound paints, unstyled text, absolute children). Use when the user asks to design, mock up or build a screen, page or dashboard in Figma with WunderUI, or to turn a React screen or a description into a Figma frame.

skills.name: wunderui-figma-sync
skills.description: Keeps Figma variables and the project's CSS tokens (styles.css) identical in both directions — reads the Figma variable collections and text styles through the Figma MCP server, diffs them against the CSS custom properties (colour per light/dark mode, spacing, radius, type, motion), lists every conflict with the measured difference, asks which side wins and writes only in that direction, then reports what changed. Use when the user asks to sync Figma and code, compare design tokens with Figma, update styles.css from Figma, push token changes into Figma, or check for design↔code drift in a WunderUI project.

skills.name: wunderui-motion-audit
skills.description: Audits a codebase's animations and transitions against the WunderUI motion rules — transition-all, raw millisecond durations, ease-in-out and other generic curves, scroll-driven animations without an @supports fallback, missing prefers-reduced-motion handling, layout-property animation and fades on the LCP element — justifies every finding with the rule from DESIGN.md, proposes and applies a patch with motion tokens and verifies the build. Use when the user asks for a motion or animation audit, wants transitions to feel less generic, asks about reduced motion, or before shipping UI built with WunderUI.

skills.name: wunderui-refactor
skills.description: Migrates an existing React app to WunderUI — scans the project and detects the UI stack per file (shadcn/ui, Radix primitives, MUI, Chakra, Headless UI, Mantine, hand-built components and hard-coded Tailwind colours), maps every component to its WunderUI equivalent with prop notes, writes a migration plan with effort and order, applies the safe codemods (shadcn imports → @wunderui/react, raw colours → token utilities) and measures before → after (raw colours, foreign UI imports, WunderUI coverage) with the project's typecheck. Use when the user wants to switch to WunderUI, migrate or refactor an app from shadcn, MUI, Chakra, Mantine or Headless UI, replace a component library, estimate how much work a switch is, or asks "how do I move this project to WunderUI".

skills.name: wunderui-uiux-design-auditor
skills.description: Evidence-based UI/UX and accessibility audit of any product — live websites, landing pages, component libraries / front-end code (React, Vue, Svelte, HTML/CSS, Tailwind) and Figma files — against a 520-rule catalog (WCAG 2.2 A/AA, platform guidance, design-system rules, responsive behaviour from 320 to 1440 px). Produces findings with evidence, severity and acceptance criteria, a coverage matrix, a change plan and a client-ready HTML report. Read-only. Use when the user asks for a UI/UX audit, accessibility or WCAG check, responsive or mobile check, design review, landing-page review, design-system or Figma audit, design↔code (token) comparison, or a re-check after fixes.
